With the N64 a similar domestic trace is missing, because by the mid-1990s the age of cloning cheap hardware was already on the decline. ### Today's scene The N64 is the trickiest of the popular consoles for retro gamers. Emulation is notoriously inaccurate — because of the unusual RCP architecture, every game behaves a little differently and no universal solution exists. On the PC, **Mupen64Plus**, **Project64** or the more accurate but demanding **Ares** serve well. On powerful machines, the popularity of "native" ports such as **Ship of Harkinian** (Ocarina of Time), built on decompilation of the original code, is growing. On handhelds with the H700 chip (better on the RG40XX/RG46R than on the weaker RG35XX Pro) a number of titles run, but expect to test them one by one and to accept that not everything will run perfectly. The reward, though, is 3D classics like Super Mario 64, **Ocarina of Time**, Banjo-Kazooie or Mario Kart 64 — experiences you won't find anywhere else and which regularly top the lists of the best games of all time.

arcade.history: Arcade machines are not a single platform — they are a whole universe. Before home consoles arrived, people played on coin-operated machines, and that is precisely where the entire gaming industry was born in the 1970s. **Pong** (1972), **Space Invaders** (1978), **Pac-Man** (1980) and **Donkey Kong** (1981) did not originate on living-room screens but in wooden cabinets under neon lights. For most of the 1980s and 1990s, arcade machines were technically always a step ahead of what you could have at home — and that was exactly their selling point. The key to understanding the arcade world is the business model: the machine was meant to take coins. That dictated the design of the games. Difficulty was often deliberately merciless so that the game would "kill" you and force you to drop in another coin. It was not a bug or developer incompetence — it was a way to make money. With home emulation today you have unlimited credits, so you can enjoy the same games without draining your wallet and get to know them from a side they never wanted to show you. ### Technology: graphics and sound You can't speak of a single "arcade hardware" — every generation of cabinets had its own board. They had one thing in common: they were built without the compromises that shackled home machines. While a console had to be cheap enough for every household, an arcade machine could afford more memory, faster processors and specialized graphics chips. The golden era for fans is the 2D period from the late 1980s to the late 1990s. Boards like the **Capcom CPS-1** and later the **CPS-2** powered fighting games and beat 'em ups with large, smoothly animated sprites and rich colors. The **SNK Neo Geo** (the MVS board) excelled with enormous sprites and a palette that was long unavailable at home — which is why games like Metal Slug or King of Fighters looked so rich. The shmup genre (vertical shooters) was brought to perfection by the Japanese studio **Cave**: bullet-hell titles like DoDonPachi or Mushihimesama filled the screen with hundreds of bullets without a stutter. Sound was similarly diverse. Early arcade machines combined simple chips and discrete circuits; in the 1980s Yamaha's FM synthesis chips reigned (the **YM** series, e.g. the YM2151 and YM2203), which gave arcades their characteristic metallically ringing sound. With the CPS-2 and Neo Geo came sampled instruments and higher-quality digitized sound. ### Connectivity and peripherals The controls of an arcade machine were part of an experience that could not be replicated at home. Alongside the classic joystick and buttons there were **pedals and steering wheels** on racing games, **light guns** on shooting machines like Operation Wolf, **trackballs** (Centipede, Missile Command) and **rotary** controls (paddles). Some cabinets were experiences in themselves — the seats tilted, the cabin shook. An important format was **cabinet versus cocktail**: the upright standing cabinet against the table-top version, where players sat opposite one another and the picture rotated between turns. Networked linking of several cabinets existed in racing games, where multiple players raced against each other on machines standing side by side. ### Models and variants Instead of "revisions of a single console", the arcade has whole families of system boards. Worth mentioning in particular: - **Capcom CPS-1 / CPS-2 / CPS-3** — successive generations with interchangeable game cartridges, the heart of 1990s Capcom (Street Fighter, Final Fight). - **SNK Neo Geo MVS** — a machine with several slots into which the operator inserted up to six different games at once; technically identical to the home variant. - **Sega System 16** and the later 3D boards **Model 1/2/3** — Sega pushed polygon graphics (Virtua Fighter, Daytona USA). - **Taito**, **Konami** and **Namco** also had their own board lines with their own sound and graphics chips. This very fragmentation is why emulating arcades is more demanding than emulating a single closed console. ### Clones and variants The arcade world was always full of **bootlegs** — unofficial copies of popular boards, often made in Asia or Italy, that circumvented licenses. Many classics thus circulated in dozens of regional versions and pirate variants; MAME today carefully catalogs them alongside the originals. The domestic trace here is indirect: SNK also sold the Neo Geo as an (extremely expensive) home console, the **Neo Geo AES**, so the richest players had an arcade machine literally in their living room. In the Czechoslovak and Eastern European context, arcades in the form of Western cabinets spread only after 1989; until then it was more a matter of isolated machines and, later, local copies of popular titles. ### Today's scene Arcade emulation stands on two pillars. **MAME** (Multiple Arcade Machine Emulator) is a huge project striving for faithful preservation of thousands of boards — it prefers accuracy over performance. **FinalBurn Neo (FBNeo)** focuses on the most popular hardware (CPS, Neo Geo, Sega) and runs briskly even on weaker hardware. One thing is crucial for a newcomer: arcade ROM files must **exactly match the version of the emulator**. The romset is tied to a specific version of MAME or FBNeo, and when it doesn't match, the game simply won't boot — which is the most common source of frustration for beginners. On handheld consoles with the H700 chip, the vast majority of 2D classics run superbly; only the most modern 3D arcade machines cause problems, and they don't belong in the retro aesthetic anyway. The arcade is thus an inexhaustible well for short, intense sessions — you toss in an imaginary coin and off you go.

neogeo.history: When SNK unveiled the Neo Geo in 1990, it was not an ordinary home console but a small miracle: literally an **arcade machine brought into the living room**. The system had two faces — the **MVS** (Multi Video System) arcade board intended for amusement arcades, and the **AES** (Advanced Entertainment System) home console. Both variants shared absolutely identical hardware, so a game that ran in the arcade looked exactly the same at home. At a time when home ports of arcade titles were usually cut-down compromises, this was an absolute sensation. But the Neo Geo came at a royal price as well: both the home system and the individual cartridges cost so much that it was a luxury item for enthusiasts with deep pockets. Even so, the Neo Geo built up a legendary status and stayed commercially alive for an incredibly long time — software for it was released officially until 2004. The strength of the Neo Geo did not lie in a technical revolution of the processor itself, but in the brutally oversized capabilities for 2D graphics and in the fact that SNK managed to keep the platform alive longer than any competitor. It became the home of iconic series that defined the genres of fighting games and run-and-gun action. ### Technology: graphics and sound The heart of the system is the **16-bit Motorola 68000 processor** clocked at roughly 12 MHz, complemented by a **Zilog Z80** as a sound coprocessor. For its time, the Neo Geo stood out with its extreme emphasis on sprites. The hardware could display a huge number of large, detailed animated characters at once, which made fighting and action games feel far smoother and "beefier" than on ordinary home consoles. The screen resolution was **320×224 pixels**. The color palette was key: the system had a **palette of 65,536 colors**, of which it could display roughly **4,096 colors on screen at once**. This gave the graphics a characteristically rich, cartoon-like look. Sprites could also be scaled and deformed, which authors used for zoom-in and "zooming" effects in fighting games such as **Art of Fighting** or **Fatal Fury**. Sound was handled by the renowned **Yamaha YM2610** chip. It combined FM synthesis with the playback of sampled (ADPCM) sounds and had several channels at its disposal — the result was unforgettable soundtracks and loud, dramatic digitized voices. It was precisely the audio side that significantly contributed to the arcade atmosphere of games like **Metal Slug** or **The King of Fighters '98**. ### Connectivity and peripherals The home AES used massive cartridges — the largest and most expensive game modules of their era, capable of holding enormous amounts of data, which enabled that rich graphics and sound. The console had two controller ports and shipped with the legendary large **joystick with microswitches**, which replicated the feel of the arcade machine. An important peripheral was the **Memory Card**. It was one of the first systems to introduce this concept: a player could save their progress onto a card, take it with them to the arcade, insert it into an MVS machine running the same game, and continue where they had left off at home. This link between home and arcade was exceptional for its time. SNK later also released a CD variant with its own optical drive (see below). ### Models and revisions The basic division is formed by the already-mentioned **MVS** (arcade machines, often with multiple cartridge slots — versions for 1, 2, 4 and 6 games) and the home **AES**. The AES was sold in various regional variants. Alongside the costly cartridge-based AES, in 1994 SNK introduced the cheaper **Neo Geo CD**, which stored games on ordinary CDs. This dramatically lowered the price of the media, but at the cost of slow loading and limited memory, so some games had to be modified. There were also revisions of the CD unit, including the faster **Neo Geo CDZ** aimed primarily at the Japanese market. Much later, in 1998, came the handheld console **Neo Geo Pocket** and shortly afterwards the color **Neo Geo Pocket Color** — but that was already a standalone handheld, not a miniature of the big system. ### Clones and variants Given the high price and the closed nature of the hardware, "classic" cheap Neo Geo clones did not spread as they did with 8-bit machines. The scene, however, long dealt with **pirate and unofficial cartridges** (especially converters between the MVS and AES formats and copies of games), which were very widespread in the community. In modern times, SNK itself released an official miniature retro variant — the **Neo Geo Mini** (2018), a compact device in the form of a miniature arcade cabinet with a built-in collection of games and a small screen, plus official controllers styled to resemble the original arcade stick. ### Today's scene The Neo Geo is among the best-documented and best-emulated platforms of all. Both MVS and AES games are faithfully run by, for example, **MAME** and specialized emulators such as **FinalBurn Neo**, so the entire library is available even on weaker devices and handhelds. Moreover, SNK actively re-sells its classics — the **ACA Neo Geo** collections are released on modern consoles and PC and make individual titles accessible in an authentic form, complete with online leaderboards. The **homebrew** community also remains alive, creating entirely new games and demos for the Neo Geo, often distributed even on real cartridges. Together with emulation and official re-releases, the platform whose software was created over more than fourteen years thus remains alive even more than three decades after its launch.

cps.history:
When the first arcade machine built on the **CP System** board (abbreviated **CPS**, often nicknamed "CPS-1") appeared in arcades in 1988, it marked for Capcom the beginning of an era that moved the company into the absolute top tier of the arcade industry for the next decade. CPS was not a console or a computer in the home sense of the word, but a family of **arcade boards** (PCBs) on which arcade cabinets for game halls ran. And it was right here that the games that defined entire genres were born — from fighting games to beat 'em ups. Without CPS there would be no phenomenon of **Street Fighter II**, which in 1991 literally flooded the arcades of the whole world and kicked off the golden era of Japanese fighting games.

Capcom gradually released three generations: **CP System (CPS-1, 1988)**, **CP System II (CPS-2, 1993)** and the technically distinct **CP System III (CPS-3, 1996)**. Each raised the bar for graphics and anti-piracy protection, and together they form one of the most influential pieces of gaming hardware of all.

### Technology: graphics and sound

The heart of both CPS-1 and CPS-2 was the 16-bit **Motorola 68000** processor. CPS-1 clocked it at around 10 MHz, CPS-2 at 16 MHz, which brought snappier logic and a greater volume of data on screen. The picture had the typical arcade resolution of **384×224 pixels**. The key to the fabled "Capcom" look was the work with **sprites** — the boards could handle large, multi-part characters composed of many tiles, smooth animation, and multi-layered backgrounds with independent **scrolling**. While CPS-1 offered a palette in the order of thousands of colors, **CPS-2 significantly expanded it** (on the order of thousands of colors on screen at once) and enabled richer shading and transparencies, thanks to which games like *Street Fighter Alpha 3* or *X-Men: Children of the Atom* looked noticeably richer than the older generation.

Sound was handled by a separate **Zilog Z80** as the sound processor, in combination with **Yamaha YM2151** FM synthesis and the **OKI MSM6295** PCM chip for samples. This combination gave the characteristic mix of melodic FM lines and sampled effects and voice clips. **CPS-3** went a completely different way: it was built on the **Hitachi SH-2** processor, used data on **CD-ROM** that was loaded into memory after startup, and excelled with huge, smoothly animated sprites of hand-drawn quality — the pinnacle being *Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike* with its breathtaking animation.

### Connectivity and peripherals

As arcade hardware, the CPS boards plugged into cabinets of the **JAMMA** standard (with CPS-2 it was a two-part cartridge: an "A-board" with the base and an interchangeable "B-board" with the game). Controls consisted of a **joystick and buttons** — typically six buttons on fighting games, fewer on action games. Most titles supported **two players** at once; beat 'em ups like *Cadillacs and Dinosaurs*, *The Punisher* or *Alien vs. Predator* could even do **three-player cooperation** on specially equipped boards. The picture went over an analog **RGB** signal to the cabinet monitor. No memory cards or modems were used here — progress and high scores lived within the machine as long as it was powered.

### Models and revisions

Development took place across three main generations. **CPS-1** went through several board revisions and even got a split version, **CPS-1.5 (CPS Dash)**, on which, for example, *Cadillacs and Dinosaurs* or *The Punisher* ran and which lay on the boundary between the first and second generation. **CPS-2** brought a fundamental novelty — strong **encryption** of the program code stored in the cartridge, backed up by a battery. This was meant to stop piracy, but it had an insidious side effect: after the battery ran out, the board "died" (the so-called **suicide battery**), because it lost the decryption keys. **CPS-3** used encrypted content from a CD loaded into battery-backed memory with the same risk; only a few games were released on it, including *Warzard/Red Earth* and the *Street Fighter III* series.

### Clones and variants

Capcom did not license the original CPS hardware for the manufacture of clones, so no official imitations in the spirit of the "Pegasus" or the *Didaktik* exist here. What did accompany both CPS-1 and CPS-2 practically from the start, however, were **pirate copies and bootlegs** — illegally copied fighting-game boards (especially *Street Fighter II* and its countless "turbo" and "hyper" hacks), which flooded the gray market even in Europe and in the countries of the former Eastern Bloc, where they made their way into arcades and pubs outside official distribution. The value of these boards, conversely, is today being raised by the collector scene, which carefully distinguishes originals from bootlegs.

### Today's scene

CPS today belongs among the best-covered arcade platforms. The **MAME** emulator (and its offshoot **FinalBurn Neo**) reliably runs the vast majority of CPS-1, CPS-2 and CPS-3 games, and the community long ago **cracked the encryption of both CPS-2 and CPS-3**, so "dead" boards can be revived (the so-called *phoenix* editions of ROMs with burned-in keys). Many titles were also released legally in modern compilations — for example the *Capcom Arcade Stadium* range or the *Street Fighter 30th Anniversary Collection*. For fans of real iron there exist **consolization kits** and speaker cabinets, thanks to which an original board can be connected to a modern display. CPS thus remains alive not only in the arcades of memory, but also on the screens of today's players.

pc-engine.history: When NEC, in cooperation with the developer studio Hudson Soft, launched the **PC Engine** in Japan in 1987, few suspected that one of the most fascinating "what if" chapters of gaming history was being born. A tiny white box about the size of a couple of cigarette packs dazzled with performance that put the reigning market leaders to shame. In Japan the PC Engine became a huge hit and for a while even outsold the Nintendo Famicom. In the West the console arrived only in 1989 under the name **TurboGrafx-16** — and due to unfortunate marketing and poor timing against the rising Sega Genesis, it remained more of a strange curiosity. The paradox starts with the name itself. Despite the "16" label, the PC Engine was powered by an **8-bit core** (a custom HuC6280 processor derived from the famous 6502 family). The secret of its success, however, was an exceptionally capable graphics chip, thanks to which the machine rivaled truly 16-bit consoles in performance. The PC Engine thus filled a peculiar mid-generation gap between the NES and the arrival of the SNES or Mega Drive. And above all: it was **the very first system with a CD add-on** (the CD-ROM² from 1988), beating the competition by years. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the graphics is a pair of chips, the HuC6270 (VDC) and the HuC6260 (VCE). The console can display up to **482 colors at once** from a palette of **512 colors** and operates with a generous count of **64 sprites** on screen, with individual sprites able to be up to 32×64 pixels large. The standard resolution hovered around 256×239, but the hardware also supported wider modes. It was precisely this combination of many large, colorful sprites and smooth scrolling that made the PC Engine **a paradise platform for both vertical and horizontal shoot-'em-ups (shmups)** — a library of titles such as Soldier Blade, Super Star Soldier or Blazing Lazers ranks among the best on any console. The sound is handled by a programmable generator right inside the processor: **six wavetable channels**, two of which can also work as a noise generator for percussion. Wavetable synthesis gave the music a characteristically clean, melodic sound. With the arrival of the CD-ROM add-on came an additional **redbook CD audio track** — games suddenly offered full recorded soundtracks, voice acting and animations, while the competition was still beeping out chip music from cartridges. ### Connectivity and peripherals Games were originally loaded from a **HuCard** (in the West the TurboChip) — flat cards roughly the size of a credit card, inspired by the then-current Hudson Bee Card memory. An absolutely key add-on was the already mentioned **CD-ROM² (1988)**, later improved with the **Super CD-ROM²** with more buffer memory; there was also a compact all-in-one model, the **PC Engine Duo**, which integrated the drive right into the body. For multiplayer there was the **TurboTap (Multitap)** adapter, which allowed connecting up to five controllers — the console itself had only a single port. Among the peripherals was also the Turbo Pad controller with an autofire switch, a light gun, and in Japan even a portable version. RF/composite AV output was the standard. ### Models and revisions A whole range of variants emerged. After the basic **PC Engine** came the smaller **PC Engine Shuttle**, the luxurious **PC Engine CoreGrafx** and the **CoreGrafx II** with improved AV output, or the portable **PC Engine GT** (in the West the TurboExpress) with a color LCD that played ordinary HuCards. The pinnacle was the integrated **PC Engine Duo** (and its successors the Duo-R and Duo-RX) combining the console and CD drive in a single piece. NEC also produced the **PC Engine LT** in the form of a small laptop with a built-in monitor. In the West the ecosystem shrank mainly to the **TurboGrafx-16** and the **TurboGrafx-CD** add-on, or the combined **TurboDuo**. ### Clones and variants Official clones of the PC Engine practically did not exist — it was a closed NEC platform. In the West the console was briefly licensed by **Telegames**. In North America, by contrast, toward the end of its commercial life the successor **PC-FX** (1994) was released, though it never repeated the success. For the Czech and Czechoslovak retro gamer it is honest to admit that **we practically don't know the PC Engine here in the 1980s and 1990s** — unlike the ZX Spectrum (and its domestic clone the Didaktik) or the NES (spread via famiclones and the Polish Pegasus), neither the PC Engine nor the TurboGrafx officially reached us. It was a purely import rarity known only to a narrow circle of enthusiasts. All the more it is a discoverer's delicacy today. ### Today's scene Right now the PC Engine is experiencing a renaissance. Emulation is mature: HuCard games run flawlessly, CD titles need only the appropriate **BIOS file** (System Card) and a bit more storage. Long-unavailable gems such as **Castlevania: Rondo of Blood** or **Ys Book I & II** have, thanks to emulation and official reissues, finally reached Western audiences. The homebrew scene is also active and collectors hunt for original HuCards. If you want to step out of the Nintendo and Sega mainstream, the PC Engine is one of the best tips — especially for lovers of shoot-'em-ups.

dreamcast.history: When Sega introduced the Dreamcast in Japan in 1998 (and a year later in Europe and North America), few suspected they were witnessing the swan song of one of the biggest names in the gaming industry. After the painful failure of the Saturn, Sega bet everything on a single card: on a technically advanced but above all **easy-to-program** machine that was supposed to beat the competition on quality, not marketing muscle. And in many respects the Dreamcast really was a generation ahead — it arrived as the very first home console with a **built-in modem** for playing over the internet. The start was great. In its first year the console sold excellently and the library filled up quickly. But then came the announcement of the PlayStation 2, which lured buyers with DVD playback and leaned on the enormous momentum of its brand. Publishers began shifting support to Sony even before the PS2 had even launched, and the financially exhausted Sega no longer had the strength to fight. In 2001 production ended and Sega withdrew from hardware for good. It was precisely this premature death that turned the Dreamcast into a cult machine with a concentrated, exceptionally high-quality library — from uncompromising arcade ports through crazy originals like **Jet Set Radio**, **Space Channel 5** or **Rez** to fantastic 2D fighters and shmups. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the Dreamcast was a 128-bit **Hitachi SH-4** processor clocked at 200 MHz with a built-in unit for floating-point work. Graphics were handled by the **PowerVR2** chip (PowerVR Series2, CLX2) from NEC/VideoLogic, which used the technique of **tile-based deferred rendering** — efficiently discarding overdrawn surfaces and thus saving computing power. The console had 16 MB of main memory and 8 MB of video memory and typically managed a resolution of 640×480 with a full palette of colors. Sound was handled by the **Yamaha AICA** processor with an ARM7 core, capable of 64 voices and PCM as well as ADPCM playback — a very solid foundation for its time for quality music and spatial effects. The result was a console that could faithfully carry over arcade games: **Soulcalibur** even looked better at home than in the arcade, and titles like **Marvel vs. Capcom 2** or **Power Stone** ran briskly and without compromise. ### Connectivity and peripherals The most famous Dreamcast peripheral was without doubt the **VMU (Visual Memory Unit)** — a memory card with its own small monochrome display and buttons, which slid right into the controller. It served not only to save positions but could also display supplementary information during a game, or even run tiny minigames as a standalone pocket toy. The aforementioned **built-in modem** (56k, in some regions later replaced by a broadband adapter) enabled online play in titles like **Phantasy Star Online** and thus was years ahead of its time. A **vibration module (Jump Pack/Puru Puru Pack)** could also be connected to the controller, and there were special arcade sticks, a fishing controller, a keyboard, a mouse, a microphone for Seaman and a light gun available. The console offered both composite/RGB SCART and VGA output for a sharp image on a monitor. ### Models and revisions The Dreamcast hardware remained fairly uniform throughout, differing mainly regionally and cosmetically. The Japanese, North American, European and Australian versions differed by regional lock and the color of the logo (an orange spiral in Europe and Japan, blue in North America due to a trademark). Besides the basic white variant, a number of **limited color editions** were released — well known are, for example, the black Sega Sports edition or various Japanese specials. A key internal difference was the GD-ROM drive and later motherboard revisions, which affected the susceptibility to running homemade copies. The **GD-ROM (Gigabyte Disc)** medium was a format developed by Sega with a capacity of around 1 GB, intended to make piracy harder — paradoxically, however, it turned out that the console could boot even from ordinary burned CD-Rs, which in later years gave it unprecedented longevity among enthusiasts. ### Clones and variants The Sega Dreamcast had no classic "clones" in the sense of, say, the ZX Spectrum or the NES, because it was a technically demanding machine of a closed generation. A related platform was the arcade board **Sega NAOMI**, which shared its architecture with the Dreamcast (the same SH-4 and PowerVR2) — thanks to which the arcade ports were exceptionally faithful and conversions in both directions were easy. In the Czech and Czechoslovak environment the Dreamcast arrived only after the revolution as standard imported hardware; the era of domestic clones that we experienced with 8-bit machines like the **Didaktik** (a ZX Spectrum clone) or with famiclones and the **Pegasus** in the case of the NES no longer applied to consoles of this generation. ### Today's scene The Dreamcast still has a remarkably lively community. For retro gamers there is great news: the most widespread emulator **Flycast** (also available as a core in RetroArch) handles the vast majority of the library very well — especially 2D titles, fighters and shmups run great even on weaker portable hardware, only the most demanding 3D games like **Shenmue** can cause trouble. On more powerful handhelds (for example an Anbernic with the H700 chip, where the RG46R is noticeably snappier than the RG35XX Pro) the Dreamcast is the most powerful console you can reasonably play. And what's rare — **new games are still being released** for the Dreamcast on real discs. The active homebrew and indie scene benefits from the fact that the console boots easily from burned media, so for fans of 2D genres and arcade action it remains a small, still-open sanctuary.

zx81.history: When Clive Sinclair unveiled the ZX81 in March 1981, it was one of the boldest attempts yet to put a computer into every home. It cost just 69.95 pounds as a ready-built unit, and even as little as 49.95 pounds as a kit that the owner soldered together at home. A flat black plastic box the size of a book, with a membrane keyboard without moving keys, it became a phenomenon: in under two years it sold more than 1.5 million units, and for an entire generation, especially in Britain, it was the very first computer they ever touched. It built on the older ZX80, but thanks to clever simplification of the circuitry it was both cheaper and more capable. The key to that incredible price was the brutal frugality of its construction. Sinclair had most of the logic that elsewhere required dozens of chips integrated into a single custom ULA (Uncommitted Logic Array) circuit, manufactured by Ferranti. At the heart of the computer was an eight-bit Zilog Z80A processor clocked at 3.25 MHz, and the machine shipped with a laughable **1 kB of RAM** (expandable via an add-on module to 16 kB and more). The ROM hid a BASIC interpreter that let you enter keywords with a single keypress. ### Technology: graphics and sound The ZX81 was spartanly stingy with graphics and sound, because every transistor saved meant a lower price. The picture was exclusively **black and white** and worked in a text mode of **32 columns and 24 rows**. There were no true pixel bitmaps: the "graphics" consisted of block characters in the character ROM set, so the effective resolution was only **64 x 48 coarse blocks**. The machine knew neither sprites nor hardware scrolling; the CPU itself had to handle everything. Its most notorious feature was its two display modes. In the basic **SLOW** mode the processor computed and generated the picture at the same time, so during calculations the screen flickered and the program run slowed down. The faster **FAST** mode turned the picture off completely during calculation and lit it up only with the result. This curiosity stemmed from the fact that generating the video signal was largely handled by the Z80 itself in cooperation with the ULA. **The ZX81 had no sound at all** — the computer had neither a sound chip nor a speaker, so games were silent, or their creators helped themselves along with the interference it radiated into a nearby radio. ### Connectivity and peripherals Input and output were likewise minimalist. The picture was sent via an **antenna (RF) output to an ordinary television**, programs were saved and loaded via an **ordinary cassette recorder** at around 250 baud, which meant long and fault-prone loading. On the rear edge was an edge **bus connector** into which modules were plugged. The most important accessory was the **16 kB RAM pack**, without which most more serious software was unthinkable. It had an unfortunate reputation, however: a mere bump against the desk was enough to shift the module in its connector, which crashed the machine and wiped out your work in progress (this was nicknamed the "RAM pack wobble"). Sinclair later also offered the **ZX Printer** thermal printer, which printed on narrow aluminium-coated paper. Classic joysticks could only be connected via add-on interfaces from other manufacturers. ### Models and variants In terms of hardware the ZX81 went through several minor board and ULA revisions during production, but outwardly it stayed the same. For the American market, the Timex company, which assembled Sinclair's machines, released it as the **Timex Sinclair 1000** — essentially an identical computer, but with 2 kB of RAM on board, adapted for the local television standard. The follow-up **Timex Sinclair 1500** got a better rubber keyboard and 16 kB of RAM in a more elegant case reminiscent of the later ZX Spectrum. ### Clones and variants The ZX81 spawned a number of official and unofficial variants around the world. In Brazil, licensed and unlicensed machines such as the **Microdigital TK82** and **TK85** were created, supplying the local market, which was protected against imports, with compatible computers. Clones existed in other countries too, often built around the same combination of the Z80 and ULA logic. For the Czech and Czechoslovak reader it is interesting that, unlike the famous ZX Spectrum, whose domestic clone was the **Didaktik**, the ZX81 does not have such a strong home footprint — in Czechoslovakia it was reached mostly by enthusiasts through imports or by building it from schematics. The main wave of domestic computer creation here came only with sixteen-bit colour machines a few years later. ### Today's scene Despite its modesty, the ZX81 has kept a loyal community. There are a number of emulators — to name a few, **EightyOne** for Windows or the cross-platform **sz81** — which faithfully reproduce even the flickering in SLOW mode. Enthusiasts still create new games and demonstration programs to this day, modern replicas of boards and keyboards are being made, and the so-called **ZX81 high-resolution** trick is popular too — by which skilful programmers coaxed out of the original hardware pseudo-graphics at a resolution that Sinclair's engineers had never even dreamed of. The legend of machines like **3D Monster Maze** with its terrifying tyrannosaur, the maze game **Mazogs**, or the incredible **1K ZX Chess**, which fit into a single kilobyte, lives on thanks to that.

zx-spectrum.history: When Sir Clive Sinclair came out with his ZX Spectrum in April 1982, it was not just another home computer — it was a machine that taught an entire British generation to program and play. Where in America the Commodore 64 was king, in Britain and much of Europe it was the Spectrum that ruled. Its secret was the price: Sinclair built the computer on a philosophy of maximum frugality, with a minimum of components, its famous rubber "calculator" keyboard and a mere 16 or 48 kB of memory. It was a people's computer in the most literal sense — and precisely because of that, one of the most inventive gaming scenes of the eighties grew out of it. The Spectrum was technically modest and had one notoriously infamous quirk that today any insider recognises at first glance. But it was precisely from these limitations that a distinctive visual style was born, one still recognisable more than forty years later. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the computer was an eight-bit **Zilog Z80A** processor clocked at **3.5 MHz**. The graphics mode offered a resolution of **256 x 192 dots**, with a palette of **15 colours** (eight basic colours at two brightness levels, where black is the same in both). Here, however, comes that famous Achilles' heel — **attribute clash**, or colour clash. The Spectrum did not store the colour for each pixel separately, but only for blocks of **8 x 8 dots**: each such block could contain only **two colours** (foreground and background). When an object moved across the background, it often "recoloured" the entire character block it passed through. Developers learned to work around this with clever graphic design, and today this phenomenon is seen as a characteristic trait of the Spectrum aesthetic. Sound on the original models was even more modest. The Spectrum 48K had only a single **"beeper"** — a one-bit speaker controlled directly by the processor. Even so, skilful programmers like Tim Follin managed to conjure multi-voice melodies from this single channel that sound incredible. The real musical leap came only with the 128K model, which added the **General Instrument AY-3-8912** sound chip with **three channels** and a noise generator. ### Connectivity and peripherals Sinclair stayed true to frugality in connectivity too. The Spectrum used an **ordinary cassette recorder** for storing data (the EAR/MIC interface), which meant long minutes of loading accompanied by the characteristic screeching. The picture was output via an **RF modulator** to the television's antenna. For expansion there was the rear **edge connector**, to which a range of peripherals was attached. The most significant were the **ZX Interface 1** with **Microdrive** micro-tape units (loop tape cartridges as a faster replacement for the tape recorder) and the **ZX Interface 2**, which added two joystick ports and a slot for a ROM cartridge. Joysticks were connected via the **Kempston** and **Sinclair** standards. The ZX Printer print unit was popular too. ### Models and revisions The line went through significant evolution over the years. The initial **ZX Spectrum 16K/48K** (1982) became famous for its rubber keyboard. In 1984 came the **Spectrum+** with a better, plastic keyboard in a new case. The turning point was the **ZX Spectrum 128K** (first for the Spanish market, 1985), which brought the aforementioned AY chip and more memory. After the brand was taken over by Amstrad, models with a built-in tape mechanism followed: the **Spectrum +2** (1986) with an integrated cassette recorder and the **Spectrum +3** (1987) with a **3-inch floppy drive**. These later variants can be recognised by their grey (+2) and black (+3) finishes. ### Clones and variants The Spectrum is among the most-cloned computers in history, and its footprint is strong in our region too. In then-Czechoslovakia the **Didaktik** enterprise in Skalica produced a series of its own clones — **Didaktik Gama**, later **Didaktik M** and **Didaktik Kompakt** with a floppy drive. These were legendary machines on which the Czech and Slovak eight-bit generation grew up; among other things they added their own memory expansions and ports. The clone scene in the **former Soviet Union** was extraordinarily extensive, where dozens of models such as the **Pentagon** or **Scorpion** were created — these effectively became a platform of their own with a rich software output that lives on to this day. In Brazil, the Microdigital company made the **TK90X** model. ### Today's scene Emulating the Spectrum is utterly trivial today — excellent examples are **Fuse** (Free Unix Spectrum Emulator) or **ZEsarUX**, available on all platforms including handhelds. A huge advantage is the **World of Spectrum** project, thanks to which thousands of games are available legally and for free with the authors' permission. The home-brew scene remains extraordinarily alive. New homebrew titles keep coming out that boldly rival the period ones — for instance the action title **Sword of Ianna**. Modern development tools are available, as are hardware novelties like the **ZX Spectrum Next**, a community-designed successor that builds on the legacy of Sinclair's machine and proves that the forty-year-old legend has by no means said its last word.

amstrad-cpc.history: When Alan Sugar decided in 1984 that he would build a computer that every ordinary person would want in their living room, the result was a machine called the **Amstrad CPC 464**. The abbreviation CPC stood for *Colour Personal Computer*, and the brand's entire philosophy could be summed up in one phrase: the complete package. Whereas with the competing ZX Spectrum you had to source a television, a tape recorder and a power supply separately, Amstrad delivered a computer with a **built-in cassette tape recorder** (later a disk drive) and **its own monitor** in a single set. That made it a practical family machine that did not have to fight over the household TV. The CPC caught on most strongly in **Britain, France and Spain**, where it still nurtures a strong nostalgic fan base to this day. In France it practically became the national computer, and a range of distinctive games and adventures were created there. It is powered by the eight-bit **Zilog Z80** processor clocked at 4 MHz, so it shared the same foundation as the Spectrum for many titles — ports between the two platforms were common, only on the Amstrad they were usually in a more colourful and visually richer form. ### Technology: graphics and sound The graphics were handled by the **CRTC (6845)** chip, complemented by a chip generating colours from a palette of **27 colours**. The CPC offered three main display modes, and choosing between them was a trade-off of resolution versus number of colours: - **Mode 0** — 160×200 pixels, but a full **16 colours** at once; ideal for colourful, "chunky" pixels in arcade games. - **Mode 1** — 320×200 pixels and **4 colours**; the most commonly used gaming mode, a good compromise. - **Mode 2** — 640×200 pixels and **2 colours**; used mainly for text and office programs. Compared to the Spectrum, the CPC had a major advantage in that it **did not suffer from the so-called attribute clash** — the colour collision where, on the Spectrum, only two colours could meet within a single character cell. The Amstrad therefore looked cleaner and more varied. Its weakness, on the other hand, was the missing hardware scrolling and sprites; everything was handled by the processor in software, so fast, smooth scrolling tended to be jerkier than on machines with dedicated hardware. Sound was provided by the well-known **General Instrument AY-3-8912** chip with **three tone channels plus a noise generator**. Owners of the Atari ST or MSX knew the same circuit, as did the 128K version of the later Spectrums. Thanks to it, the CPC could handle decent music and sound effects, and the music scene flourished on it. ### Connectivity and peripherals From the outset the CPC had a convenient **joystick** connection right on the back (a standard nine-pin Atari connector), so there was no need to buy an interface as with the Spectrum. A key role was played by the **monitor**, which came in two variants: the monochrome green **GT-65** and the colour **CTM-644**. The base unit itself drew its power from the monitor, so it was a well-thought-out but at the same time tightly bound system. The **MP-1 / MP-2** modulator and adapter served to connect it to an ordinary television or another image source. Among the other accessories worth mentioning are printers via the Centronics port and, within the broader ecosystem, the possibility of a memory expansion. ### Models and revisions The CPC line went through several important variants: - **CPC 464** (1984) — the first model with 64 KB of RAM and an integrated **cassette tape recorder**. - **CPC 664** (1985) — a briefly produced model that was the first to bring a built-in **3-inch disk drive**. - **CPC 6128** (1985) — the most capable classic model with **128 KB of RAM** and a disk drive; also popular for working with the CP/M operating system. The use of **3-inch disks** was distinctive (rather than the more common 3.5"), which Amstrad also adopted for its PCW word processors. At the twilight of the era, in 1990, the **modernised Plus line** arrived under new ownership — the **464 Plus** and **6128 Plus** models with an extended palette of **4096 colours**, hardware sprites and cartridge support. Alongside them, the **GX4000** games console was also created, built on the same foundation, though it failed to succeed on the market. ### Clones and variants The Amstrad CPC did not spawn as many unofficial clones as the Spectrum, but this architecture appeared in the **Eastern Bloc** too. The most notable mark was left in the **German Democratic Republic** by the **KC compact** computer (1989), which was an East German clone of the CPC compatible with its software. From the standpoint of the **Czechoslovak footprint**, the CPC remained rarer here than the ubiquitous Spectrums and their domestic Didaktik clones — Amstrad hardly ever reached us officially and was more a matter of imports. Historically, machines compatible with the Spectrum dominated here, while the CPC remained a more exotic choice for most Czech and Slovak players. ### Today's scene Emulation of the Amstrad CPC is trouble-free today. Among the top emulators are **WinAPE** and the multiplatform **CPCEC** or **Caprice32**; they also run comfortably within the collecting frontend **RetroArch**. Original game recordings are distributed as disk images (.DSK) or cassette images. But what is nicest of all, the scene around the CPC is still alive. New **homebrew** titles and remakes are being created, among them for instance the acclaimed adventure **Orion Prime**. Competitions for new games and demos are held regularly, thanks to which the eight-bit Amstrad keeps pixelling on even four decades after its launch. For the retro gamer who already knows the Spectrum and the Commodore, the CPC is a pleasant discovery — a European 8-bit classic in a more colourful coat, full of gems like **Prince of Persia**, **Gryzor**, **Rick Dangerous** or **Chase H.Q.**

msx.history: When Microsoft and the Japanese ASCII Corporation joined forces in 1983, they had in mind an idea that sounded almost heretical: to create a unified standard for a home computer that a whole range of companies could manufacture. Instead of one manufacturer, one machine and one software library, this was to give rise to an open platform — something like the later PC, only a few years earlier. Brands such as **Sony, Panasonic, Philips, Sanyo, Toshiba, JVC** and **Canon** gradually signed up under the MSX banner. Commercially, the standard succeeded mainly in Japan, the Netherlands, Spain and Brazil; on the English-speaking markets, where Commodore and Sinclair already reigned, it failed to break through. Yet for gaming history the MSX is indispensable. It was here, after all, that **Hideo Kojima** created the very first **Metal Gear** (1987) and, a year later, the more advanced **Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake**. Konami gave it the original **Vampire Killer**, that is the MSX version of Castlevania, and a whole series of superb action games and shooters. The MSX was the home of Konami in its golden era in Japan — and the platform's library remains to this day a treasure trove of titles that never reached the West. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the first MSX was the eight-bit **Zilog Z80A** processor clocked at 3.58 MHz. The image was handled by the **Texas Instruments TMS9918** video chip (or rather its variants), that is the same family used by the **ColecoVision** and **Sega SG-1000**. It offered a resolution of 256×192 pixels, a palette of **16 colours** and hardware support for **32 sprites**. The weakness of this chip was the limited number of colours per line and the notoriously well-known problem of sprites disappearing when there were more than four of them on a line. Basic sound was provided by the **General Instrument AY-3-8910** chip with three tone channels and a noise generator — the same principle as with the ZX Spectrum 128 or the Amstrad CPC. A real leap came in 1985 with the **MSX2**. The new **Yamaha V9938** video chip could handle a resolution of up to 512×212, a palette of **512 colours** (with modes displaying 16 or 256 colours at once) and, above all, **hardware scrolling and bitmap modes**, which made the MSX2 a markedly more capable gaming machine. The later **MSX2+** added smooth horizontal scrolling and further colour modes; the final **MSX turbo R** (1990) deployed the faster R800 processor. Many Japanese machines also contained a Yamaha sound chip, which was followed up by expansion music modules as well. ### Connectivity and peripherals The MSX was a full-fledged computer, so it had a keyboard — some games require it, and on handhelds that tends to be the only complication of emulation. The standard provided for **two joystick ports** (compatible with the Atari connector), so a two-player game could be played without any problem. A key element was the **cartridge slot** (often two), into which game modules and expansions were plugged, and a port for a **cassette tape recorder** for saving programs. Later, **disk drives** (3.5") became widespread and became the main medium, especially in Europe. The peripherals included a mouse, a light pen, data storage and music modules. A chapter of its own is the expansion sound cartridges such as the **Konami SCC**, thanks to which the later Konami games (for example Space Manbow or Nemesis 2) sounded markedly richer than the standard AY chip. Some modules brought **FM synthesis** (Yamaha OPLL), so the MSX's audio could grow beyond its modest foundation. ### Models and revisions The standard developed in clearly defined generations. **MSX (1983)** was the base with the Z80 and the TMS9918 chip. **MSX2 (1985)** brought the Yamaha V9938, a larger palette and more memory. **MSX2+ (1988)** extended the graphics with smooth scrolling and new colour modes and remained practically exclusively a Japanese affair. The pinnacle was the **MSX turbo R (1990)** from Panasonic with the 16-bit-tuned R800 processor. Within each generation there then existed dozens of specific models from various manufacturers — from the compact Sony HitBit-series machines through the Philips VG-8000 to the Panasonic FS ones — which differed in memory, number of slots or built-in drives, but thanks to the standard remained mutually compatible. ### Clones and variants Because the MSX was an open standard, "clones" in the true sense of the word do not entirely make sense — there was a whole range of legal manufacturers right from the start. The Eastern trace is interesting, however. In the **Soviet Union**, MSX and MSX2 machines (for example the **Yamaha YIS** imported for schools) were used extensively in computer-science education and became the first computer for a whole generation. The MSX also caught on in South Korea and in Brazil, where local firms manufactured it under their own brands **Gradiente** and **Sharp/Epcom**. In Czechoslovakia the MSX was not widespread — the local scene was dominated rather by the ZX Spectrum and its Didaktik clones, so the MSX remained here primarily a matter for later collectors and emulation. ### Today's scene The MSX belongs among the very liveliest retro communities. Emulators such as **openMSX** or **blueMSX** handle the whole family of machines faithfully and without trouble, so getting Metal Gear or Aleste running is a matter of a moment. The scene is moreover extraordinarily prolific thanks to the annual **MSXdev** competition, from which dozens of new games emerge each year. Among the best modern homebrew is the precise metroidvania **Pampas & Selene** — proof that a forty-year-old standard still has something to offer.

colecovision.history: When Coleco launched the ColecoVision in August 1982, the console felt like an apparition from the future. While the Atari 2600 was already beginning to show its age and its games looked like clusters of blocky smudges, the ColecoVision brought arcade hits home in a quality no home machine had managed before. The bundled port of **Donkey Kong** was a perfect killer app: for the first time you could play the popular arcade game at home and the picture actually resembled what you knew from the arcade. The console is therefore sometimes nicknamed the „Dreamcast of its era" — a technically outstanding machine that outpaced the competition, yet was doomed to an early end. That end was the great North American video game crash of 1983. The ColecoVision initially sold superbly, but the collapse of the entire industry swept it away along with the others. Coleco moreover bet on the unsuccessful Adam home computer, which drained the company financially and effectively brought it down. The console thus had only a short life — production ended in 1985 — but it managed to assemble a surprisingly high-quality library of arcade ports, which still earns it respect among collectors today. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the ColecoVision is an eight-bit **Zilog Z80A** processor clocked at around 3.58 MHz. The picture is handled by the **Texas Instruments TMS9928A** video chip (a variant of the TMS9918 series), which manages a resolution of 256×192 pixels and a palette of **15 colors** plus transparency. Key was the support for **32 hardware sprites** — it was precisely thanks to them that moving objects such as Donkey Kong, barrels or Mario could glide smoothly across the screen without the processor having to laboriously redraw the background. This was a huge leap over the Atari 2600, which had only a few primitive sprites at its disposal and had to painstakingly assemble the picture „on the fly" line by line. Sound is provided by the **Texas Instruments SN76489** chip, which offers **three tone channels and one noise channel**. By 1982 standards this was decent equipment, allowing simple melodies and sound effects at the same time. The same video chip and sound circuit were used by other platforms of the period, which we will come back to — and it is precisely this kinship that makes the ColecoVision a technically very interesting piece of history. ### Connectivity and peripherals The ColecoVision connected to the television via an **RF modulator** (antenna input), which was the standard at the time. The controller was a unique design of its kind: it combined a classic joystick with a **numeric keypad** and two side buttons. The keypad served for entering difficulty levels, menu choices or special actions in games — many titles used the included plastic overlays, which the player placed onto the keypad according to the specific game. Coleco also offered a varied range of expansions. The most famous was the **Expansion Module #1**, an adapter that allowed you to play Atari 2600 games directly on the ColecoVision — a bold move over which Atari even filed suit. The **Expansion Module #2** added a steering wheel and pedal for the racing game Turbo. There was also the **Roller Controller** (trackball) and the **Super Action Controller** with additional buttons. The pinnacle of the ecosystem was to be the **Adam** computer module, which turned the console into a full-fledged home computer with a keyboard, tape drive and printer. ### Models and revisions The ColecoVision essentially existed in a single main hardware form, so hardware revisions were sparse and, for the ordinary player, unimportant. Far more important were the aforementioned expansions, which transformed the console. The most striking transformation was precisely the **Coleco Adam** — a computer built on the same foundation, available both as a standalone machine and as an add-on to an existing console. The Adam, however, was notorious for its faultiness and for problems with data erasure caused by a magnetic field at startup, which further damaged Coleco's reputation. ### Clones and variants Thanks to the kinship of the chips, the ColecoVision is close to other platforms of its time. The same (or very similar) TMS9918/9928 video chip and SN76489 sound circuit can be found in the Japanese **Sega SG-1000** and in the **MSX** computer standard, so games ported between these systems relatively easily — something the homebrew scene still takes advantage of today. Among the official variants, the European distribution through the CBS company under the **CBS ColecoVision** brand is worth mentioning. There was also a later clone, the **Telegames Personal Arcade** (also sold as the Dina), which combined compatibility with both the ColecoVision and the Sega SG-1000. In the Czechoslovak or Eastern European context the ColecoVision was practically nonexistent — the region was flooded instead by NES famiclones (known here as the **Pegasus**) and ZX Spectrum clones of the **Didaktik** type, whereas Coleco left no significant trace here. ### Today's scene Emulating the ColecoVision is trivial today and can be handled by practically any modern hardware — from PCs through the Raspberry Pi to pocket handhelds. Among the emulators, **BlueMSX**, **openMSX** or the multi-emulator **MAME** are popular; on RetroArch there is the **Gearcoleco** core. The main draw remains the faithful period arcade ports and a surprisingly active homebrew community, which still releases new games for this nearly half-century-old machine on physical cartridges as well as for download. For retro gamers the ColecoVision thus represents a short but very pleasant excursion into the beginnings of home consoles.

intellivision.history: When Mattel launched the **Intellivision** (short for „Intelligent Television") on the market in 1979, it was not just another box for the TV — it was the first serious challenge to the then-dominant Atari 2600. Mattel bet on the strength of both marketing and hardware: in the famous comparative advertising campaign hosted by writer and actor George Plimpton, it placed side by side the crude graphics of the Atari and the noticeably more colorful, finer picture of the Intellivision. The console had the ambition to come across as the „smarter" choice for the whole family and became one of the pillars of the so-called second generation of gaming consoles. By the time production ended in 1990, roughly three million units had been sold, and it left behind a rich library of sports, strategy and action titles. The unconventional controllers became a characteristic feature: flat gamepads with a numeric keypad, a rotating disc instead of a stick, and a set of side buttons. Many games moreover came with paper „overlay" templates that were placed on the keypad and described what each digit did in the game. It was a solution both ingenious and frustrating at once — the disc was more precise than a joystick for some genres, but stiff and, over time, prone to failure. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the Intellivision was the 16-bit **General Instrument CP1610** processor, clocked at around 0.9 MHz. The sixteen-bit architecture was unusual for its time — the Atari 2600 and the later NES ran on 8-bit chips — even though real-world performance was limited by slow memory and clock speed. It was precisely this detail that Mattel liked to emphasize in its marketing. Graphics were handled by the specialized **STIC (Standard Television Interface Chip), AY-3-8900** video chip. It displayed a resolution of 159 × 96 pixels and a palette of **16 colors**. It featured a background assembled from tiles and eight moving objects (sprites, here called MOB — Moving Object Block), which could be enlarged and mirrored. The resulting picture had rounder, less „blocky" shapes than the competition, which gave the console its typical look. Sound was provided by the **General Instrument AY-3-8914** chip, a relative of the famous AY-3-8910 from home computers. It offered **three tone channels and a noise generator**, so games sounded fuller and more musical than the beeping of simpler rivals. The later Intellivoice expansion module even added human speech synthesis. ### Connectivity and peripherals The console connected to the television via an RF output. In the base version the controllers were permanently attached by cable, which meant they could not be easily swapped — that only changed with later revisions. The best-known accessory was the **Intellivoice Voice Synthesis Module**, a voice module inserted into the cartridge slot, into which a special game was then plugged. Titles such as *B-17 Bomber* or *Bomb Squad* spoke thanks to it — at a time when speech synthesis in the home felt like science fiction. The planned **Keyboard Component** (an add-on computer module with a tape drive and its own memory) became a notorious fiasco: it was repeatedly delayed, overpriced, and because of it Mattel even faced regulatory intervention. It was replaced by the simpler **Entertainment Computer System (ECS)** with a keyboard, which allowed programming in BASIC, and there was also a **Music Synthesizer** music keyboard as an add-on. There was also the **System Changer**, an adapter that allowed the Intellivision II to play Atari 2600 cartridges. ### Models and revisions The original 1979 model bore the simple designation **Intellivision (Master Component)** in a wooden design. In 1982 came the redesigned, cheaper **Intellivision II** with detachable controllers and a more angular appearance; the System Changer was intended precisely for it. Other manufacturers also sold the console under their own brands — **Sears** offered it as the *Super Video Arcade*, and in Europe it appeared for instance under the **Radofin** or **GTE Sylvania** name. After Mattel's collapse in the gaming market, the rights were taken over by the **INTV Corporation**, which continued production and in 1985 introduced the **INTV System III** model (also known as the Super Pro System). INTV kept the console alive through mail-order sales until 1990, when the last new games were released. ### Clones and variants The Intellivision did not have as extensive a clone scene as the NES or the ZX Spectrum — its closed, specific hardware was difficult to imitate. The main „variants" were therefore more likely licensed rebranded versions (Sears, Radofin, GTE Sylvania) than illegal clones. In Czechoslovakia or elsewhere in the Eastern Bloc the Intellivision hardly spread; the local home scene centered around the ZX Spectrum computer and its **Didaktik** clone, or Pegasus-type famiclones, while American second-generation consoles remained a rarity behind the Iron Curtain. A valuable trace for historians, on the other hand, is the fact that INTV, after years, made part of the original source material available, which helped the later documentation of the platform. ### Today's scene The Intellivision has maintained a surprisingly lively community. Emulation is well solved — there are dedicated emulators (e.g. **jzIntv**) as well as cores for the multiplatform **RetroArch**, so you can play the original library on PCs, handhelds and single-board computers. Mattel moreover officially revived the brand: it released collections of classic games and collectible miniatures. The **homebrew** scene also remains active, still writing new titles for the CP1610 to this day, distributed on physical cartridges as well as in digital form, thereby keeping the legacy of the „intelligent television" alive.

jaguar.history: When Atari unveiled the Jaguar in the autumn of 1993, it bet everything on one bold number: **64 bits**. At a time when the world was ruled by the sixteen-bit duo of the Super Nintendo and the Sega Mega Drive, this angular black box, advertised with the slogan „Do the Math“, was supposed to leap over an entire generation and shame the competition before it could even get going. The Jaguar was the last home console Atari ever made, and it became a symbol of ambitions that outgrew the company itself. It was a commercial flop, with only around 150,000 units sold, and yet it still holds cult status to this day: it was a machine that could do things for which it lacked the games, the documentation and the time. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the Jaguar sat a pair of custom chips code-named **Tom** and **Jerry**. Tom contained the graphics processor (GPU), an object processor for rendering sprites, and a blitter for fast data transfers; Jerry handled sound and contained a second programmable processor (DSP). Together they formed the backbone of an architecture built around a **64-bit data bus** to memory — that is exactly where the marketing „64-bit“ came from. The reality, however, was more prosaic: the main control processor remained the aging **16/32-bit Motorola 68000** at 13.3 MHz, which many developers used out of convenience for the game logic itself, instead of harnessing the faster and harder-to-program RISC cores. This was one of the main reasons why a number of games looked more like enhanced sixteen-bit titles. But when a team mastered the whole architecture, the results were impressive: the Jaguar could handle **thousands of colors** from a palette of up to 16.7 million, smooth scrolling, sprite scaling and rotation, and in games like **Tempest 2000** it delivered effects the contemporary competition could not manage. The Jerry sound chip offered multichannel synthesis as well as playback of digitized samples in stereo, and the music for Tempest 2000 remains to this day one of the legends of game soundtracks. ### Connectivity and peripherals The console output a composite and RF signal to the television and had an unusual controller with a numeric keypad of twelve buttons, over which paper overlays with per-game functions were laid — a solution inherited from the era of Atari home computers. A later expanded **Pro Controller** was released, with six action buttons and shoulder buttons, better suited to fighting games. The most important accessory was the **Atari Jaguar CD** unit, which mounted on top of the console and added a CD-ROM drive. It came out in 1995, sold miserably, and today it is a collector's item because of its rarity and unreliability. Further peripherals were also planned, among them a modem and **Jaguar VR** virtual-reality goggles, but most of them never got past the prototype stage. ### Models and revisions There were few hardware variants of the console itself — it was a single basic version. The essential expansion was the aforementioned **Jaguar CD** add-on, which effectively turned the console into a two-part assembly. In parallel, Atari was developing a successor under the working name **Jaguar II** and a professional arcade board, but none of these devices reached the market because of the company's collapse. In 1996 Atari merged with the disk maker JT Storage, and development of both games and hardware effectively came to an end. ### Clones and variants Genuine period clones of the Jaguar essentially do not exist — it was too complex and commercially marginal a platform for anyone to imitate, unlike, say, the NES with its famiclones. The rights to the hardware were later acquired by **Hasbro Interactive**, which in the late 1990s officially released the Jaguar as an open platform and gave up enforcing licenses, thereby stirring up homebrew development. In more recent times a curiosity has appeared — the **Atari Jaguar GameDrive** and similar flash cartridges, which allow ROM images to be run from a memory card. In the Czech and Czechoslovak setting the Jaguar left no clone trail of its own; it reached the region only in small numbers as an expensive imported piece, which makes it a sought-after rarity here more today than back then. ### Today's scene Today the Jaguar lives on mainly thanks to emulation — the **Virtual Jaguar** core (also available within RetroArch) handles most commercial titles, though accurate emulation of the demanding Tom and Jerry chips remains difficult. The homebrew community is remarkably alive: new games, conversions and demos are being made that only now are drawing out of the hardware what studios of the day lacked. Collectors hunt for original cartridges and the rare CD unit, and so, after years, the Jaguar has earned itself the position of a beloved flop — a machine that was ahead of its time more in its ambitions than in reality.

amiga-cd32.history: When Commodore unveiled the **Amiga CD32** in the autumn of 1993, it was a bold attempt to turn the Amiga home computer into a living-room game console. From a technical standpoint it was nothing brand-new from the ground up: at its core the CD32 was an **Amiga 1200** supplemented with a CD-ROM drive and stripped of its keyboard and floppy drive. Even so, the console deserves an honorable place in history — it is often described as the **world's first 32-bit game console with a CD drive**, one that reached the market before the Atari Jaguar with its CD as well as the later Sega Saturn and Sony PlayStation. Commodore was desperate for a hit. The company was drowning in debt, sales of the classic Amigas were falling, and the CD32 was meant to be the lifebuoy that would draw players toward the medium of the future — the compact disc. In Europe, where the Amiga had an enormous installed base, the console sold decently and for a while became very popular. But the story ended quickly and sadly: because of a patent dispute and manufacturing problems, Commodore went bankrupt in the spring of 1994 and the CD32 passed into history after only a few months on the market. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the CD32 is a **Motorola 68EC020** processor clocked at **14.18 MHz** and **2 MB of Chip RAM**. Graphics are handled by the **AGA (Advanced Graphics Architecture)** chipset, the same as in the Amiga 1200. It can work with a **palette of 16.8 million colors**, while it can render up to **256 colors** on screen at once in indexed mode, or **262,144 colors** in the special **HAM8 (Hold-And-Modify)** mode. Standard game resolution hovered around **320×256** pixels (PAL), though AGA could handle higher modes too. The Amiga was renowned for its **specialized coprocessors** — the Blitter for fast moving of graphics blocks, the Copper for controlling the image line by line, and hardware sprites. Thanks to these, smooth scrolling and color gradients stood out, things that required far more effort on competing machines. Sound is provided by the legendary **Paula** chip with **four hardware channels** and **8-bit PCM** playback of samples (sampled sound), split classically into stereo pairs. Above-average sound for its time was one of the great strengths of the entire Amiga line. The CD drive also made it possible to play **music directly from an Audio CD**, and the console worked as an ordinary CD player too. ### Connectivity and peripherals The CD32 had a **two-button gamepad** (with a D-pad, two action buttons, buttons for browsing and pause), connectable to two ports. There was a **composite video and RF output** for connecting to a television, and on some variants also **S-Video**. An interesting chapter is the **FMV (Full Motion Video) module** peripheral, which slotted into the expansion connector and added hardware decoding of **MPEG-1 video**, so the owner could play films from **Video CD (VCD) and CD-i** format discs. The console also had an **expansion connector**, through which projects existed to turn the CD32 back into a full-fledged computer (adding a keyboard, floppy drive, mouse and serial port) — effectively creating devices close to the Amiga 1200. ### Models and revisions The CD32 was made in essentially a single basic form, differing mainly in regional versions for **PAL** (Europe, Australia) and the planned **NTSC** versions for North America. The North American market, however, the console practically failed to reach — because of a **patent dispute with Cad Track** (concerning XOR rendering), Commodore's imports were blocked and a large part of the stock got stuck in warehouses, which was one of the nails in the coffin of the whole company. In hardware the CD32 is so close to the **Amiga 1200** that a large part of the software and know-how was transferable between the two machines. That, incidentally, explains why many games arose as simple conversions of Amiga titles to CD. ### Clones and variants No official clones of the CD32 were made — Commodore went bankrupt before the market could develop, and the brand was later acquired by another company. There are, however, **modifications and expansion kits** made by enthusiasts that turn the console into a computer, or address the faulty internal battery and the replacement of the outdated CD drive with a modern solution. As for the **Czechoslovak trail**, it is tied more to the whole Amiga family than to the CD32 directly: both eight-bit and sixteen-bit Amigas had a devoted community of users here in the 1990s, the Amiga demoscene was extraordinarily lively, and the machines were imported here in large numbers. The CD32 itself was rather a rarity here because of its price and short lifespan — all the more prized among collectors. ### Today's scene The CD32 lives on splendidly today thanks to emulation. Emulators like **WinUAE** (and its variants for various platforms) can faithfully simulate the AGA chipset and the CD drive, so you can play the titles on a PC as well as on more powerful handheld emulation devices. The community around the Amiga is one of the most active in the retro world — new **homebrew games**, demo productions and hardware add-ons (drive replacements, flash solutions instead of CD) are being created. For collectors the CD32 remains an attractive piece: a reminder of the time when Commodore made its last attempt to conquer the living rooms — and almost pulled it off.

atari-2600.history:
When the **Video Computer System** — only later renamed the Atari 2600 after its CX2600 ordering code number — rolled out of Atari's factories in 1977, few suspected it was launching an era that would last over forty years. The console was not the first of its kind, but it was the first to commercially establish the idea of **interchangeable cartridges**. Instead of hard-wired games like those offered by predecessors such as the Magnavox Odyssey or home Pong units, you could now buy any number of titles for a single device. This idea, obvious today, defined the entire industry for decades to come.

The machine sold for an astonishingly long time — from 1977 all the way to 1992, when Atari officially ended production — and for an entire generation it became synonymous with the word "video game." Games like **Pitfall!**, **River Raid**, and **Adventure** (which contained the very first "easter egg" in history — the hidden name of programmer Warren Robinett) showed what creativity could achieve even on extremely stingy hardware.

### Technology: graphics and sound

The heart of the console is the eight-bit **MOS 6507** processor, a cheaper, cut-down variant of the famous 6502, clocked at roughly 1.19 MHz. It had a mere **128 bytes of RAM** — not kilobytes, bytes — and cartridges initially carried typically just 2 or 4 KB of code. This is why programming for the 2600 was notoriously demanding.

Graphics and sound were handled by the **TIA (Television Interface Adapter)** chip. It had no classic framebuffer; the image had to be "drawn" in real time, line by line, synchronized with the movement of the electron beam in the television. This technique was nicknamed **"racing the beam"** — the developer literally competed with the beam and the code had to be cycle-exact. The TIA could display five moving objects: two player sprites (**players**), two shots (**missiles**), and one "ball" (**ball**), plus a symmetric background (**playfield**). The palette in the NTSC version comprised **128 colors**, though only a limited number could be used on a single line without tricks.

Sound was provided by **two independent channels** in the TIA with a coarse, characteristically "buzzing" tuning — clean music was nearly impossible on them, but they sufficed for arcade effects. That playable and still-admired games arose on such a minimalist foundation is a small technical miracle.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The standard controller was a simple **digital joystick** with a single button (the famous black CX40). The console had two ports, so two could play. Besides the joystick, Atari also offered **paddles** (rotary controllers) — two in each connector, thus up to four players — ideal for Kaboom! or Breakout, as well as a numeric **keypad controller** for educational and quiz titles.

The output went through an **RF modulator** into the television's antenna input, with a channel 2/3 switch and a color/black-and-white selector. Switches on the front of the console also set the difficulty for the left and right players. A true rarity was the **Starpath Supercharger** peripheral — a device that loaded games into the console from an ordinary audio cassette and added extra RAM, enabling richer titles.

### Models and revisions

The original 1977 model, nicknamed the **"Heavy Sixer,"** had six switches and a robust construction with a wooden front panel. It was soon succeeded by a lighter version (the "Light Sixer") and later by four-switch variants, in which the two difficulty switches were moved to the back. In 1980 came a model with a full **wood-grain imitation**, subsequently replaced by an all-black design.

In 1982 Atari introduced the shrunken and cheaper **Atari 2600 Jr.** with a flat plastic design and a rainbow stripe. There was also the curious **Atari 5200** (1982) as a technically more powerful but incompatible sibling, and later the backward-compatible successor **Atari 7800** (1986), which could play most 2600 cartridges. The 7800 came late, faded in the shadow of the NES, though it was more capable in terms of hardware.

### Clones and variants

Given its long lifespan and popularity, a range of unofficial clones arose. Cheap Asian **"retro" versions** in the form of a joystick with built-in games are still produced today. In the Eastern Bloc the 2600 was not officially distributed, but clones like the **Rambo TV Game** and other Taiwanese variants did appear. Collectors also prize a number of licensed versions sold under other brands (for example Sears Tele-Games in the United States, where Sears distributed the console under its own name). In Brazil, thanks to the company Polyvox, the Atari 2600 lived on long after it had gone out of fashion in the West.

### Today's scene

The Atari 2600 is excellently supported by emulators — the best known is **Stella**, an open and very accurate emulator running practically everywhere. The **homebrew scene** is also remarkably alive: enthusiasts still release new cartridges to this day, for instance **Halo 2600** by Ed Fries (former head of Microsoft Games) or the action title **Draconian**. People still enjoy taming this "impossible" machine — and for retro gamers the 2600 is more a fascinating trip into the prehistory of video games than a source of long gaming evenings. But no one can take away the magic of the beginnings.

atari-5200.history: When Atari unveiled the **Atari 5200 "SuperSystem"** console in the autumn of 1982, it was meant to be a dignified farewell to the era of the simple VCS (Atari 2600) and an entry into a new generation. The machine arrived at a time when Atari's 400/800 series home computers had already been earning praise for their graphics for several years, and the 5200 was technically based on them. The console was to face the rising Intellivision and ColecoVision, but it met an unfortunate fate: it arrived shortly before the crash of the American gaming market in 1983, and due to a problematic controller and the lack of backward compatibility with the 2600 library it never won broader favor. Nonetheless, it is a technically interesting and today prized piece of history. ### Technology: graphics and sound The heart of the Atari 5200 is the proven trio of chips from Atari's home computers.
