The image is handled by the **ANTIC** and **GTIA** coprocessors, which cooperate with the main **MOS 6502C** processor (a variant with bus-sharing support, designated "Sally") clocked at around 1.79 MHz. For its time this architecture enabled excellent smooth scrolling, display lists (programmable graphics modes line by line), and hardware sprites, which Atari called **player/missile graphics** – up to four "players" and four "missiles." The console handled a palette of **256 colors** and roughly dozens of colors on screen at once, which placed it above the competition in terms of color range. Sound is handled by the **POKEY** chip with four independent audio channels. POKEY also handled reading the controllers and generating noise, so it was suitable for both gunfire and melodies. Thanks to this foundation, games like *Star Raiders* or *Centipede* looked and sounded markedly richer on the 5200 than on the older VCS. ### Connectivity and peripherals A characteristic yet at the same time most problematic element was the **analog controller**. It was one of the first analog joysticks in a home console – it did not return to center on its own, had a numeric keypad, START/PAUSE/RESET buttons, and two side fire buttons. In practice, however, it was unreliable and prone to failure, which famously harmed the console. The console had **four ports** for controllers, so it allowed multiplayer games; but only a few games for four simultaneous players were released (e.g. the *Realsports* titles). A peculiarity of the first version was the **automatic RF switch** powered by a special cable – after being turned on, the console switched itself to the television input. Peripherals also included the **Trak-Ball** controller, suitable for games like *Centipede* and *Missile Command*, and planned (but effectively never released) voice and keyboard hardware. A planned adapter for playing games from the Atari 2600 did appear later, but only in a limited way. ### Models and revisions The Atari 5200 came first as a **four-port version (1982)**, which in 1983 was succeeded by a redesign with **two ports**. The two-port variant abandoned the automatic RF switch in favor of an ordinary switching cable and gained a new connector on its left side – this was precisely where the adapter for Atari 2600 games was to be connected. The internal board also changed, so some games sensitive to timing did not get along equally with both revisions. A large part of the library was essentially conversions of games from the Atari 400/800 computers, because they shared the same architecture. This also meant that anyone who owned an Atari computer had access to similar games by another route – and so the console lost part of its distinctiveness. ### Clones and variants Outright standalone clones of the Atari 5200 practically do not exist – the console was not sold for long or widely, so no one copied it the way it happened with, say, the NES (famiclones) or the ZX Spectrum. Worth mentioning, though, is the close kinship with the **Atari 400/800** computers and later XL/XE models: at its core it is the same hardware family. In Czechoslovakia, the interest of retro enthusiasts focused rather on the related Atari eight-bits (the XL/XE series), which were imported here even through second-hand shops and which had a lively demoscene here, while the 5200 console itself remained a rarity that practically never reached us. ### Today's scene The Atari 5200 is today reliably run by emulators focused on eight-bit Ataris, primarily **Altirra** (excellent accuracy) and the cross-platform **Atari800**, and it is also supported by a number of cores in **RetroArch**. Playing on a keyboard or on a gamepad, moreover, also solves the original problem with the unfortunate analog controller. The community around Atari is still active: new homebrew titles are created, corrected releases of old games, and hardware projects such as replacement controllers and flash cartridges, thanks to which one can play the whole library on real iron. For collectors, the 5200 is today a prized, if bulky, piece for the display cabinet – a reminder of an ambitious console that was sunk by bad timing and one botched joystick.

atari-7800.history: The Atari 7800 ProSystem is one of the most intriguing "what if" chapters in the history of the gaming industry. The console was ready as early as **1984**, when General Computer Corporation designed it for Atari as the successor to the famous but technically aging 2600. However, the North American video game crash and the subsequent sale of Atari's home division to Jack Tramiel got in the way. The finished console thus ended up in a warehouse, and its official market launch only came in **1986**. By then, though, Nintendo dominated the scene with its NES, and the Atari 7800 was cast from the start as an outsider fighting for the scraps of attention. Even so, it was a machine with several clever ideas. The biggest draw for owners at the time was **backward compatibility** with the Atari 2600 library – you just plugged in an old cartridge and the console behaved like its predecessor. Atari thus offered instant access to hundreds of games, which was a strong argument in its day. The 7800's own library was never large, but it contained solid arcade conversions such as **Ms. Pac-Man**, **Centipede**, **Asteroids**, as well as unconventional titles like **Ninja Golf** and **Food Fight**. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the console is the eight-bit **Atari SALLY (6502C)** processor running at roughly 1.79 MHz. The real star, however, is the graphics chip nicknamed **MARIA**. It worked differently from the competition of the time: instead of a fixed number of hardware sprites, it processed so-called "display lists," which let it put a large number of moving objects on the screen at once. For games full of enemies and projectiles this was a major advantage, and in this respect the 7800 even outdid the NES. MARIA could handle a palette of **256 colors**, and games commonly displayed more colors on screen than many of its rivals allowed. The weak point, on the other hand, was **sound**. The console relied on the old **TIA** chip inherited from the Atari 2600, which offered only two simple channels and belonged sonically to the previous generation. On top of that, MARIA consumed so many system resources that little power was left for music. Atari therefore counted on more demanding games getting a **POKEY** sound chip placed directly in the cartridge – but this succeeded with only a handful of titles, for example the home version of **Ballblazer**. Most games thus sound significantly poorer than they look. ### Connections and peripherals The Atari 7800 built on the proven standard of its older sibling. The console had **two controller ports** compatible with the Atari 2600 connector, so classic joysticks worked too. The bundle included a two-button **controller with a dial (Pro-Line)**, which many players did not particularly like due to its ergonomics. Thanks to compatibility with the older system, paddles could also be used for games that required them. In terms of connecting to a television, the console offered a standard **RF output** via the antenna input, a solution typical for the home devices of the era. Planned expansion peripherals, including a keyboard and a high-speed module, either never achieved wide distribution or remained only in the prototype stage – toward the end of the console's life, Atari no longer invested in developing further accessories. ### Models and revisions The console underwent cosmetic tweaks rather than a fundamental redesign during its life. The original 1986 model had a bulkier body with a detachable dial for the expansion connector on the right side. The later variant received a **slightly reduced and simplified case**, while the aforementioned expansion port (which never had any real use) disappeared from some units. These were cost-saving redesigns typical of a console that Atari kept on the market more out of inertia – official support ran out at approximately **1992**. ### Clones and variants Unlike the Atari 2600 or the ZX Spectrum, the Atari 7800 did not become a target of massive cloning. There were several reasons: a small installed base, weaker worldwide reach, and the fact that its MARIA graphics architecture was harder for unofficial manufacturers to imitate. In the Eastern Bloc, where the systems copied were mainly those built around the NES (the famous Famiclones and the **Pegasus** sold here) or the ZX Spectrum (the domestic **Didaktik**), the 7800 therefore left practically no trace. This console thus remained more of an American affair without any notable Czechoslovak echoes. ### Today's scene Today the Atari 7800 is well covered by **emulators** – alongside the specialized **ProSystem**, it is handled by a number of multi-system solutions and cores within RetroArch. The console also has a surprisingly lively **homebrew community**, which to this day releases new games on physical cartridges and uses MARIA's capabilities to the fullest – often better than the titles from the 1980s managed. For collectors and retro enthusiasts, the 7800 thus represents an underappreciated machine whose graphical potential only gained full recognition decades later.

atari-8bit.history: When Atari introduced the **400** and **800** models in 1979, it raised the bar for home computers considerably. The machine, built around a pair of custom coprocessors — the **ANTIC** video chip and the **GTIA/CTIA** multimedia chip together with the **POKEY** sound chip — surpassed the competition of its time in both graphics and sound and stood a class above the consoles of the era, including the home Atari 2600, in gaming quality. Its development involved engineers around **Jay Miner**, who later designed the Amiga, so the Atari 8-bit architecture is in a sense a forerunner of what computers became famous for a few years later. Crucially, this was not a gaming machine but a **full-fledged computer** with a keyboard, programmable in BASIC, loading software from cassettes, floppy disks, and cartridges. The library is therefore enormous and diverse in genre — from arcades through strategy games to text adventures. The flagship titles are the legendary **Star Raiders** (a space battle from the cockpit, astonishing for 1979), the economic strategy **M.U.L.E.**, and the Lucasfilm experiments with fractal landscapes **Rescue on Fractalus!** and **The Eidolon**. ### Technology: graphics and sound The heart of the machine is a trio of chips. **ANTIC** is essentially a standalone graphics processor that reads from memory a so-called **display list** — a program describing how the screen is to be assembled from lines of various graphics modes. This makes it possible to mix text and graphics modes on a single screen and easily create smooth **hardware scrolling** (fine pixel-by-pixel movement) as well as interrupts on a specific line. Colors are handled by **GTIA** (still **CTIA** in the first units) with a palette of **128 colors** (GTIA can do 256). Standard resolution reaches up to **320 × 192** points; low resolution draws in more colors, high resolution in fewer. GTIA also provides **Player/Missile Graphics** — hardware sprites (four "players" and four "missiles") with collision detection, which for games meant smooth character movement independent of the background. The **POKEY** sound chip offers **four channels** of sound with adjustable frequency, volume, and distortion (they can be paired into two 16-bit channels for cleaner tones). But POKEY doesn't serve only sound — it also handles reading the keyboard, joysticks (paddle inputs), and serial communication. The processor is a **MOS 6502** clocked at around **1.79 MHz**. ### Connections and peripherals Atari bet on its own serial bus **SIO** (Serial Input/Output), into which peripherals were daisy-chained: the **Atari 410** cassette recorder, the **Atari 810** floppy disk drive (and later the **1050**), and printers. It was a pioneering concept of intelligent peripherals with their own logic — a distant relative of today's USB. Games and joysticks used the standard **9-pin Atari ports** (compatible with Commodore joysticks and others); the 400/800 models had four ports outright, so they allowed multiplayer play on a single machine (e.g., M.U.L.E.). **Paddle controllers** were available, later also a mouse (an ST mouse/Amiga mouse can be used in the connection) and modems for connecting to a telephone line. The image was output via an **RF modulator** to a television, while higher models and variants also offered better-quality **composite/AV** output. ### Models and revisions The family went through several generations. After the original **400** (membrane keyboard, cheaper) and **800** (full keyboard, expandable memory), the early 1980s brought the **XL** line — the **1200XL**, the popular **600XL**, and the **800XL** — with a more modern design and built-in BASIC. After Jack Tramiel took over the company, the more economical **XE** line arrived: the **65XE**, the **130XE** (with 128 KB of RAM), and the game-oriented **XEGS** (Atari XE Game System) from 1987, which was sold as a console with a keyboard but hardware-wise remained the same old 8-bit Atari. High software compatibility was maintained across generations. ### Clones and variants Unlike the ZX Spectrum, for which the domestic clone **Didaktik** was created in Czechoslovakia, the Atari 8-bit was officially imported and cloned in few places. All the stronger, however, was the **user and gaming scene in the Eastern Bloc**, especially in **Poland** and **Czechoslovakia**. Atari was more accessible and popular behind the Iron Curtain, and a devoted community grew around it that still creates to this day. The Polish puzzle classic **Robbo** became a legend, and the modern scene churns out new titles — the annual Polish competition **"Fujicup"** brings dozens of fresh games. Among the technical variants, the **stereo POKEY** sound expansion (two chips) and the memory expansions, which became a standard among enthusiasts on many XE/XL machines, are worth mentioning. ### Today's scene Emulation is trouble-free today — the reference **Atari800** (and its core in RetroArch) runs at full speed even on small handheld consoles. For the classics, extensive archives such as **AtariMania** serve well, while news and home-grown production are gathered by the legendary website **Fandal**. Homebrew is alive: besides the annual competitions, new demoscene productions and games making use of expanded memory and modern flash cartridges are being created. For the retro gamer, the Atari 8-bit is thus an exploratory territory with its own atmosphere — and a scene that is close to us both geographically and at heart.

vic20.history: When Commodore launched the VIC-20 in 1980, it had no ambition to become a technical marvel. It was meant to be something far cleverer: the first color home computer for less than 300 dollars. Jack Tramiel pushed the slogan "computers for the masses, not the classes" and the VIC-20 fulfilled it completely. The machine was sold not only in specialized stores but also in ordinary department stores, and it became the first computer in history to cross the mark of one million units sold. For an entire generation of people, the VIC-20 was the very first computer they ever touched, and a springboard to a much more famous successor. At the heart of the machine was the eight-bit **MOS 6502** processor clocked at around 1 MHz and a mere **5 KB of RAM**, of which only a little over 3.5 KB remained available to the user after startup. That was a modest portion even for its time, one that almost every owner addressed with add-on memory modules. Even so, the VIC-20 was a friendly and open machine: after powering on, the **Commodore BASIC 2.0** interpreter from Microsoft booted up and the user could start programming immediately. ### Technology: graphics and sound A single universal chip handled both picture and sound, and the computer was even named after it — **VIC** (Video Interface Chip, MOS 6560 in the NTSC version and 6561 in the PAL version). The text mode offered **22 columns and 23 rows**, which was little even by the standards of the day and meant that an unusually short word fit on the screen. This narrow screen became one of the VIC-20's distinguishing traits. **16 colors** were available, and thanks to redefinable characters and so-called semigraphics, programmers could create surprisingly colorful and lively games. The VIC did not have hardware sprites like the later Commodore chips, so all object movement had to be handled by redrawing the character matrix — which makes games like **Gridrunner** by Jeff Minter, who squeezed a brisk shooter out of the limited hardware, all the more admirable. Sound was provided by **three tone channels** complemented by one noise channel, all likewise integrated directly into the VIC chip. It was not enough for serious music, but it was fully sufficient for game effects and simple melodies. ### Connectivity and peripherals The VIC-20 was designed as the heart of an entire home setup. Programs and games were loaded either from ROM modules inserted into the **cartridge slot** (this was how titles like **Omega Race**, **Jupiter Lander** or **Radar Rat Race** arrived), or from the **Datasette** cassette tape unit. Anyone who could afford the luxury connected a **VIC-1540** disk drive (later the 1541), which communicated over the IEC serial bus. The machine had one **joystick port** compatible with Atari connectors, so the vast majority of period joysticks worked. Through the user port and modules, it was also possible to connect the **VICMODEM**, one of the first affordable modems for the household, which opened the door to online services. The picture was sent to the television via a radio-frequency modulator, while newer and more professional monitors could also handle a composite signal. A key role was played by the **memory expansion modules** (3 KB, 8 KB, 16 KB), without which many more demanding programs could not be run at all. ### Models and variants The basic form of the VIC-20 remained essentially the same throughout its production run — a cream keyboard case in the style Commodore later repeated with the C64 model. The main variations were regional and dictated by the television standard: the North American version with the **6560 (NTSC)** chip and the European version with the **6561 (PAL)** chip, which differed in timing as well as resolution. In Germany and some European countries the machine was initially sold under the name **VC-20** (interpreted as VolksComputer), to avoid the unfortunate phonetic association of the German word "vic". In Japan it bore the designation **VIC-1001**. ### Clones and variants The VIC-20 was not cloned as massively as later platforms, partly because its narrow screen and small memory quickly pushed it aside in favor of the C64. Even so, a Czechoslovak user could come across it — in the 1980s they reached us through imports, though more as a rarity than a mass-available machine. The main trail of clones and unofficial variants in our region, however, was carried by other platforms: **Didaktik** as the domestic clone of the ZX Spectrum, and among game consoles the **Pegasus** as a NES famiclone. The VIC-20 remained in Czechoslovakia rather the domain of enthusiasts who came to it through foreign contacts. ### Today's scene Even after more than four decades, the VIC-20 retains a devoted community. It is reliably emulated by the **VICE** (Versatile Commodore Emulator) package, which today is practically the standard for all eight-bit Commodores. The machine is a popular target for homebrew creators: thanks to its simple hardware, it is a joy to program for, and every year new games, demos and musical compositions are created. Modern memory and flash modules are also appearing, replacing the period cartridges and making it easier to run software from SD cards. The VIC-20 thus remains living proof that a computer's timelessness does not rest on the amount of memory, but on how many people it opened the door to the world of programming and games for.

c64.history: When Commodore introduced the Commodore 64 in August 1982, few suspected that it was launching a machine that would enter the Guinness Book of Records as the best-selling computer model of all time. Estimates vary between 12 and 17 million units sold, and even the lower bound is a figure no other home computer came close to. The secret of its success lay not only in the technology but in the price — Commodore owned the chip maker MOS Technology, and so it could wage an aggressive price war that literally forced competitors like Texas Instruments out of the market. The C64 brought computing and gaming into millions of living rooms and became the uncrowned king of the European gaming scene of the eighties. While consoles ruled in the USA and Japan, in Europe people played on the "sixty-four". ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the computer was the eight-bit **MOS 6510** processor (a variant of the famous 6502) running at roughly 1 MHz and 64 kB of RAM, after which the computer was named. The picture was handled by the **VIC-II** graphics chip, which managed both text and bitmap modes, a palette of **16 colors** and hardware support for **eight sprites** (movable objects) per line. It was precisely the sprites and hardware smooth scrolling that enabled fluid arcade action, for which the ZX Spectrum, for instance, was short of breath. The demoscene moreover discovered a range of tricks to overcome the limits — sprite multiplexing for dozens of objects on screen, or opening up the top and bottom borders of the image. The real secret weapon, however, was the **SID** sound chip (officially the MOS 6581, later revised to the 8580). For 1982 it was an incredibly capable music processor with **three independent voices**, four waveforms (sawtooth, triangle, square/pulse and noise), ADSR envelopes, ring modulation and a programmable analog filter. The SID turned the C64 into a full-fledged musical instrument. Composers like **Rob Hubbard**, **Martin Galway** or **Chris Hülsbeck** (Turrican) coaxed music out of it that remains among the icons of game sound to this day. An entire genre of "SID music" grew up around the chip and lives on to this day. ### Connectivity and peripherals The C64 sat in the middle of a rich ecosystem of accessories. Games were loaded from the **Datasette** cassette recorder; faster was the **1541** disk drive for 5.25" floppy disks (notorious for its slowness as well as its characteristic clattering, which the demoscene learned to use as a rhythm). The computer had two ports for Atari-standard joysticks, so an ordinary paddle was all it took and multiplayer was ready to go. Among the other peripherals, mention should be made of the light pen via the joystick port, the single-button mouse and later the **1351 device** with a proper mouse for programs like GEOS. Connection to the television was handled by an RF modulator, while a better picture was offered by composite/S-Video output via a DIN connector. For the online world there were modems and services popular in their day; the user port and serial port allowed printers and other hardware to be hooked up. ### Models and revisions The original "breadbin" with its beige keyboard was replaced in 1986 by the **C64C** redesign in a flat, lighter form matching the 1541-II drive. Inside, newer revisions of the motherboard and the aforementioned newer 8580 sound chip were gradually added. Commodore also offered a portable variant, the **SX-64** — the first color "luggable" computer with a built-in monitor and disk drive. The line was continued by the more powerful **Commodore 128**, which could also run in a fully compatible C64 mode, so owners did not lose their game library. A more professional offshoot was represented by a business model with expanded memory, which however never caught on as a gaming machine. ### Clones and variants Commodore held the C64 architecture firmly in its own hands (it even owned chip production), so few direct unofficial clones came about — unlike, say, the ZX Spectrum, whose **Czechoslovak clone Didaktik** was made in Skalica, or the NES with its famiclones and the Polish Pegasus. The C64 thus spread in the Eastern Bloc mainly as gray-imported original units. Among the later official variants, the **C64 Games System (C64GS)** game console from 1990 is worth mentioning — a keyboardless computer intended only for cartridges, which however flopped on the market. Present times are recalled by the miniature replica **THEC64 Mini** and the full-fledged **THEC64** with a working keyboard, released by Retro Games Ltd. ### Today's scene The C64 remains an inexhaustible treasure trove. The benchmark of emulation is the open-source **VICE**, which runs practically everywhere — on PCs, phones and retro handhelds. The **demoscene** is inseparably linked with the C64, a community of programmers competing to see who can wring the impossible out of the hardware. This scene arose on the C64 and lives on to this day; its archive, **CSDb**, is a bottomless well. Modern homebrew that looks like console games is also being released — the flagship is **Sam's Journey** by Knights of Bytes. For a European, a return to the "sixty-four" is a little bit of a return home.

amiga.history: When Commodore unveiled the Amiga in 1985, it felt like a machine from another planet. At a time when the IBM PC was filling a green screen with characters and home eight-bits were scrapping over a handful of colours, the Amiga offered a full palette, smooth scrolling, multi-channel sampled sound and — something almost unheard of for its era — a genuine preemptive multitasking operating system. This was no accident. Behind the design stood the team around Jay Miner, the father of Atari's graphics chips, and at the heart of the computer sat a trio of specialised coprocessors that took work off the Motorola 68000 processor and turned the Amiga into a multimedia marvel. No wonder that a large part of the television graphics, music and video of the late 1980s and 1990s was created on it. For games this meant a leap into another league. **Shadow of the Beast**, with its multi-layered parallax backgrounds and dozens of colours, stunned the whole world with what a home computer could actually do. The Amiga became home to genres and brands we still know today: **Lemmings**, **Worms**, **Speedball 2**, the cult **Another World** and **Flashback** were born here, and above all **point & click adventures** flourished — Monkey Island and Beneath a Steel Sky belong to the golden age of the genre. Britain's Bitmap Brothers, with stylish titles such as Chaos Engine, became icons of the Amiga scene. In Europe the Amiga dominated much as the Commodore 64 had before it. ### Technology: graphics and sound The Amiga's secret lay in a set of custom chips named after women — **Agnus**, **Denise** and **Paula**. Agnus contained the Blitter for lightning-fast movement of blocks of graphics in memory and the Copper, a coprocessor able to change display settings in the middle of a frame (hence those gorgeous colour gradients in the sky). Denise handled sprites and image generation, Paula the sound and the disk drive. The standard resolution was 320×256 in PAL (or 320×200 in NTSC), with a palette of **4096 colours**, of which 32 could commonly be displayed at once. Special modes pushed the boundaries further: **HAM** (Hold-And-Modify) allowed all 4096 colours to be shown at once, while EHB (Extra Half-Brite) offered 64. The hardware sprites, Blitter and Copper together enabled that famous smooth scrolling and dozens of moving objects without loading the processor. The sound chip **Paula** was revolutionary: it offered **4 independent channels** with 8-bit **PCM samples** and stereo output (two channels left, two right). Instead of purely chip-based synthesis the Amiga thus played real recordings of instruments — which gave rise to the phenomenon of **tracker music** (the MOD format) and to the whole demoscene, which wrung wonders out of the chips. ### Connectivity and peripherals The Amiga was generously equipped for its time. Standard fare included two ports for joystick and mouse (the 500 model came with a mouse in the box — adventures and drawing programs would make no sense without it) and both serial and parallel ports. The **AV output** was crucial for games: composite video and separate stereo RCA jacks, so the sound from Paula rang out in full from a hi-fi system. The floppy drive used a proprietary **880 KB** format on a 3.5" disk. Available extras included a memory expansion card (typically into the so-called trapdoor slot beneath the computer, which expanded the A500 to 1 MB), external floppy drives, hard disks via controllers and accelerators with faster processors. Later models offered internal Zorro expansion slots. ### Models and revisions The Amiga line was broad. It began with the expensive professional **Amiga 1000** (1985), soon followed by two pillars: the home **Amiga 500** (1987) in the form of an all-in-one keyboard, which became the best-selling and most popular gaming model, and the desktop **Amiga 2000** with slots for professional deployment. At the turn of the decade came the **Amiga 3000** and, in 1992, the generation with the new **AGA chipset**: the affordable **Amiga 1200** (successor to the A500 with 256 colours from a palette of 16.8 million) and the powerful **Amiga 4000**. Commodore also tried a console, the **CDTV** (1991), and later the gaming **Amiga CD32** (1993) with a CD-ROM drive — the first 32-bit games console with CD on the market. Commercially it came too late; in 1994 Commodore went bankrupt. ### Clones and variants Because of its custom chips, the Amiga was not "cloned" as easily as the PC or the ZX Spectrum, so genuine hardware clones practically never appeared. There were, however, **emulation add-ons** in the opposite direction: cards and software that turned the Amiga into a PC (the Bridgeboard range) or a Macintosh (Emplant, ShapeShifter). In Czechoslovakia the Amiga was a worshipped yet expensive and hard-to-obtain imported machine — unlike the ZX Spectrum, whose domestic clone **Didaktik** was made by Skalica and Didaktik. Here the Amiga was bought mainly by graphic artists, musicians and television studios; it kept its gaming popularity mostly within the community of enthusiasts and at floppy-disk swap meets. ### Today's scene The Amiga has one of the most devoted communities of all, and emulation today is mature. On the PC **WinUAE** reigns, while on handhelds and Linux its variant **Amiberry** does. The emulator needs a **Kickstart ROM** (a system file from the original machine) and games are best sourced in the **WHDLoad** format, which loads them quickly and reliably from disk instead of the tedious swapping of floppies. Most classics targeted the A500 model, which also serves as the basis for the recommended settings; for the most demanding AGA titles some minor performance tuning is occasionally needed. But the scene is not just a museum — modern **homebrew** is being released too, for example stylish shmups such as **Reshoot**, new demo productions and even community hardware. The Amiga remains a symbol of "what might have been", a machine that was years ahead of its time.

atari-st.history: When Atari launched the ST range in the mid-1980s, a machine entered the fray that immediately shifted the balance of power among home computers. Under the leadership of Jack Tramiel, who came to Atari after leaving Commodore, a computer was born built around a powerful sixteen-bit processor, yet at a price an ordinary household could afford. The **520ST** model appeared in 1985, and according to the interpretation of the day the abbreviation ST referred to "Sixteen/Thirty-two" — the Motorola 68000 processor, which worked with a sixteen-bit data bus and an internal thirty-two-bit architecture. The Atari ST quickly became an icon of two worlds. In homes it served for games and drawing, while in the professional environment it became an unrivalled tool for musicians. It was the ST that opened the way to affordable computer music, and its legacy in recording studios outlived the brand itself by many years. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the computer was the **Motorola 68000** processor clocked at 8 MHz. Graphics were handled by the Shifter chip working together with the MMU controller and video logic. The ST offered three graphics modes: low resolution **320×200 pixels with 16 colours**, medium resolution **640×200 with 4 colours** and high monochrome **640×400**, which required a special monochrome monitor and ran at a higher refresh rate so the image did not flicker — this made the ST a pleasant machine for working with text and DTP. The colour palette was derived from the basic **512 colours** (three bits per RGB component). Unlike the competing Amiga, the ST lacked a dedicated blitter in its base version and had no hardware sprites, so the processor had to handle object movement and scrolling. This long disadvantaged the ST in arcade games, but programmers gradually refined tricks that squeezed the maximum out of the 68000. Sound was handled by the three-channel **Yamaha YM2149** chip (a variant of the General Instrument AY-3-8910), capable of three square-wave voices plus a noise generator. That was enough for games, but the ST's real strength was something else: the built-in **MIDI ports**. ### Connectivity and peripherals The ST's connector complement was exceptionally rich for its time. As standard it had **two MIDI ports** (In and Out/Thru) right on the motherboard — no other home computer of the period had them integrated. Thanks to this the ST became the heart of countless music studios, and software such as Cubase or Notator was created here or scored its first successes. The computer also offered a serial and a parallel port, a port for the floppy drive, a DMA interface for hard disks, two ports for joysticks and a mouse (the ST came with a mouse as standard) and an RF/monitor output. The floppy drive used **3.5-inch disks**, at first single-sided 360 KB, later double-sided 720 KB. ### Models and revisions The first **520ST** shipped with an external floppy drive and the TOS operating system on a floppy. Soon came the **520ST+** and, above all, the **520STFM** (1986), which integrated the floppy drive, the modulator (FM = Floppy + Modulator) and TOS directly in ROM. The **1040STF/STFM** version doubled the memory to 1 MB and became the most widespread model. For musicians and professionals the **Mega ST** was created, in a separate flat chassis with a detached keyboard and an optional blitter. The later **STE** (1989) brought fundamental improvements: a hardware blitter, **4096 colours** in the palette, hardware scrolling and stereo **8-bit DMA sound channels**. The pinnacle of the range was the more powerful **Mega STE** and the completely redesigned **Atari Falcon030** (1992) with a 68030 processor and a Motorola DSP56001 signal processor, which, however, already came too late. ### Clones and variants Direct clones of the Atari ST practically never appeared — the architecture around TOS and its custom chips could not be imitated as easily as with the simpler eight-bits. There were, however, professional add-ons and turbo cards from third parties, and in the segment of TOS replacements the alternative operating system **MagiC**. In Czechoslovakia the ST spread less than the eight-bit computers because of its high price and the technology embargo. While the ZX Spectrum had its domestic clone in the form of the **Didaktik** and eight-bit Ataris flowed in in large numbers, the sixteen-bit ST belonged rather to the dreamed-of imports for enthusiasts and musicians who appreciated its MIDI capabilities. The ST's true domain was Western Europe, especially Germany, where it also established itself in offices. ### Today's scene The Atari ST lives on thanks to advanced emulators. Among the most popular are **Hatari** (built on accurate hardware emulation) and **Steem SSE**, both of which can run period software and games from floppy disk images. The community around the ST remains active: new games are being made, demos on the demoscene, and hardware expansion cards such as **UltraSatan** or solutions that replace the floppy drive with flash memory. Classics like **Dungeon Master** — which on the ST became one of the best-selling titles of all — or the distinctive **Llamatron** and **Oids** by Jeff Minter still find their players today. The Atari ST thus remains not only a museum exhibit but a living platform with its own devoted scene.

game-watch.history: When we hold a powerful hybrid console in our hands today, or launch hundreds of games at once on a phone, it is easy to forget that the whole story of portable gaming began with a single calculator-like board with a clock. **Nintendo Game & Watch** (1980–1991) is exactly the place where it happened. It was devised by **Gunpei Yokoi** — according to the famous story, the idea came to him on a train while watching a bored businessman kill time by fiddling with a calculator. Yokoi combined a cheap LCD display, of the kind then used in calculators and digital watches, with a simple game and a clock function. This created pocket entertainment you could carry with you at any time — years before the arrival of the Game Boy. The magic lay in its simplicity. Each unit was single-purpose and contained just one hard-wired game. Yet the result was so addictive that Nintendo sold over **43 million** units. These humble devices financially saved the company and earned the money that later made the development of the NES possible. Their legacy, however, is even greater than the revenue: it was on the Donkey Kong version here that Yokoi first used the **cross-shaped controller (D-pad)** — an element that then became a standard on literally every game controller in the world. ### Technology: graphics and sound Game & Watch used no framebuffer or true moving graphics. The display was made up of **fixed LCD segments** — pre-drawn shapes of characters, objects and obstacles that only lit up and switched off. Animation therefore came about in the same way as with the indicators on digital watches: the game gradually turned the prepared shapes on and off in fixed positions, so movement was actually a switching between several drawn states. This has its charm — everything is sharp and perfectly legible — as well as its limits, because nothing that the manufacturer had not etched into the segments in advance could ever appear on the display. The image had no color; it was a monochrome LCD, where the impression of the environment and background was completed by a printed mask and colored backdrops directly on the panel. Sound was handled by a simple **piezoelectric buzzer** with a few tones — beeping on a jump, a catch or a loss. No melodies, no channels in the sense we know from gaming chips; the purpose was instant audio feedback, not music. The whole thing ran on a simple microcontroller and got by on button cell batteries for long months of operation. ### Connectivity and peripherals Here we have to be honest: Game & Watch was not a modular system with accessories. There was no link cable, no interchangeable modules and no memory cards — the game was fixed and self-contained. Nevertheless, several ingenious hardware ideas appeared across the range. The **Multi Screen** series versions (for example Oil Panic or Donkey Kong) had **two displays** in a fold-out case resembling a compact case — an arrangement that evidently inspired the Nintendo DS decades later. There was also the **Table Top** and **Panorama** series with a more colorful optical design and the **Crystal Screen** edition with a transparent panel. Most models also served as an alarm clock and a clock, which was a welcome added value at the time. No TV output, no modem — it was purely a standalone pocket thing. ### Models and revisions Game & Watch was not released as a single device, but as a whole family of **series** that differed in the construction of the case and in the controls. The main ones include **Silver** and **Gold** (the earliest simple titles such as Ball, Fire or Octopus), then **Wide Screen** with a larger display area, the aforementioned **Multi Screen** with two displays, **Table Top**, **Panorama**, **Super Color**, **Micro Vs. System** and **Crystal Screen**. A crucial milestone was the **Donkey Kong** version from the Multi Screen series, because it was on it that the cross-shaped D-pad debuted. As collector's items, the individual series are today valued very differently according to rarity and condition. ### Clones and variants The success of Game & Watch logically attracted crowds of imitators. All over the world, the Eastern Bloc not excepted, dozens of **LCD games of the same principle** arose from various manufacturers. The best-known domestic trace belongs to the **Soviet Union**: the local **Elektronika** series (for example the famous "Nu, pogodi!" with a wolf catching eggs) was essentially a not-particularly-licensed variation on the Game & Watch concept, and in Czechoslovakia and other Comecon countries it was an extraordinarily widespread and affordable pocket game. A whole generation remembers these "electronic games with eggs". It is, however, fair to add that these were related products of the same type, not direct copies of specific titles — which is why we class them as variants rather than official clones. ### Today's scene For today's retro gamer, Game & Watch is more of a historical curiosity and nostalgia than a source of deep gaming — they are simple reflex games for a few minutes. Emulation is possible, typically via **MAME** with accompanying artwork files (which fill in the printed background and the shape of the display), or via dedicated cores in RetroArch. The most pleasant way to get to know them today, though, is the **Game & Watch Gallery** compilation on the Game Boy, which offers both faithful original versions and modernized remakes with characters from the Mario cast. In 2020, moreover, Nintendo released the collector's devices **Game & Watch: Super Mario Bros.** for the anniversary and later **The Legend of Zelda**, thereby reminding a whole new generation of that little yellow marvel. Trying them out is worth it at least once — for you are holding in your hand the very roots of all portable gaming.

pico-8.history:
PICO-8 is something of an intruder in this whole retro hardware guide — because **there is no hardware**. It is a so-called **fantasy console**: a software environment from the New Zealand studio **Lexaloffle** (author **Joseph White**, alias zep), which came out in 2015. Instead of simulating some specific period machine, it invented its own, deliberately strict rules — few colors, low resolution, tiny memory — and thereby imitated the feeling of programming and playing on the 8-bits of the 1980s. But with modern comfort: you have the editor for code, graphics, sound and maps all in one window, and to run a game you just type `run`.

The magic lies precisely in those limitations. When you cannot have everything, you have to be inventive — and because it is so easy to start, an enormous and active community grew up around PICO-8. The most famous story is **Celeste**: it arose as a four-day project at a game jam in PICO-8 (under the name *Celeste Classic*) and later became one of the most acclaimed modern platformer hits. The original PICO-8 version is still playable for free today. This perfectly captures what PICO-8 is: nostalgia for an era that younger creators often did not even experience, recast into a creative playground.

### Technology: graphics and sound

Lexaloffle set the specifications firmly and programs cannot get around them. The image has a resolution of **128×128 pixels** and a fixed **16-color palette**. That palette is iconic — shades such as dark blue, salmon, yellow-green or light beige give games an instantly recognizable "pico" look. Newer versions added a so-called hidden palette of a further 16 colors, from which the basic sixteen can be remapped, so creators have a wider register at their disposal, albeit still only 16 colors at once.

Graphics are based on **8×8 pixel sprites**: there are 256 of them in the sprite sheet (plus another 128 shared with the map). The map for levels has a size of 128×32 tiles. Rendering runs at **30 or 60 frames per second** depending on whether you use the `_update()` or `_update60()` function.

Sound is handled by a **4-channel synthesizer**. The creator has 64 sound patterns at their disposal and can compose melodies and effects using several basic wave shapes (square, sawtooth, triangle, noise and others), which corresponds sonically to the era of chip music. The whole program — code in the **Lua** language, graphics, map and music — must fit within the limits of the "cartridge": around **32 kB** of compressed data for the code and fixed slots for graphics and sound. The cartridge itself is a technical treat: it is an ordinary **PNG file** of 160×205 pixels, in whose data the game is hidden. The image thus serves at once as an icon and as the carrier of the game.

### Connectivity and peripherals

Because it is software, the "peripherals" are control schemes, not physical boxes. PICO-8 reckons with **two virtual gamepads**, each with six buttons: a four-way cross plus two action buttons (internally marked O and X). This is deliberately minimalist — it maps easily onto a keyboard, a game pad and the buttons of retro handhelds. Some games also use a **mouse and keyboard**, if the author allows it in the cartridge.

An interesting feature is the so-called **splore** — a built-in browser through which you download and run cartridges directly in PICO-8 from the online BBS database. Games can also be exported as standalone HTML5 versions for a web browser, or as executable files for Windows, macOS and Linux. For local multiplayer, sharing gamepads on one machine is available.

### Clones and variants

Fantasy consoles have meanwhile grown into a whole genre, and PICO-8 is its flagship. The most significant relative is **TIC-80** (author Vadim Grigoruk, 2017) — open-source and free. It has a somewhat larger resolution of **240×136 pixels**, a full 16-color palette, supports more programming languages (Lua, JavaScript, MoonScript, Wren and others), and you browse games in it with the `surf` command. The library is smaller than PICO-8's, but the philosophy is identical.

Besides PICO-8, Lexaloffle also released **Voxatron** (a 3D fantasy console with voxels) and a standalone music instrument. Other projects in the genre include, for example, **LIKO-12** or **WASM-4**. Do not look here for a direct "Czech trace" — unlike the ZX Spectrum with the Didaktik or the NES with the Pegasus: fantasy consoles are a purely internet, global phenomenon of the last decade, and no period Eastern European clone of them exists.

### Today's scene

Here the situation is the reverse of the old classics — no emulation of the past, but living creation of the present. PICO-8 is a paid tool, but the resulting games are often free, and the community has produced thousands of them: from miniature metroidvanias through logic games to shooters. Besides *Celeste Classic*, it is worth trying, for example, **Dank Tomb**, **Just One Boss**, **Hexagravity**, **Subsurface** or **Pico Racer**.

For retro gamers with handhelds, the good news is that on Anbernics with the **H700** chip (and similar), PICO-8 runs via its own core and TIC-80 natively, though graphically more demanding cartridges may slow down a little on weaker cards. It is "new retro" in its purest form — games made today, but with the soul of the eighties. An ideal choice when you want to discover something beyond the period classics.

tic-80.history:
There is a whole category of gaming platforms that never got a plastic case, a chip, or a connector to plug into a TV — and yet they behave as if they had. **TIC-80** is one of them. It is a so-called **fantasy console**: a purely software environment that has voluntarily imposed on itself the strict limitations of the 8-bit era (few colors, low resolution, modest memory) in order to awaken in the creator the same feeling that programmers once had on machines like the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, or NES. It is not an emulation of any existing computer — it is an invented machine that could easily have come from 1985, but was actually born in 2017.

The author of TIC-80 is **Vadim Grigoruk** (working under the Nesbox label), and from the very beginning he conceived it as an **open-source and freely distributable** project. In doing so, he set himself apart from his more famous model, the commercial console **PICO-8** from the Lexaloffle studio (2015). While PICO-8 bets on being a closed system with finely tuned simplicity, TIC-80 offers a somewhat more generous resolution, open code, and a choice of several programming languages. The philosophy, however, is the same: limitation is creative fuel. Communities have grown up around both consoles, producing hundreds to thousands of small, clever games — platformers, puzzles, shooters, and miniature metroidvanias. It is "new retro" in its purest form: games made today, but with the soul of the eighties.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At the heart of TIC-80 is a screen with a resolution of **240×136 pixels** and a palette of **16 colors**. That is roughly twice the area compared to PICO-8 (128×128), and it is precisely this small generosity that gives creators a bit more room for detail and text. The palette is editable — fifteen colors plus one transparent one, so the author can recolor the default set to suit the game's taste. Graphics are made up of **8×8 pixel tiles and sprites**; the console has banks for both sprites and for the map, which are used to render the background and scrolling.

Sound is handled by **four channels** with programmable waveforms. TIC-80 offers a wavetable editor, so the creator can draw their own waveform shape, plus a sequencer for compositions and a set of effects. The result sounds typically "chiptune" — buzzy, raw, but surprisingly musical. The entire game, including code, graphics, maps, and music, is saved into a single **cartridge** (a `.tic` file), which nicely references the game modules of the era, only in the form of one small file.

### Programming and tools

This is where TIC-80 shines most. It is essentially an **entire development environment in a single window**: right inside the console you will find a code editor, a sprite editor, a map editor, a sound editor, and a music sequencer. You do not need to install anything else — you open the console and create.

A great advantage over PICO-8 is **support for multiple programming languages**. Alongside the default **Lua**, TIC-80 can also handle **MoonScript, JavaScript, Wren, Fennel, Squirrel**, and others (the set expanded over successive versions). You run a game with the `run` command, and you browse and play finished cartridges from the online database directly in the console via **`surf`** — you flip through the offering as if it were a jukebox and launch the titles right away. Games can also be exported to standalone executable files or to HTML, so they run in a browser too.

### Editions and versions

Because TIC-80 is not hardware, "models and revisions" here are replaced by **versions of the program** and distribution variants. The basic edition is free and open-source (the code is publicly available). At the same time, the author offers a paid **PRO** version, which mainly adds convenience for developers — for example, saving cartridges in a text form suitable for version control in Git, or more memory banks for larger projects. The engine itself is **multiplatform**: it runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, on the web via a browser, and thanks to its open code it has been ported to a number of other devices as well.

### Clones and variants

Talking about "clones" in the case of a fantasy console is a bit of a paradox — TIC-80 itself is, in a sense, an open answer to PICO-8. The whole genre of fantasy consoles is diverse today: alongside PICO-8 and TIC-80 there are, for example, **PixelVision8**, **WASM-4**, or **LIKO-12**, with LIKO-12 being directly designed as an open counterpart to PICO-8. Each chooses slightly different limitations and a different "period character."

For players on **Anbernic** devices and similar handhelds, it is important that, thanks to its open-source code, TIC-80 runs **natively** directly on the device (on chips like the H700 it runs smoothly, though with more demanding cartridges it may stutter on weaker cards). PICO-8 on the same machines is typically launched through a separate core. For retro gamers this means access to a huge stock of small, often entirely free games beyond the classics of the era.

### Today's scene

TIC-80 is in a way an "eternally living" platform — it is both a tool and an arcade at once. The community around it keeps releasing new cartridges, game jams are held, and the online game database keeps growing. Among the titles you might come across are, for example, **Bombic**, **ESCAPE**, **Sumico**, **RobomanIA**, **Bunny Maze**, **Knight's Quest**, **Tic Tank**, or the tongue-in-cheek **ASCII Game**. None of them cost a single penny in licenses, and you can play most of them in your browser within a few seconds. If you are drawn to the retro feeling but do not want to just play forty-year-old hits over and over, TIC-80 is the ideal gateway to a world where the eighties are being made anew — today, with love and open code.

ps2.history:
When Sony launched the PlayStation 2 in Japan in March 2000 (and in Europe and North America in the autumn of that same year), it built on the phenomenal success of the first PlayStation from the position of a self-assured leader. But this was no mere sequel — the PS2 became a cultural phenomenon that defined an entire generation and ultimately went down in history as **the best-selling gaming console of all time**, with more than 155 million units sold. The key to this triumph was not just performance, but a brilliant strategic decision: the PS2 could play back **DVD films**. At a time when standalone DVD players were expensive, plenty of households bought a PS2 essentially as a cheap player — and the game library then won them over on its own.

Sony also cleverly bet on continuity. The PS2 was **backward compatible with PlayStation 1 games**, so a new owner did not lose their existing collection. Thanks to its enormous installed base, strong publisher support and a library of thousands of titles, the PS2 stayed on the market for an incredibly long time — official production only ended in **2013**, a full thirteen years after its debut.

### Technology: graphics and sound

The heart of the console was the famous Emotion Engine processor, a 128-bit CPU clocked at just under 300 MHz with vector units (VU0 and VU1) optimised for physics calculations and 3D geometry transformations. Rendering was handled by the Graphics Synthesizer chip with extremely fast embedded video memory, which relied more on enormous fillrate than on the modern effects of the day. The console had **32 MB of main RDRAM memory**, which was relatively little in the context of the era and forced developers into ingenious optimisation.

The PS2's architecture was notoriously **difficult to program** — squeezing the most out of it took years. While early titles sometimes looked awkward, late games like **God of War II**, **Shadow of the Colossus** and **Gran Turismo 4** showed what truly lay dormant inside the machine. Sound was handled by the dedicated SPU2 processor with 48 voices and support for surround sound, allowing games to offer rich orchestral soundtracks and Dolby effects.

### Peripherals and accessories

The console shipped with a reworked DualShock 2 controller — outwardly almost identical to the original, but with **analogue pressure-sensitive buttons**, which in a number of games brought more nuanced control of the throttle or the force of a press. An outright revolution was the EyeToy camera, which captured the player and drew their movements directly into the on-screen action; it thus anticipated the era of motion controls by several years.

There was also a Network Adapter card for online play (already integrated in later Slim models), dance mats for the Dance Dance Revolution series, microphones for SingStar, plastic guitars for Guitar Hero, buzzers for the Buzz! quizzes and countless steering wheels. Saving was handled by **memory cards** with a capacity of 8 MB.

### Models and revisions

The original **"fat" PS2** was a hefty black box with a vertically oriented stand and a front slot for memory cards. A key feature was the **expansion bay** on the rear, into which a **hard drive (HDD)** could be installed — used by the legendary version of **Final Fantasy XI** or the game SOCOM, and above all it enabled the installation of games via homebrew.

In 2004 came the dramatically shrunk PS2 Slimline (Slim) revision, thin as a book, with an integrated network adapter but without an internal bay for an HDD. It was the Slim that became a long-term bestseller and continued selling well into the PlayStation 3 era.

### Significance and legacy

The PlayStation 2 is, without exaggeration, **the most successful and influential console in history**. Its huge library covers absolutely every genre — from monumental JRPGs through brutal action games, racers and fighters to artistic gems like **ICO** and **Okami**. It was on the PS2 that a number of series were born which to this day form the backbone of the games industry: God of War, Kingdom Hearts, Devil May Cry, Ratchet & Clank and Jak and Daxter.

For today's retro gamers there is great news in the mature PCSX2 emulator, which on a powerful PC handles the vast majority of the library at higher resolution. The PS2 thus remains a living treasure trove — perhaps the largest any single console has ever offered.

gamecube.history:
When Nintendo launched the GameCube in Japan and North America in 2001 (and in Europe in 2002), it introduced its most unconventional home console ever. A small purple cube with a **carrying handle** looked more like a toy than a next-generation gaming machine — and that was exactly what Nintendo wanted. After the commercially lukewarm Nintendo 64, the company decided not to follow the multimedia-hub path taken by Sony, but to offer clean, powerful and above all **easy-to-program** gaming hardware focused on one thing: great games. The GameCube was also Nintendo's first home console to abandon cartridges and switch to optical media.

The console's launch was decent, but it was clear from the start that the fight against the PlayStation 2 phenomenon could not be won. Sony had an enormous head start, a strong brand and the trump card of DVD film playback. Against that, the GameCube offered quality, not quantity — and although it sold "only" around **21.7 million units** (behind both the PS2 and the Xbox), it left behind one of the most concentrated and beloved libraries of all. It was here that **Luigi's Mansion**, **Pikmin**, **Metroid Prime** and the superb **The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker** first shone.

### Technology: graphics and sound

The heart of the GameCube was the 32-bit IBM PowerPC "Gekko" processor clocked at 485 MHz, built on the proven PowerPC architecture and supplemented with custom instructions for floating-point work. Graphics were handled by the ATI "Flipper" chip running at 162 MHz, developed in collaboration with ArtX — a remarkably efficient GPU for its time with an excellent performance-to-price ratio.

The memory architecture was unusual: the console had **24 MB of fast main memory (1T-SRAM)** supplemented by another **16 MB** of slower memory for auxiliary tasks. The result was hardware that in real games often surpassed the PS2 in texture cleanliness and frame-rate stability. Titles like **Rogue Squadron II** or **Resident Evil** showed what Flipper could do — and **Star Wars Rogue Leader** was among the most technically impressive games of the entire generation.

### Peripherals and accessories

The most famous accessory was the wireless WaveBird controller — a revolutionary radio-frequency pad for its time with excellent range and long battery life, which to this day counts as one of the best wireless controllers in history. The wired GameCube controller itself, with its distinctive large green **A** button and analogue triggers, gained cult status and is still used today at Super Smash Bros. tournaments.

Nintendo also bet on linking with the Game Boy Advance handheld: via a special Link Cable, the GBA functioned as a second screen or an additional controller in games like **Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles** or **Four Swords Adventures**. The Game Boy Player add-on, attached to the bottom of the console, additionally allowed the entire Game Boy, GBC and GBA library to be played directly on the television. There were also exotic peripherals like the bongos for **Donkey Konga**.

### Models and revisions

The GameCube's hardware remained fairly uniform throughout its life. The console came in several colours — besides the iconic **purple (Indigo)**, also in black, silver (Platinum) and in Japan, for instance, in orange (Spice). The most notable revision was the DOL-101 model, which compared to the original DOL-001 omitted the port for the digital AV output (Digital AV Out), thereby ending the possibility of connection via a component cable — which is why these cables and early models are today prized collector's items.

An interesting side note was the Panasonic Q, a Japanese hybrid version combining the GameCube with a full-fledged DVD player in a metal case. It thus responded to one of the main criticisms of the console — the use of **proprietary 8 cm miniDVD discs** with a capacity of only **1.5 GB, which moreover could not play back DVD films**, a noticeable disadvantage compared to the PS2.

### Significance and legacy

The GameCube never won the sales war, but in hindsight it is one of Nintendo's most highly rated consoles. Production ended in **2007** and the baton was taken up by the immensely successful Wii, which incidentally retained backward compatibility with GameCube games and controllers. The console's legacy lives on not only in remasters (**Wind Waker HD**, **Twilight Princess HD**, **Metroid Prime Remastered**), but also in the community around the Dolphin emulator, which handles GameCube titles superbly in high resolution.

For collectors and retro gamers alike, the purple cube remains a symbol of an era when Nintendo went against the current and bet solely on gameplay. Compact, reliable and packed with jewels — the GameCube is proof that the winner of a generation need not necessarily be the one who sells the most units.

xbox.history:
When Microsoft launched its first gaming machine in North America in November 2001 (and in the spring of 2002 in Europe and Japan), it was a minor earthquake. The software giant from Redmond, until then known mainly for Windows, decided to enter the console world ruled by Sony and Nintendo — and it did so its own way. Instead of an exotic, custom-tailored architecture, it built the **Xbox essentially as a powerful PC in a black case**: with an Intel processor, NVIDIA graphics and a system derived from Windows. This "brute force" approach paid off — the Xbox became the technically strongest console of its generation and laid the foundations of a brand that to this day belongs among the three biggest.

The project originally began as the "DirectX Box", hence its later name. The goal was to bring PC developers under one roof and offer them a familiar, easy-to-program environment. The Xbox never really caught on in Japan, but in North America and Europe it built a strong position. In total it sold roughly **24 million units** — a more than respectable result for a newcomer to the field.

### Technology: graphics and sound

Under the Xbox's hood beat a heart from the computer world. Computation was handled by a **modified Intel Pentium III processor** clocked at **733 MHz**, complemented by the NVIDIA NV2A graphics chip — a relative of the GeForce 3 series cards of the time. The console had **64 MB of shared DDR memory**, a generous portion for its era, which allowed titles rich textures, dynamic lighting and advanced shaders.

The real revolution, however, was the **built-in hard drive** — the Xbox was the very first console with an HDD as standard equipment. It served to save games without memory cards, to cache data for faster loading and to rip music from CDs directly into games. The optical drive already handled **DVDs**, so with a remote control connected the Xbox also functioned as a full-fledged film player. Sound supported surround **Dolby Digital 5.1**, which made the console an appealing piece of kit for home cinema too.

### Xbox Live and online play

The original Xbox's greatest legacy, though, lies not in silicon but in the network. In the autumn of **2002**, Microsoft launched the Xbox Live service — and forever changed the idea of online console gaming. While the competition relied on clumsy solutions, Xbox Live brought a unified system with a **persistent gamertag**, a friends list, voice chat and matchmaking, all built on a broadband connection. For the first time, online gaming on the couch was truly comfortable and well thought out.

The phenomenon that raised the service to the heavens was **Halo 2** in 2004. Its multiplayer over Xbox Live literally defined online console shooters and for years glued millions of players to their screens. The subscription model and sophisticated infrastructure then became the template that the whole industry copies to this day.

### Peripherals and controllers

The original Xbox controller went down in history under the nickname **"Duke"** — a giant, heavy controller that became a target of ridicule because of its dimensions, which did not suit smaller hands (and the Japanese market in particular). Microsoft quickly responded to the criticism and introduced the smaller, more ergonomic Controller S, which subsequently became the standard and inspired even the later Xbox 360 controllers.

A range of other accessories was available too: a **DVD remote control** with an IR receiver for watching films, memory cards for transferring saves between consoles, or a headset for Xbox Live. Also characteristic were the controller ports, which were based on the USB standard — just with their own connector.

### Significance and legacy

Although the original Xbox could not match the PlayStation 2 in unit sales in a head-to-head contest, its significance cannot be measured in numbers alone. It **established Microsoft as a serious player** in the console field, brought the concept of modern online gaming and raised brands that endure to this day — above all **Halo**, one of the most important gaming series of all. The Xbox thereby paved the way for its immensely successful successor, the **Xbox 360**.

Production of the console ended in **2008/2009**. But the machine's legacy lives on: many of its games received **backward compatibility** on Microsoft's later consoles, so classics like Halo, Fable or Knights of the Old Republic are available to modern players as well. For collectors and enthusiasts, the first Xbox remains a symbol of a bold entry that paid off — and a machine with an unexpectedly rich and, to this day, prized library.

xbox-360.history:
When Microsoft unleashed the Xbox 360 upon the world in November 2005, it instantly put the competition a generation behind — it was, after all, the very first seventh-generation console, beating Sony and the PlayStation 3 to market by a full year. After the original Xbox's not entirely convincing debut, Microsoft went for a decisive strike: a technically ambitious machine built around full HD resolution, a polished online service, and the bold idea that gaming should be a social experience connected over the internet. The bet paid off — the Xbox 360 became one of the most influential machines of its era and defined what online console gaming still looks like today.

The launch was accompanied by shortages on store shelves, but the library quickly filled up with titles like **Perfect Dark Zero** and **Project Gotham Racing 3**, and a year later **Gears of War** arrived, which together with **Halo 3** (2007) made the Xbox 360 the home platform for a whole generation of third- and first-person shooters. Microsoft managed to attract both exclusives and multiplatform titles at the same time, and for most of the generation the Xbox 360 version was the technical reference — the platform developers targeted first.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At the heart of the console was the triple-core **IBM PowerPC "Xenon"** processor clocked at 3.2 GHz, with each core handling two hardware threads — six simultaneous computation threads in total. Graphics were handled by the **ATI "Xenos"** chip, designed together with ATI (later absorbed into AMD), which was one of the first in the world to use a **unified shader architecture** — shaders capable of computing both vertices and pixels as needed, instead of fixed, separate units. Xenos also included 10 MB of fast eDRAM memory directly on the chip, which made antialiasing easier without a performance hit.

The console had 512 MB of shared memory and was built primarily for the HD era: it supported 720p and 1080i output, and later 1080p as well, which in 2005 was a major leap over the standard-definition resolution of the previous generation. Sound was handled via multichannel Dolby Digital output, later supplemented by formats like Dolby TrueHD in select titles. An HDMI port only appeared in later revisions — the first models relied on component and composite video.

### Xbox Live, Achievements, and online

If the Xbox 360 has one truly groundbreaking contribution, it's turning **Xbox Live** into the standard against which online console gaming is still measured today. A unified Gamertag account, a clear friends list across every game, integrated voice chat, simple matchmaking, and downloadable content through the **Xbox Live Marketplace** — all of it worked smoothly and consistently no matter which game you were playing.

A key innovation was **Achievements** — points (Gamerscore) awarded for completing specific in-game challenges, visible on your profile and comparable with friends. This seemingly minor idea proved extraordinarily addictive and is now a standard feature of practically every gaming platform, from PlayStation to Steam to mobile games. Xbox Live Arcade, meanwhile, opened up space for smaller, cheaper, and more experimental games, becoming a forerunner of today's digital distribution.

### Peripherals (Kinect, controllers)

The standard Xbox 360 controller became the reference template for game pads for years to come, thanks to its comfortable grip and asymmetrical stick layout. Both wireless and wired versions were available, along with special editions tied to specific games and a range of accessories — from steering wheels to arcade sticks to headsets for voice chat.

The biggest peripheral event came in November 2010 with **Kinect** — a motion sensor with a camera and microphone that could track full-body movement and recognize voice commands without needing to hold a controller. Kinect sold in the millions and even briefly made it into the Guinness Book of Records as the fastest-selling consumer electronics device. Although it never delivered the promised revolution at the core of gaming in the long run, it opened the door to fitness and family party games and pointed the way that other platforms would later follow.

### Models, revisions, and the Red Ring of Death

Over its lifetime, the Xbox 360 went through several hardware waves. The first generation offered the **Core** variant (no hard drive, just the basics) and **Premium/Pro** (with a hard drive and wireless controller); in 2007 the premium **Elite** model arrived with a larger drive and HDMI output. In 2010 came the completely redesigned **Xbox 360 S (Slim)** — quieter, smaller, with built-in Wi-Fi and a Kinect port, followed in 2013 by the stripped-down **Xbox 360 E**, styled after the by-then-released Xbox One.

The first generation of consoles, however, also earned a dark chapter in history: the notorious **Red Ring of Death** — three flashing red lights around the power button signaling a fatal hardware failure. The problem was caused by chips overheating due to inadequate cooling and lead-free solder that cracked under thermal cycling. The failure rate was so high that Microsoft extended the warranty to three years and set aside over a billion dollars for repairs. Later revisions (especially the Slim model, with a redesigned, cooler-running chipset) essentially solved the problem.

### Significance and legacy

Over its lifetime the Xbox 360 sold roughly 84 million units, and production officially ended in 2016, after a decade of uninterrupted games and updates. Its true legacy, though, isn't just the sales figures — it's a platform that normalized online multiplayer with voice chat, Achievements as a universal measure of gaming progress, and digital distribution as a full-fledged alternative to physical media. Today it's a popular target for both emulation (Xenia) and collecting, and many of its generation-defining classics, from Mass Effect to Halo, remain genre-reference titles to this day.

ps3.history:
When Sony launched the PlayStation 3 in Japan and North America in November 2006 (and a year later, in March 2007, in Europe too), it was building on its predecessor's success with the feeling that it could afford almost anything. The result was a machine full of bold decisions — its own exotic processor, a built-in Blu-ray drive, a free online network — but also a high price that made the PS3 the most expensive console of its generation. The base model cost $499 in the US, the better-equipped version $599, and Sony lost money on every unit for a long time. The high price combined with the inaccessible architecture gave the PS3 a slow start, with the Xbox 360 holding almost a year's head start. Even so, the PS3 eventually grew into one of the most successful consoles in history, with a rich library of exclusives.

### Technology: Cell and graphics

At the heart of the PlayStation 3 was the **Cell Broadband Engine** processor, developed jointly by Sony, Toshiba, and IBM. It was a radically different architecture: a single main **PPE** core based on PowerPC was supplemented by eight secondary **SPE (Synergistic Processing Elements)** units for massively parallel computation. Theoretically enormous performance, but in practice the Cell placed unusual demands on developers — code had to be manually split across the units, and as a result many early multiplatform games ran worse on PS3 than on the Xbox 360.

Graphics were handled by Nvidia's **RSX** chip, derived from the GeForce 7 series, with 256 MB of dedicated memory. It communicated with the Cell over a fast bus, and together they could render scenes at up to 1080p — one of the first consoles with full HD support. Mastering the combination of both architectures took time, so sweeping titles like **Uncharted 2**, **The Last of Us**, and **God of War III** only appeared later.

### Blu-ray and multimedia

One of Sony's most significant moves was building a **Blu-ray Disc** drive into every console. This made the PS3 the cheapest Blu-ray player on the market and unwittingly gave it a role in the **format war against HD DVD** — thanks to the PlayStation's huge installed base, Sony's format won out, and the competing HD DVD (backed by Microsoft, among others) disappeared from the market in 2008. Blu-ray also solved a practical problem: PS3 games took up tens of gigabytes, more than DVD could handle. The console also played music, photos, and video, serving as the living room's media hub.

### PlayStation Network and online

The PS3 also introduced **PlayStation Network (PSN)** — a service that, unlike Xbox Live, Sony offered **free** for online gaming. That was a strong argument for many players, even though PSN long lagged behind the competition in convenience and stability (the most painful moment was the 2011 security breach, which took the network down for weeks). Over time it grew to include the **PlayStation Plus** subscription and a digital store, and became the foundation for subsequent console generations.

### Models and revisions (fat, Slim, Super Slim)

The first generation, today nicknamed the **'fat' PS3**, came in versions based on drive capacity — the priciest models had backward compatibility with the PlayStation 2, initially hardware-based, later software-only, and eventually dropped entirely on cheaper models. In 2009 came the smaller, quieter **PS3 Slim** with reduced power draw and price, followed in 2012 by the even more compact **PS3 Super Slim** with a sliding drive cover. The redesigns helped Sony cut costs enough to turn money-losing hardware into a profitable product.

### Significance and legacy

Despite its slow start, the PlayStation 3 ultimately sold approximately **87 million units** and became home to games that still rank among the most significant in the medium's history — from **Metal Gear Solid 4** and **Demon's Souls**, which laid the foundation for the soulslike genre, to **Journey** and **Heavy Rain**, up to the crowning achievements of Naughty Dog. The Cell's demanding architecture may have slowed the PS3 at launch, but it also forced developers to find unexpectedly efficient solutions. Production wound down gradually between 2015 and 2017. Today the PS3 is one of the toughest targets for emulation out there — the combination of Cell and RSX is difficult to replicate (though the RPCS3 project keeps making remarkable progress), so for many players the original remains the most reliable way to play the classics.

ps4.history:
When Sony launched the PlayStation 4 in November 2013, it did exactly the opposite of what it had done a generation earlier with the PlayStation 3. Instead of the exotic Cell architecture, which had drained developers' blood for years, the company bet on **standard PC hardware** built around an x86-64 processor, making clear that its priority would be easy development and strong third-party support. It was the move of the century — the PS4 became the dominant console of the eighth generation, and with an estimated **over 117 million units sold**, it ranks among the most successful gaming machines in history, second only to the PlayStation 2.

Sony took developer criticism from the PS3 era to heart and delivered a powerful yet, above all, **predictable** machine. While the Xbox One bet on multimedia ambitions and controversial policies, the PS4 presented itself primarily as a console for gaming. A strong lineup of exclusives, an aggressive price, and developer trust made it the console the vast majority of players of this generation took home.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At the heart of the PS4 was an **AMD APU codenamed "Jaguar"** — an eight-core x86-64 processor paired with a graphics core based on the **AMD Radeon (GCN)** architecture.
