It was a single-chip solution combining CPU and GPU on the same silicon, complemented by **8 GB of GDDR5 memory** shared between the processor and the graphics. This unified memory eliminated the bottlenecks known from the previous generation and gave developers greater freedom.

Graphics performance amounted to roughly 1.84 teraflops, enough for a stable **1080p** in most titles. An architecture close to a regular PC fundamentally simplified porting games between platforms, a key advantage throughout the machine's entire life cycle.

### DualShock 4 and peripherals

The **DualShock 4** controller marked the most significant redesign in the history of the lineup since the original PlayStation. Its most striking novelty was the **touchpad** on the front, which developers used for everything from menu gestures to unconventional mechanics. Beneath it sat the **Share** button, allowing screenshots and videos to be shared to social networks with a single press.

The controller also gained a **light bar**, used to identify players as well as a gameplay element reacting to on-screen events, and combined with the **PlayStation Camera** it also enabled motion tracking. The camera and DualShock 4 formed the foundation for the **PlayStation VR** headset, which brought virtual reality into homes on a mainstream scale.

### PSN, online, and services

A major, if controversial, milestone was making online play a paid feature through **PlayStation Plus** — unlike the PS3, multiplayer online required a subscription. In return, subscribers received free monthly games, store discounts, and cloud storage.

The **PSN** network grew over the PS4's lifetime into one of the largest gaming platforms in the world, with features like streaming to Twitch/YouTube and gradually expanding cross-play. The **PlayStation Now** service offered streaming of older games without the need to download them, foreshadowing the direction the gaming industry would start to take.

### Models and revisions (Slim, PS4 Pro)

The original PS4 model was slimmed down in 2016 into the **PS4 Slim** — a smaller, more energy-efficient case with the same performance. That same year, however, brought a far more important novelty: the **PlayStation 4 Pro**.

The PS4 Pro offered significantly boosted graphics (around 4.2 teraflops), enabling gameplay in **4K resolution** (often via checkerboard rendering) and support for **HDR**. It was the first example of a so-called mid-generation console — Sony did not force players to buy new hardware, only offering an upgrade for those who wanted better graphics, while games remained compatible across models. Microsoft later adopted the concept with the Xbox One X.

### Significance and legacy

The PlayStation 4 went down in history as the console that **corrected its predecessor's mistakes** and showed that developer-friendliness is valued more than exotic performance on paper. A strong lineup of exclusive titles, openness toward the indie scene, and a smart business strategy made it the winner of the eighth console generation. Today the PS4 is gradually passing into the hands of emulators and retro enthusiasts, but in significance it stands alongside the PlayStation 2 as one of the pillars of Sony's dominance in the home console market.

xbox-one.history:
When Microsoft unveiled the Xbox One in May 2013, a confident answer to the successful Xbox 360 was expected. Instead came one of the most unfortunate reveals in the history of the gaming industry. The company chose to present the console as a universal "all-in-one" living-room entertainment hub — emphasizing television, movies, and voice control via **Kinect** — while games briefly seemed like an afterthought. Rival Sony reacted cleverly: the PlayStation 4 offered a simpler, cheaper, and more player-friendly solution, kicking off one of the most decisive generational victories in console history.

Still, the Xbox One ultimately wasn't a flop — it merely lost the battle for first place. Microsoft managed a sharp course correction after a disastrous start, listened to the community, and gradually built the console into a platform that still defines today's Xbox Game Pass and the philosophy of services layered over hardware.

### A controversial start (DRM, Kinect)

Xbox One inflicted the biggest blow on itself, even before launch. Microsoft planned an **always-online DRM** system — the console was to connect to the internet at least once every 24 hours to verify licenses, and games could only be installed and resold under restrictions resembling digital distribution. On top of that came the requirement to have the **Kinect** sensor connected and switched on (it was included with every unit), which watched the living room via camera and microphone — sparking a wave of privacy concerns. A price of 499 dollars, a hundred dollars higher than the PS4, only underscored the whole package.

The reaction from players and journalists was so strong that Microsoft capitulated within a few weeks: in June 2013 it announced the cancellation of the always-online requirement, the removal of restrictions on sharing and reselling games, and made the Kinect detachable. The reputational damage, however, had already been done, and the Xbox One entered the generation with a lost head start it never fully made up.

### Technology: graphics and sound

Microsoft built the Xbox One around its own AMD APU with an **x86-64** architecture, containing eight **Jaguar** cores and a graphics core from the **Radeon** (GCN) family. It was the same philosophy as the PlayStation 4 — a unified, PC-like architecture that finally made it easier for developers to port games between platforms and to computers.

The difference lay in memory: while the PS4 bet on faster 8 GB of GDDR5 shared between CPU and GPU, the Xbox One used 8 GB of slower **DDR3** supplemented by 32 MB of fast **ESRAM** cache meant to compensate for the bandwidth shortfall. In practice, this meant the Xbox One had, proportionally, lower net graphics performance than the competition, and many multiplatform games ran on the PS4 at a higher resolution or higher frame rate — a gap that journalists and players tracked title after title throughout the entire generation.

### Xbox Live, backward compatibility, and Game Pass

Where the Xbox One lost on paper specs, it made up for it in services. **Xbox Live** remained the generation's most advanced online infrastructure, but the real turnaround came with **backward compatibility** — Microsoft gradually enabled playback of hundreds of games from the **Xbox 360** and even the original **Xbox**, making the Xbox One the only console able to play titles from three generations back. It was a technically demanding hardware-level emulation project that earned praise even from players who otherwise remained skeptical of Microsoft.

An even bigger impact came in 2017 with the launch of **Xbox Game Pass** — a subscription that, for a monthly fee, unlocked a growing library of downloadable games, including Microsoft's new releases on day one. This model, later expanded to PC and cloud, became the core of the company's entire strategy and is still regarded today as one of the most significant moves in modern console history.

### Models and revisions (S, One X)

The base Xbox One from November 2013 got a successor in 2016, the **Xbox One S** — smaller, quieter, without an external power brick, supporting **4K video and HDR** for movies and streaming, even though it still rendered games at a lower resolution.

The true technical peak of the generation was the **Xbox One X** of 2017, which Microsoft marketed as "the most powerful console in the world." It brought a significantly stronger GPU, 12 GB of GDDR5 memory, and the ability to render a number of games in genuine **4K resolution**, for the first time in the generation surpassing the PlayStation 4 Pro in raw hardware terms. It was a smaller but enthusiast-cherished machine that showed Microsoft had learned from the mistakes of 2013.

### Significance and legacy

The Xbox One ultimately sold roughly **50 million units** — noticeably fewer than the PlayStation 4's more than 117 million — and in console history remains a reminder of how costly a poorly handled product reveal can be. At the same time, it's also an example of a turnaround: a company that in 2013 nearly lost the trust of its own community laid, in the years that followed, the foundations for what Xbox is today — a platform built on subscriptions, backward compatibility, and cross-device availability rather than the raw power of a single piece of hardware. The Game Pass and cross-generation gaming philosophy that the Xbox One generation kicked off leads directly to today's Xbox Series X/S and defines how Microsoft positions itself in the console market to this day.

switch.history:
When Nintendo launched the Switch in March 2017, it bet on a concept that no one had ever fully pulled off before: a console that is both a home system hooked up to the TV and a full-fledged handheld in your pocket. After the commercial flop of the Wii U, it was a huge gamble — and it paid off completely. The Switch launched alongside **The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild**, a title that instantly showed what the hybrid design could do and became one of the most acclaimed games of all time. Within a few years, the Switch became one of the most successful consoles in gaming history, with sales exceeding 140 million units.

### Hybrid concept (dock, handheld, tabletop)

The foundation of the whole success was a simple yet brilliant idea: one device, three ways to play. In **docked mode**, the tablet slots into a dock connected to the television, and both the picture and performance scale up for the big screen. Pull it out of the dock and the game transitions without interruption to the built-in display, turning the Switch into a classic **handheld**. The third option is **tabletop mode** — the console stands on its own flip-out kickstand, the controllers detach, and two people can play directly off the display without a TV. It was this flexibility, not raw power, that defined the entire generation.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At the heart of the Switch is the **NVIDIA Tegra X1** chip with an **ARM** architecture (a quad-core ARM Cortex-A57 CPU and graphics based on the Maxwell architecture), paired with 4 GB of RAM. Performance scales dynamically depending on the mode — docked, the chip runs at a higher clock and games typically target 900p to 1080p, while in portable mode the clock drops to save battery and resolution falls to match the 720p display. This scalability made it possible to bring even graphically demanding titles like **The Witcher 3** or **DOOM** to the system, though often at the cost of compromises in frame rate and detail.

Audio is handled through standard stereo speakers built into the console body, with output via a 3.5mm jack or HDMI when docked. Built-in storage (32 GB on the base model, later 64 GB) is supplemented by a microSD card slot, since games are distributed both physically on **cartridges** and digitally through the eShop.

### Joy-Cons and peripherals

The Switch's most distinctive feature is its detachable **Joy-Con** controllers, which clip onto the sides of the tablet via rails, or can be separated to function as a pair of independent mini controllers — ideal for spontaneous multiplayer without any extra hardware. Each Joy-Con includes **HD rumble** (finely graded vibration feedback capable of simulating things like dice rattling in a cup) and **motion sensors** used in games like 1-2-Switch or Mario Kart 8 Deluxe. The right Joy-Con additionally carries an infrared camera. For television play there's the classic **Pro Controller**. Nintendo also built an experimental peripheral line around the hardware called **Nintendo Labo** — cardboard construction kits that the Joy-Cons slot into, turning the console into a fishing rod, a robot, or a motorbike using infrared sensing and vibration.

### Models and revisions (Lite, OLED)

The original model stayed on sale unchanged for several years, later receiving only quieter cooling and a slightly longer battery life. In 2019 came the **Nintendo Switch Lite** — a lightened, purely handheld version with no docking capability and fixed-in-place controllers, aimed at players who don't use TV mode. Then in 2021 came the **OLED model**: a larger 7-inch screen with richer colors and deeper blacks, an improved kickstand, and steadier battery life, while the chip's raw performance stayed unchanged. All three variants are mutually compatible with the same game library and peripherals.

### Significance and legacy

The Switch conclusively proved that the hybrid approach isn't a compromise but a full-fledged design philosophy — a console that goes anywhere with the player while still offering an experience comparable to sitting in front of the TV. The combination of a strong lineup of exclusives, the social potential of the Joy-Cons, and clever performance scalability made it one of the best-selling platforms of all time and a blueprint that other portable and hybrid systems are now modeled after.

ps-vita.history:
When Sony unveiled the PlayStation Vita on December 17, 2011 in Japan (and in February 2012 in western markets), it looked like a dream come true for anyone who'd ever complained about the PSP's missing second stick. The Vita was an almost absurdly well-built piece of hardware: a gorgeous OLED display, a quad-core processor, and touch controls on both the front and back. It was also **Sony's last major attempt at a classic handheld** — and although it's technically one of the best-designed pocket machines in history, commercially it fell flat.

There were several reasons. Standing directly against the Vita was **Nintendo's 3DS**, with cheaper hardware, stronger brands, and a year's head start. But a far bigger enemy that nobody had counted on was **smartphones**. By 2012, almost everyone already had a device in their pocket that could run games for free or for pocket change, and the market for expensive dedicated handhelds began to collapse. On top of that, Sony largely stopped supporting the Vita with its own big-name titles after a few years and let it survive on Japanese games and the indie scene.

And yet — or perhaps precisely because of that — the Vita has earned a cult reputation today. Whoever bought one back then rarely regretted it.

### Hardware: graphics and sound

At the Vita's heart sits a **quad-core ARM Cortex-A9**, paired with **PowerVR SGX543MP4+** graphics — the same quad-core variant of the chip that powered top-end tablets at the time. The system has **512 MB of RAM plus another 128 MB of VRAM**, which in 2012 made it the most powerful handheld gaming machine on the market by a wide margin.

The pride of the original model is its **5" OLED display at 960 × 544 pixels**, exactly four times the resolution of the PSP. The combination of absolute black and saturated colors was genuinely shocking at the time and still ranks among the most beautiful things you can look at on a handheld console today. The later PCH-2000 model switched to LCD, which is the one thing fans have never forgiven it for.

Control-wise, the console was revolutionary above all thanks to its **two analog sticks** — the first time in the history of a Sony handheld. Alongside them, the Vita offers a **front touchscreen as well as a rear touchpad**, a gyroscope with accelerometer, and **two cameras**. The rear touchpad, however, was an idea developers never quite figured out what to do with — it ended up used more as a curiosity than as a fully-fledged input method.

Audio is handled by stereo speakers and a quality headphone output; even with basic headphones, the Vita sounds clean and loud.

### Connectivity and peripherals

Games shipped on **proprietary PS Vita cards** — small flash media that replaced the PSP's optical UMDs. Alongside them, full **digital distribution through the PlayStation Store** eventually became home to the vast majority of the indie catalog.

The platform's biggest pain point was **Sony's memory cards**. The Vita refused to work with ordinary microSD cards and demanded its own proprietary format, priced absurdly — a 32GB card could easily cost as much as half the console itself. A textbook example of a decision that hurt the platform more than any competitor did.

Connectivity itself, on the other hand, was strong: **Wi-Fi** on all models, and **3G** on select versions. **Remote Play** worked beautifully — streaming games from the PlayStation 3 and, above all, from the PlayStation 4, where the Vita served as a second screen for the whole household. Sony also added **cross-buy** (buy a game once, play it on both PS4 and Vita) along with cross-play and cross-save between the platforms.

### Models and revisions

The PS Vita family stayed fairly compact:

- **PCH-1000** (2011) — the original model with a **5" OLED display**, available in Wi-Fi and 3G versions. Heavier, but with the best picture.
- **PCH-2000 "Slim"** (2013) — a thinner and noticeably lighter revision with an **LCD display** instead of OLED, longer battery life, 1 GB of internal storage, and microUSB charging. More practical, but a visual step backward.
- **PlayStation TV (Vita TV)** (2013) — a small **set-top box** built on Vita hardware that displayed games on a television and was controlled with a DualShock. Due to limited compatibility (titles relying on touch and gyroscope controls fell away), it was more of an interesting experiment than anything else.

### Clones and variants

No classic clones of the Vita ever appeared — the hardware was closed and complicated to replicate. Its legacy lies elsewhere: the Vita was **the first console to convincingly prove that full-fledged games belong in your pocket**, and it's exactly that idea that the wave of handheld gaming PCs would carry to completion a decade later. The **Steam Deck**, the ASUS ROG Ally, and other machines are essentially doing what the Vita did — just with a library no longer locked to a single manufacturer.

Sony returned to the idea in 2023 with the **PlayStation Portal**, though it isn't a standalone console at all: it's purely a streaming screen for the PS5. The irony is that the Vita could already do exactly that function a decade earlier — and it could also play its own games on top of it.

### The scene today

The Vita has one of the best **homebrew scenes** around, period. The breakthrough came with **HENkaku** and the tools that followed, which made it possible to run custom code on practically every firmware version. The result is a console that can be turned into an excellent emulation machine — handling everything from 8-bit systems through PS1 and GBA to a solid chunk of the PSP library — and one that also supports ordinary microSD cards via an adapter that fits into the game card slot. That neatly sidesteps the original sin of the platform's expensive memory cards.

Production of the console ended in **2019**, and along with it went the ability to buy new titles from the store. Even so, the Vita doesn't feel like a dead platform. Its catalog — packed with **JRPGs** (Persona 4 Golden, Danganronpa, Ys, Trails), superb ports, and indie gems like Hotline Miami or Spelunky — remains a very good reason to pick one up today. And whoever holds an original OLED model in their hands will understand within seconds why it's called the most beautiful handheld console ever made.

pc-dos.history:
When IBM introduced its **IBM PC** in 1981, nobody was thinking about games. It was an expensive office machine with an **Intel 8088** processor, a text screen, a beeping speaker, and an **MS-DOS** system controlled from the command line. Next to the colorful Commodore 64, it looked like an accountant in a suit who wandered into a kids' birthday party. Yet it had one quality nobody else offered: an **open architecture**. Expansion cards, documented interfaces, and readily available components meant that anyone could build a computer.

And that's exactly what happened. Through the **XT** (1983) and **AT** with the 80286 processor (1984), all the way to the **386** and **486** generations, the PC became the world's most widespread platform, driven by an army of clones and a merciless price war. The hardware improved every year, while the closed sixteen-bit machines stayed frozen in time. By around 1992 it was clear: the DOS PC had steamrolled both the Amiga and the Atari ST.

The era of DOS gaming peaked in the first half of the nineties. **Doom**, **X-COM**, **Dune II**, **Civilization**, and adventure games from LucasArts and Sierra were made for a machine that, barely ten years earlier, could only manage four colors and a single beep.

### Technology: graphics and sound

Graphics went through generations of cards that players bought separately. The oldest, **CGA**, handled 320×200 pixels in **4 colors** from brutally limited palettes (including the infamously ugly cyan-and-magenta combo). **Hercules** offered sharp monochrome graphics, great for spreadsheets and lousy for games. **EGA** (1984) raised the bar to **16 colors** and a resolution of 640×350.

The real turning point, though, was **VGA** in 1987. Its legendary **Mode 13h** offered 320×200 pixels in **256 colors** out of a palette of 262,144 shades, all in simply addressable linear memory — a gift for programmers. Suddenly it was possible to do digitized images, smooth transitions, and palette animation. VGA gave the PC visual superiority over the Amiga and became the standard for the entire DOS era; **SVGA** cards with higher resolutions later supplemented it.

Sound was a weak point for a long time. The default output was the **PC speaker**, a piezo speaker capable of essentially nothing but square-wave beeping. Salvation came with the **AdLib** card (1987) with the **Yamaha OPL2** chip, which brought **FM synthesis** and nine channels of real music. It was soon overtaken by Creative's **Sound Blaster**: compatible with AdLib, but also able to play **digital samples**, so explosions, voices, and drums arrived in games. It became the standard that practically every game targeted. At the top of the heap sat the expensive external **Roland MT-32** module, whose sound FM synthesis couldn't match.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The **keyboard** was the foundation, literally: games from simulators to adventures assumed the player had both hands on the keys and remembered dozens of shortcuts. The **mouse** went from an office accessory to a gaming necessity with the rise of **point-and-click adventures** and strategy games; without it, neither Monkey Island nor SimCity would make sense.

The **joystick** plugged into an analog **game port**, initially found on a separate card, later standardly moved to the sound card — so a single connector served both the joystick and MIDI. Analog controllers were beloved by flight simulators. Enthusiasts added a modem to play over a phone line, and networks for deathmatch play started appearing in offices and schools.

### Models and revisions

PC development wasn't measured by one manufacturer's models but by processor generations. The **8088** in the original PC and XT was enough for text adventures and simple arcade games, the **80286** in the AT brought higher performance, but it was the **386** and especially the **486** that defined the gaming era — only on the 486 did Doom or Wing Commander run the way they were meant to. There were differences within the lines too: the 486SX without a math coprocessor, the 486DX with an integrated FPU, and earlier standalone coprocessors like the **8087**, **287**, and **387**.

A typical curiosity was the **turbo button** on the case. It didn't speed anything up, as everyone assumed — quite the opposite, it slowed the computer down to its original clock speed so older games tied to processor clock speed would still work properly. Just as typical was the fight over **conventional memory**: the **config.sys** and **autoexec.bat** files, the **himem.sys** and EMM386 drivers, **EMS** and **XMS**, boot disks with different configurations, and the eternal out-of-memory message a few kilobytes short of the goal.

### Clones and variants

The key to the PC's rise was **IBM compatibility**. After companies like **Compaq** legally cloned the BIOS, an avalanche of clones followed — manufacturers around the world built these computers, and prices fell. This is what set the PC apart from the Amiga and Atari ST, which rose and fell with a single company.

Media went through its own evolution: from **5.25" floppy disks** (360 kB, later 1.2 MB) through **3.5" floppy disks** (720 kB and 1.44 MB) to **CD-ROM** in the early nineties. CDs brought spoken dialogue, digitized music, and video — and a wave of games with recorded actors. Installing from eight floppy disks was a ritual of the era.

In Czechoslovakia, PCs appeared in significant numbers mainly after 1989, once import restrictions fell and the first computer shops and markets sprang up. The machines were expensive, often assembled from imported parts, and games spread mainly on **copied floppy disks** that circulated among friends and around schools.

### The scene today

Playing DOS games today is easy thanks to emulation. The standard is **DOSBox** and its more advanced variant **DOSBox-X**, which can handle even the trickier period configurations. On retro handhelds the same foundation is used — both **Batocera** and **RetroArch** (via the **dosbox-pure** core) get a DOS game running without needing to fuss over sound card drivers or autoexec lines.

A legal source is **GOG.com**, which sells the classics pre-configured and set up in an emulator. Adventure games deserve **ScummVM**, which launches game data directly instead of emulating an entire computer. **Source ports** are a special chapter of their own: once the source code was released, dozens of Doom engines emerged — from the purist **Chocolate Doom**, which faithfully replicates the original behavior, to modern variants with high resolution. On top of that, the community supplies fan patches, bug fixes, translations, and new levels. The DOS era hasn't stayed a closed chapter — it's a living scene.

pc-9x.history:
The second half of the nineties was the period when the office box became the most powerful gaming machine in the world. It kicked off with the arrival of **Intel Pentium** processors and, in 1995, **Windows 95** with its 32-bit environment and unified hardware interface. Until then, every game handled its own drivers — during installation, the player manually picked the sound card model and set the **IRQ**, DMA channel, and port address, and if you got it wrong, the game stayed silent or crashed. With the arrival of **DirectX**, the era of magic numbers ended.

The transition wasn't instant: 1995 to 1997 belonged to titles released in both DOS and Windows versions, and only by the end of the decade did Windows fully take over. At the same time, the fastest technological spiral in gaming history got underway — whatever was cutting-edge in spring was average by Christmas. In terms of games, this was a golden age: the modern **FPS** was born here in the shape of Quake, Unreal, and Half-Life, real-time strategy games and simulators flourished along with the first big 3D RPGs — and because the PC wasn't a closed console, an enormous modding scene grew up around it.

### Technology: graphics and sound

The biggest topic of the era was **3D accelerators**. Until 1996, all 3D graphics were calculated in software on the CPU — hence the coarse, juddering textures at 320×200 resolution. Then along came 3dfx with the **Voodoo Graphics** card and the **Glide** interface, and the difference was night and day. Hardware acceleration brought **bilinear texture filtering**, perspective correction, transparency, higher resolution, and above all smoothness. For a lot of people, GLQuake on a Voodoo was the moment PC gaming changed for good.

The first Voodoo was still an add-in card connected by a cable to regular 2D graphics; **Voodoo2** could run SLI mode with two cards side by side. But the competition quickly caught up: NVIDIA came out with the **RIVA TNT** and TNT2 chips, which combined 2D and 3D on a single card and bet on **OpenGL** and Direct3D, and in 1999 released the **GeForce 256** — the first mainstream card with hardware **T&L**, meaning geometry and lighting calculations right on the graphics chip. ATI, meanwhile, offered the **Rage** line and, in 2000, the first **Radeon**. The 3dfx era was over.

Sound had its own development. The **Sound Blaster** line remained the standard, from the SB16 through the **AWE32** and AWE64 with wavetable synthesis for better MIDI music; later came cards with hardware acceleration and 3D sound via **A3D** and **EAX**, which let you actually hear that the gunfire was coming from behind you. The **CD-ROM** was crucial too: games started playing full **CD Audio** tracks instead of chip music. Toward the end of the era, **MP3** joined in.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The baseline system moved from tens to hundreds of megahertz within a few years. Pentium gained **MMX** instructions, memory moved from **EDO RAM** to **SDRAM**, and graphics moved from the **PCI** bus to the dedicated **AGP** port with faster access to main memory.

For control, the standard that still holds today was established: **keyboard and mouse**. In shooters, the **WASD + mouse** scheme took hold — moving with the left hand and looking with the right — a combination born in the community around Quake. Simulators called for **joysticks** and flight control sets, racing games called for force-feedback **steering wheels**.

The biggest social change was online gaming. It started with a **modem** and a direct dial-up connection between two computers, then **dial-up** connections with high ping and a phone bill nobody wanted to explain at home. The first online services and lobby systems appeared. **LAN parties** became legendary — weekends when towers, monitors, and metres of cable got hauled into one room for a game of Quake or StarCraft.

### Models and revisions

The PC differed from consoles in that no single "model" existed — a build was always an assembly of parts. Still, the era can be divided by processor: **Pentium** and its MMX version, then **Pentium II** in a slot-in cartridge, and finally **Pentium III**. Media changed in parallel: **floppy disks** were phased out, and the **CD-ROM** became the sole medium. Installations of hundreds of megabytes stopped being unusual, and big games shipped on several discs.

### Clones and variants

The openness of the architecture was the PC's greatest strength. Compatible computers could be built by anyone, and Intel wasn't the only one supplying processors — the rival was **AMD** with its **K6** line and, from 1999, the **Athlon**, which for the first time genuinely gave Intel a run for its money; **Cyrix** also offered a cheap alternative. Thanks to this competition, prices stayed low and performance climbed at a breathtaking pace.

In the Czech environment, this meant a boom of custom-built systems from computer markets and small local vendors. Companies mainly bought branded complete PCs, while gamers assembled their own machines piece by piece and upgraded gradually — new graphics card this year, processor next year. Gaming magazines with cover-mounted CDs were a source of demos and drivers.

### The scene today

Retro PC gaming today has several paths. For transitional DOS titles, **DOSBox** helps; for classic adventure games, **ScummVM**. Windows games from the late nineties, however, often run directly on a modern system, or in **compatibility mode** with community patches for fast processors and widescreen resolutions. For titles written for Glide there are **wrappers** like **nGlide** and **dgVoodoo**, which translate the old calls to today's graphics interfaces.

The most convenient legal source is **GOG.com**, with pre-configured versions free of copy protection. For the biggest classics there are also **source ports** built on released source code — engines derived from Quake offer higher resolutions, modern controls, and online play. And then there's the most honest option of all: building a period-correct **retro rig** with a Pentium, a Voodoo card, and a Sound Blaster. Hunting down the parts has become a collector's hobby in its own right, and emulation can't replace the feel of a CRT monitor.

pc-modern.history:
The break between the "old" and "modern" PC has no single date, but it has clear markers. Sometime around 2001, the gaming PC stopped being a box you stuffed with the fastest possible processor and became a machine where the heavy lifting is done by a **programmable graphics card**. Shortly after, a second revolution arrived: in 2003 AMD launched the **Athlon 64** processor along with the **x86-64** architecture, a 64-bit extension that — unlike various exotic dead ends — stayed fully backward compatible with everything that came before it. Intel adopted it too after some initial resistance, and x86-64 became the industry's common language, including on game consoles.

The era's third pillar arrived with **multi-core processors**. Clock speeds hit a physical ceiling, and instead of more gigahertz, cores started multiplying, forcing game studios to rewrite the way they built their engines. From the middle of the decade onward, game development stopped being a matter of a single fast loop and became a discipline of parallel programming — with separate threads for physics, audio, data streaming, and rendering.

And above all of this came a change that hit players harder than any piece of silicon: **digital distribution**. The box on the shelf gave way to an account, a library, and background downloads. The PC, a platform console gamers were writing off in the mid-2000s, became the most open and the largest gaming platform of all.

### Technology: graphics and sound

The key moment was **programmable shaders**. Until then, graphics cards could only perform a fixed set of operations; with **DirectX 8** and the **GeForce 3** card (2001), developers could for the first time write their own short programs running directly on the GPU for every vertex and every pixel. **DirectX 9** and the **ATI Radeon 9700** (2002) pushed the boundary further, and the result was visible at a glance: real reflections on wet asphalt, rippling water, soft shadows, skin and fabric that actually looked like skin and fabric. Games like Half-Life 2 and Far Cry showed what that meant in practice.

The next step brought **unified shaders** — instead of separate units for vertices and pixels, a universal array of compute cores arrived, one that could also be used for general-purpose computation. This was followed by **DirectX 11** with tessellation and compute shaders, and later **DirectX 12** and the open **Vulkan**, which gave developers access closer to the hardware and reduced driver overhead.

At the same time, the "raw" numbers kept climbing. From a resolution of 1024×768, gaming moved through 1080p and 1440p to **4K**, refresh rates rose from 60 Hz to 144 Hz and beyond, **antialiasing** smoothed jagged edges, and **HDR** widened the range of brightness and color. The latest major chapter is **ray tracing** — calculating reflections, shadows, and lighting by tracing rays, the same approach once used to render film overnight. Because it remains demanding, it's accompanied by **upscaling techniques** like Nvidia's **DLSS** and AMD's **FSR**, which render the image at a lower resolution and reconstruct it to full size.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The **keyboard and mouse** remained the foundation — a pairing no console has ever matched for aiming precision and the sheer number of instantly available commands. Alongside it, though, the PC gained full **gamepad** support: the Xbox controller became the de facto standard, games recognize it automatically and display its icons, so platformers and racing games play just as comfortably as on a console.

Peripherals that consoles simply don't have also arrived — **VR headsets**, high-refresh-rate monitors, wheels and sticks for simulators. On the memory side, generations of **DDR** cycled through all the way to DDR5, but the biggest practical difference came from storage: the move from hard drives to **SSDs** and then to **NVMe** drives connected via PCI Express cut loading screens from tens of seconds down to a handful, and let games stream vast open worlds on the fly.

### Digital distribution and services

Valve launched **Steam** in **2003**, and players openly hated it at first — mainly because, in 2004, there was no way to launch Half-Life 2 without it, an utterly unheard-of condition at the time. Within a few years, though, this necessary evil became the most convenient way to buy games, keep them updated, and have them available forever. **GOG.com** followed, with DRM-free games and care for old titles, along with the **Epic Games Store** and the **Game Pass** subscription.

This changed a game's entire life cycle. Boxed releases disappeared, along with the idea that a game was finished the moment it was pressed — regular **patching** took over, along with additional content, **Steam Workshop** for easy distribution of mods, and **early access**, where players buy a title while it's still in development and watch it grow. For small studios, this was a fundamental turning point: the road to market no longer had to run through a publisher and distributor.

### Modding, indie games, and openness

Openness is precisely the trait no one ever took away from the PC. **Modding** grew from a fringe pastime into a phenomenon — **Skyrim**, years later, has thousands of mods changing its graphics, mechanics, and even entire new regions, **Minecraft** built its own culture around modifications, and more than one of today's standalone games began life as a mod of someone else's title.

Alongside this, the **indie scene** grew up. Digital distribution gave it a storefront, and tools like **Unity** and the open-source **Godot** gave it a way to build; games that never would have made it past approval in the boxed era suddenly found hundreds of thousands of players. And third, the PC is home to **emulation** — this is precisely where emulators for consoles from the 8-bit era to recent generations are built and run.

### Todays scene

Recent years have brought something that would have sounded like a contradiction at the start of the era: the **handheld gaming PC**. Valve's **Steam Deck** and machines like the **ROG Ally** look like handhelds, but inside is an ordinary x86-64 PC. The Deck, moreover, runs on Linux and launches Windows games through the compatibility layer **Proton**, which worked well enough to turn a purchased game library into essentially portable property across systems and devices.

And with that, the circle closes. Today's PC isn't just the platform with the newest games — it's the one place where practically the entire history of gaming can be played at once: today's ray-traced blockbusters, indie gems, old classics from GOG.com, and emulated titles from consoles of every generation. The modern PC is at once the most powerful gaming machine of our time and the finest museum gaming has ever had.

wii.history:
When Nintendo unveiled a console in autumn 2006 that had gone by the codename **Revolution** during development, few suspected it would become one of the biggest hits in gaming history. The Wii was small, quiet, white, and at first glance almost unassuming — next to the bulky cases of the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, it looked like a set-top box. Nintendo had deliberately refused to join the performance race its rivals were running, betting everything instead on a single card: **the way games are controlled**.

That card was the **Wii Remote** controller, shaped like a TV remote control. Thanks to accelerometers and infrared sensing against a **sensor bar** placed on top of the television, it could react to tilting, swinging, and pointing at the screen. The accompanying **Nunchuk**, connected by cable, added an analog stick and a second set of sensors for the left hand. The controls were so intuitive that people who had never held a gamepad before sat down at the console for the first time — grandparents, parents, whole families.

The result surpassed even the most optimistic expectations. The Wii sold **over 101 million units**, more than the PlayStation 3 and the Xbox 360, despite being the technically weakest console of the generation. Nintendo proved that the winner doesn't have to be the one with the best graphics — it's enough to offer something no one else has, at a price almost everyone can afford.

### Technology: graphics and sound

Inside the Wii lay an evolution of the GameCube hardware, not a revolution. The **IBM PowerPC “Broadway”** processor was essentially a faster version of the older Gekko chip, graphics were handled by **ATI “Hollywood”**, an improved successor to the Flipper chip. The console had **88 MB of memory** split between fast 1T-SRAM and slower GDDR3, used **12cm optical discs** as its medium, and stored games on **512 MB of internal flash memory** expandable with an **SD card**.

The most glaring technical limitation was resolution: the Wii offered **a maximum of 480p** — merely standard definition at a time when competitors were running in HD and households were switching en masse to large flat-panel TVs. On a modern display, the Wii therefore looks soft and blurry. Nintendo offset this disadvantage with **a bold, clean, colorful art style** — games like **Super Mario Galaxy** or **The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword** have aged visually far better than their technical specs would suggest.

### Peripherals and accessories

The bundled game **Wii Sports** played a key role. Five simple disciplines — tennis, bowling, boxing, golf, and baseball — controlled by swinging your arm became the best possible demo for the console, and in many households it was the very first title people ever tried. Wii Sports essentially sold the console all by itself.

A huge number of peripherals followed. **Wii MotionPlus** added a gyroscope to the controller and dramatically improved motion tracking accuracy; **Wii Sports Resort** made full use of it. The **Wii Balance Board**, a platform that reacted to shifts in weight, opened up a whole wave of fitness and wellness titles with **Wii Fit**. Plastic add-ons arrived too, like the **Wii Wheel** for **Mario Kart Wii** or the **Wii Zapper** for shooters, along with the more traditional **Classic Controller** for Virtual Console games.

A major strength was **backward compatibility with the GameCube**. The original model had four GameCube controller ports and two memory card slots hidden under a flip-down cover, so older games ran natively and players didn't have to throw anything away.

### Models and revisions

From the start, the Wii was distinctly an **online console**. Built-in Wi-Fi, the **WiiConnect24** system, and an interface divided into “channels” offered the **Wii Shop Channel** digital store, the **WiiWare** service for smaller original games, and above all **Virtual Console** — a legal way to access classics from the NES, SNES, Nintendo 64, Sega Mega Drive, and other platforms. For a lot of players, it was the very first easy way to get their hands on old games. The **Mii** channel, with its custom avatar creation, became one of the defining symbols of the whole era.

The hardware went through several revisions. The **Wii Family Edition** from 2011 was designed to lie flat only and **dropped GameCube support** — the ports and memory card slots disappeared entirely. The **Wii mini** from 2012 went even further: a cheap, compact version with a top-loading disc drive, no Wi-Fi or online functions, no SD card slot, no GameCube support, and only composite video output. It served as a budget machine for the platform's final years, before being replaced in 2012 by the backward-compatible Wii U.

### The scene today

The Wii is today one of the most accessible retro consoles around — so many units and games were made that both are cheap to find. On a modern TV it's worth using a component cable or an external upscaler, otherwise composite output looks very soft. The **Wii Shop Channel has been shut down**, so digitally purchased titles can no longer be bought; the legal options left are physical discs and modern remasters or remakes of select games on the Nintendo Switch.

Emulation is in excellent shape. **Dolphin** handles both Wii and GameCube in high resolution, with anti-aliasing and widescreen hacks; controls can be handled with a mouse and keyboard, or by connecting an original Wii Remote over Bluetooth. The Wii is also supported by **Batocera**, so the platform can be run on a gaming PC or a beefier mini-PC — weaker handhelds generally aren't up to the task of motion-controlled games, though.

The **homebrew scene** is also alive and well. Through the **Homebrew Channel**, the console can run custom software, emulators for older platforms, media players, and tools for launching games from a USB drive or SD card. It's precisely this combination of low price, a huge library, and an open community that makes the Wii one of the most rewarding consoles a retro gamer can pick up today.

wii-u.history:
Nintendo's Wii U arrived on the market in autumn 2012 with a task that was almost unsolvable from the start: following up on the Wii, one of the best-selling consoles ever. By then Nintendo realized the magic of waving a controller around had worn off, and it came up with an idea that looked great on paper — the **GamePad**, a large controller with its own **touchscreen** functioning as a **second screen** alongside the television. Maps, inventories, or moves hidden from other players moved into your hands, and when someone in the living room needed the TV, the game simply continued on the GamePad in **off-TV play** mode. It was also Nintendo's very first **HD console**.

Yet the Wii U became a textbook example of how to sell a good idea badly. The **confusing name** suggested an accessory for the Wii rather than a new console, and the ads focused so heavily on the GamePad that many customers never grasped it was a different machine altogether. The result was a **commercial failure**: only around **13.5 million units** sold. Third-party publishers left quickly after a lukewarm start, and in 2013 the PlayStation 4 and Xbox One arrived, against which the Wii U simply couldn't compete on power.

Ironically, the library itself ranks among the best Nintendo has ever released in a single generation. This is where **Mario Kart 8**, **Splatoon**, and **The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild** debuted first — games that only became massive hits in their reworked Switch versions. Today the Wii U looks like an underappreciated laboratory that gave rise to the following console's success.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At the heart of the console sits the triple-core **IBM Espresso** processor built on the **PowerPC** architecture, a direct descendant of the Broadway chip from the Wii and the Gekko chip from the GameCube. This family lineage ensured smooth backward compatibility, but it also meant the Wii U entered the HD era with a conservative, none-too-fast CPU. Graphics are handled by the **AMD Latte** chip, based on the Radeon architecture and supplemented with fast **eDRAM** memory built right into the package.

The console carries **2 GB of DDR3 memory**, though only half of that belongs to games — the second gigabyte is reserved for the system, so multitasking, the browser, and social features can run in the background. Video output goes out over **HDMI** at up to **1080p**, though most games targeted 720p with stable frame rates instead. The hardware sat roughly at the level of the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, just with a more modern graphics architecture and considerably lower power consumption. Even so, Nintendo's studios squeezed visually gorgeous games out of it — **Super Mario 3D World**, **Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze**, and **Bayonetta 2** rank among the cleanest-looking titles of their era.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The GamePad is, without question, the star of the system. Besides the touchscreen, it carries analog sticks, motion sensors, a camera, a microphone, and an **NFC reader**, on which the **amiibo** figures launched in 2014. Video streams to it wirelessly from the console, so its range is limited to roughly one room — the GamePad isn't a standalone handheld, but an extension of the console's reach.

The Wii U is **backward compatible with the Wii**: in so-called Wii mode it runs practically the entire original library and can use old accessories too, namely the **Wii Remote**, **Nunchuk**, and **Balance Board**. For classic television play there was the comfortable **Wii U Pro Controller**. The online side was handled by the **Nintendo Network**, along with the social **Miiverse**, where players drew messages and left them directly inside other people's games. The **eShop** store also offered **Virtual Console**, for the first time including games from the Game Boy Advance and Nintendo DS.

### Models and revisions

Hardware variants are few and differ mainly in storage capacity. The base **Basic** model was white with **8 GB** of built-in storage, while the pricier **Deluxe** (called **Premium** in Europe) was black with **32 GB** and a stand. Since even 32 GB isn't enough for modern games, the console can connect an **external USB drive** and reads SD cards. Nintendo released a number of collector's bundles, including editions tied to **The Wind Waker HD**, Mario Kart 8, and Splatoon. No major revision ever arrived; production ended in **2017**, just a few weeks before the Switch launched. The Wii U is also Nintendo's last **regionally locked** home console.

### Clones and variants

True clones don't exist — the architecture was closed and commercially unattractive enough that nobody bothered copying it. The **homebrew scene**, on the other hand, is remarkably alive. The community gradually developed methods like **Haxchi**, and later **Tiramisu** and **Aroma**, which open the console up to custom apps and emulators. Even the built-in Wii mode (**vWii**) can be unlocked, turning the Wii U into a very capable emulation machine for older Nintendo systems.

### The scene today

On PC, the clear choice is the **Cemu** emulator, which has matured into remarkable quality — a number of games run on it at higher resolutions and more smoothly than on the original hardware, with its handling of Breath of the Wild being especially legendary. Cemu is demanding on performance, though, and targets classic x86 computers, so you can run it under **Batocera** on a regular PC as well, but cheap ARM handhelds like the Anbernic or R36S aren't anywhere close to enough for the Wii U. The **eShop was shut down in 2023**, so digital purchases are no longer possible and games have to be sourced as secondhand discs.

On the resale market the Wii U is still **cheap**, while offering dozens of excellent games, some of which never appeared anywhere else — Xenoblade Chronicles X, for instance, or the GamePad-driven minigames in Nintendo Land. Its usual weak point is the GamePad itself: batteries fade after years of use, and finding a replacement is harder than finding a whole console. Even so, the Wii U is growing into a **prized collector's item** — a console the world passed by, even though it deserved so much more.

ps5.history:
When the **PlayStation 5** arrived on the market in November 2020, it landed in a world that wasn't exactly in a celebratory mood. The pandemic had shut down stores, production lines were faltering, and Sony's new console became, for a large portion of gamers, more of a hunt than a routine purchase. Yet — or perhaps precisely because of that — the PS5 went down as one of the most anticipated hardware launches in the history of the gaming industry. The bulky black-and-white machine with its dramatic curves divided opinions at first glance, but what it could do on the inside was far more interesting than its design.

This time, Sony didn't arrive with an architectural revolution the way it had with the PlayStation 3. On the contrary — it continued the proven path set with the PS4 and built the console on **standard x86-64 hardware from AMD**. The real novelty lay elsewhere: in storage. The extremely fast **custom SSD** wasn't just a marketing figure but an element that changed game design itself — the end of long loading screens, the end of hidden "elevators" and corridors meant to mask data loading.

The PS5 is also the only platform in this overview that is **not retro**. It's the current generation, a machine that's still on sale today and for which new games are still being released. We include it in the list for the sake of completeness — as the latest chapter in a long line that began with a gray box with a CD drive in 1994.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At the heart of the PS5 is an **eight-core AMD processor built on Zen 2 architecture**, paired with an **RDNA 2** graphics core. Both are based on technologies AMD was deploying in PCs at the same time, reaffirming the strategy of "PC-adjacent hardware, easy porting." For the first time in the history of Sony consoles, the graphics chip handles **hardware-accelerated ray tracing** — calculating reflections, shadows, and lighting by tracing rays, a technique that used to belong exclusively to the world of film production and expensive workstations.

The key weapon, though, is the aforementioned **SSD with its own controller** and a dedicated unit for data decompression. This offloads the processor and allows content to stream into memory at a pace classic console hard drives never offered. Thanks to this, developers could design worlds with instant transitions between locations and considerably more detailed textures. A showcase example where the benefit was obvious at first glance was **Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart**.

On the audio side, Sony introduced its own spatial audio solution, which tries to place sound sources in three-dimensional space around the player even on ordinary headphones. On the video side, the console targets **4K resolution**, higher frame rates, and **HDR**, with many games offering a choice between a quality-focused mode and a performance-focused mode.

### DualSense and peripherals

The PS5's biggest surprise, however, was hidden in the controller. **DualSense** abandoned the twenty-year-old DualShock name, and with it the classic rumbling vibration. It was replaced by **haptic feedback**, capable of simulating surprisingly subtle sensations — grainy sand underfoot, raindrops, the click of a mechanism. Added to that were **adaptive triggers**, which apply variable resistance: a taut bowstring, a jamming weapon, or a stiff brake could suddenly be felt in your fingers.

The pre-installed game **Astro's Playroom** served as an impressive showcase of both and remained, for many players, the best demonstration of what the controller can do. The console was later joined by the **PlayStation VR2** headset, which continued the virtual reality line from the PS4 era, this time with its own motion tracking that requires no external camera.

### Models and revisions

Alongside the standard model, Sony also introduced the **Digital Edition** — a variant **without an optical drive**, cheaper, but relying exclusively on digital purchases. The choice between the disc and the purely digital version became a regular part of the buying decision.

Later came the **Slim** revision with a smaller, lighter case and the option to attach the disc drive to the base unit afterward, and finally the more powerful **PS5 Pro** for players who wanted to squeeze the maximum visual quality out of the console. As with the PS4 Pro, games remain compatible across models — the Pro offers better visuals, not a different library.

### PSN, backward compatibility, and games

The PS5 is **backward compatible with the PlayStation 4**. The vast majority of previous-generation games run on it, often with smoother performance and a more stable image, and saved games can be transferred as well. For owners of large libraries, this was a major argument — switching to the new console didn't mean starting from scratch.

The PS5's catalog leaned on strong single-player franchises: the **Demon's Souls** remake, **Marvel's Spider-Man: Miles Morales**, **Returnal**, **Horizon Forbidden West**, and **God of War Ragnarök**. Meanwhile, the **PlayStation Plus** subscription branched out into several tiers, with the higher ones offering a catalog of downloadable and streamed games, including older titles from Sony's back catalog.

For roughly the first two years, however, the platform fought a different battle than competition: **a shortage of units**. A worldwide chip shortage crippled production, consoles vanished from online stores within seconds, and scalpers resold them at steep markups. The situation only evened out later, bringing the PS5 back to the status of a normally available product.

### The scene today

Because it's a **current generation** console, none of what we're used to with older platforms applies to the PS5. **Emulation practically doesn't exist** — and even if it appeared, it would have no purpose: the console is still being sold and games for it are still being released. You won't be able to play the PS5 on devices like Batocera or a handheld Anbernic, and you won't be able to for the foreseeable future.

The path to games is the standard one: physical discs for disc-equipped models, digital purchases through the PlayStation Store, or a subscription. The second-hand market for both consoles and games is rich, and previous-generation games on disc can often be had for a fraction of their original price. For collectors, it's also worth noting that the disc-equipped PS5 can play **physical PS4 games** — from the perspective of long-term library preservation, that's not a small thing. In a few years the PS5 will become another chapter of retro history; for now, though, it's still writing the current one.

xbox-series.history:
When Microsoft launched the new generation of Xbox in November 2020, it did almost everything the opposite way from seven years earlier. No grand presentation of the future of the living room, no voice-controlled TV, no Kinect in every box. Instead, a quiet, matter-of-fact launch in the middle of a pandemic — and, above all, two consoles at once. The powerful **Xbox Series X**, shaped like a black monolith resembling a small refrigerator, alongside the slim white **Xbox Series S**, a disc-less digital model meant to make the new generation accessible to those for whom the flagship's price was too high.

Splitting the lineup into two machines of different performance levels was unusual in the console world and still sparks debate today. The Series S is noticeably weaker and aims more at gaming around 1440p resolution than true 4K, but it shares the same architecture, the same interface, and the same game library as its bigger sibling. For Microsoft, this was a logical step: if the strategy's center of gravity is a subscription rather than a box, then the cheaper the ticket into the ecosystem, the better.

That's exactly the key to understanding the whole generation. While the competing PlayStation 5 built its identity on major exclusives, Microsoft bet on **Xbox Game Pass** — a subscription library that its own titles land in on day one of release. The launch lineup reflected that: no major system exclusive, but instead instant access to hundreds of games from all previous Xbox generations.

### Technology: graphics and sound

Both consoles are powered by a custom APU from **AMD**, combining an eight-core processor core built on **Zen 2** architecture with graphics based on **RDNA 2**. For the first time in Microsoft consoles, this brought hardware-accelerated **ray tracing** — realistic ray tracing for reflections, shadows, and lighting — along with techniques like variable rate shading and mesh shading.

The difference between the two models lies mainly in graphics performance and memory. The Series X has a significantly wider GPU, 16 GB of **GDDR6** memory, and targets 4K at 60 frames per second, with support for up to 120 Hz in titles that can handle it. The Series S has a smaller graphics chip and less memory, so developers usually lower the resolution, reflection quality, or detail density for it. On the audio side, both consoles rely on spatial sound — they support **Dolby Atmos**, **DTS:X**, and **Windows Sonic**, and have hardware assistance for processing audio effects, which is most noticeable on headphones.

### Speed: SSD, Quick Resume, and backward compatibility

The generation's biggest practical leap didn't come from graphics but from storage. A custom **NVMe SSD**, combined with a package of technologies Microsoft calls the **Xbox Velocity Architecture**, virtually eliminated long loading screens and let games stream data from the drive continuously instead of holding the entire surrounding area in memory.

That gave rise to the whole generation's most beloved feature — **Quick Resume**. The console can keep several in-progress games frozen in a suspended state and switch between them within a few seconds, even surviving a console restart. Once you get used to it, it's hard to give up.

Equally important is **backward compatibility**, which Microsoft continued from where it left off with the Xbox One. The Series X and S play Xbox One titles, a large part of the **Xbox 360** library, and even games from the original **Xbox** — often at a higher resolution, with a more stable frame rate, and with automatically computed HDR thanks to the **Auto HDR** feature. The **FPS Boost** feature can double the frame rate for select older games, while **Smart Delivery** ensures that a purchased game automatically downloads the best available version for that particular model.

### Game Pass instead of exclusives

Microsoft's strategy became clearly defined over the course of the generation: sell the service, not the box. Game Pass expanded to PC and to the cloud, where it can be played through a browser, TV, or phone, and Microsoft backed it with extensive studio acquisitions — most notably **ZeniMax Media** (the parent company of **Bethesda**) and later **Activision Blizzard**.

Among the games that defined the generation, the ones most often mentioned are **Forza Horizon 5**, **Halo Infinite**, **Microsoft Flight Simulator**, **Starfield**, and the continually expanded **Sea of Thieves**. At the same time, Microsoft gradually abandoned the idea that games must stay exclusive to its hardware, and it began releasing some titles on competing platforms too — a move that would have been unthinkable just a few years earlier.

### Models and revisions (Series X, Series S)

The original pair from November 2020 was gradually joined by variants that were more cosmetic than technical. The Series S got a **1TB** storage version in black, while the Series X gained a purely **digital white variant without a disc drive** and limited editions with a larger drive. Internal performance stayed the same across revisions, which marks a major difference from past generations — no "Pro" version arrived mid-cycle.

Storage can only be expanded via a proprietary **expansion card** plugged into the back of the console; a regular external USB drive only works for archiving and for playing older titles. The controller stayed faithful to the proven Xbox One shape, gaining a share button, a finer directional pad, and a **USB-C** connector.

### Significance and legacy

The Xbox Series X|S is still the current generation, so its place in history is still settling — we include it in the platform overview mainly for the sake of completeness. Microsoft apparently didn't win the sales battle against the PlayStation 5 again, but that clearly wasn't the main goal anyway. Instead, it produced a platform that, thanks to backward compatibility, works as one of the best legal ways to play older titles from the brand's entire history today.

For retro gaming, the Series X|S has one more interesting property: after switching into **Developer Mode**, it can also run emulators such as **RetroArch**, turning the console into a surprisingly capable machine for eight- and sixteen-bit classics. Those who just want to play games from the Xbox 360 and original Xbox era, though, don't even need that — a digital store, Game Pass, and an old disc copy in a drawer will do just fine.

switch-2.history:
Eight years is an eternity in the console world. By the time Nintendo unveiled the **Nintendo Switch 2** in 2025, the original Switch had already enjoyed a lifespan no one would have dared predict back at launch — and with it, a library far too valuable to simply abandon. Nintendo therefore chose a path it rarely takes with a successor: instead of revolution and a new concept, it went with evolution. The Switch 2 looks like a Switch, behaves like a Switch, and plays Switch games. It just does everything noticeably better.

That approach is itself a small event. For decades Nintendo was known for starting each generation from scratch and presenting the audience with some new gimmick — motion controls on the Wii, dual screens on the DS, a tablet on the Wii U. This time it bet that the hybrid design no longer needs any justification, since it has since become a standard the entire handheld gaming PC market now imitates. The Switch 2's job wasn't to sell players on a new idea, but to take the old one further than the original 2017 hardware technically allowed.

The launch was accompanied by **Mario Kart World**, an openly reimagined entry in the famous racing series that, as the flagship title, played a role similar to Breath of the Wild once did — showing what the new console can do without needing a lengthy explanation.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At the heart of the console is a **custom chip from NVIDIA**, continuing a partnership that began with the Tegra X1 in the first Switch. The major new feature is support for **DLSS**, an image-reconstruction technology that lets a game run internally at a lower resolution while still reaching the screen in a sharp result without the corresponding load. That is precisely the key to a handheld console with a limited thermal budget managing **4K resolution when docked**. The chip also supports hardware-accelerated ray tracing, so modern lighting techniques are no longer principally out of reach for the Switch 2.

The built-in display has grown noticeably — larger than both the original model and the later OLED version, with higher resolution, HDR support, and a high, variable refresh rate. Compared to its predecessor's seven-inch screen, handheld play feels considerably more generous. Internal storage is an order of magnitude larger than before and expands with **microSD Express** memory cards, which are substantially faster than regular microSD cards; older cards from the Switch don't work in the new console. Audio remains the tried-and-tested stereo setup with built-in speakers, a 3.5mm jack, and digital output via the dock, now enhanced with spatial effects.

### Joy-Con 2 and peripherals

The controllers underwent the most visible change. The **Joy-Con 2** no longer attaches to the console via rails but **magnetically**, which speeds up both attaching and detaching and removes one of the system's most mechanically fragile points. The controllers are larger and fit the hand better, so playing with a single Joy-Con is no longer a compromise reserved for emergencies.

The real novelty lies elsewhere, though: each Joy-Con 2 can function as a **mouse**. Set it on a table or on your thigh and it tracks motion across the surface, so the console natively supports control schemes typical of PC genres — strategy games, shooters, or drawing and creative applications. It's a classically Nintendo idea in the sense that it grows out of hardware you're already holding rather than another extra box. The console also keeps the classic **Pro Controller** for playing on a TV, along with expanded options for voice and video communication between players during a game.

### Models and revisions

The Switch 2 is so far available in a single configuration — no Lite or OLED variant of the kind that gradually rounded out the previous generation's lineup. Color and collector's editions are available for purchase, along with accessories like spare Joy-Cons, a camera, or protective cases, but the hardware itself doesn't yet split into performance or build tiers. The dock has been redesigned and, besides 4K output, also handles the improved heat dissipation the more powerful chip demands.

### Backward compatibility and game library

The new console's biggest practical advantage is **backward compatibility with Nintendo Switch games** — both physical and digital. An owner of the older console therefore doesn't start with an empty library, and a number of titles run more smoothly on the new hardware, in better resolution, or in a directly updated form prepared for the Switch 2. Given that the original Switch sold tens of millions of units and amassed an enormous number of games, this is a bridge the new generation crosses with a considerable head start.

Alongside its own franchises — Mario, Zelda, Metroid, Pokémon, Kirby — Nintendo has from the start also relied on collaboration with third-party studios, for whom the new chip with DLSS is a substantially friendlier target than the eight-year-old Tegra. The Switch 2's competition, meanwhile, isn't just the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, but above all handheld gaming PCs led by the **Steam Deck** — a category the original Switch's success itself helped bring into being.

### Today's scene

The Switch 2 is the newest console on this site, and from the retro scene's perspective it's essentially ground zero: no usable emulation exists for it, you won't find it in Batocera or on any handheld emulation device, and any experiments in that direction remain purely theoretical for now. The only path to its games is the official one — the console itself, game cards, and the digital store, or else original Switch games that run on it.

For collectors and players interested in platform history, it's interesting mainly as a milestone. It shows that a concept which, in 2017, looked like a risky bet following the Wii U's failure, became so self-evident within a single generation that its successor no longer needs to justify it — it only needs to make it faster, sharper, and more comfortable. How the Switch 2 will be remembered is something only time will tell; for now, it's a console that is still writing its first page.

mega-cd.history:
At the turn of the 1980s and 1990s, the games industry embraced the notion that the future lay on optical disc. A compact disc holds hundreds of megabytes where a cartridge offers mere units, it can play back a studio recording at CD quality, and — as it seemed at the time — it can even play video. Sega jumped on that wave as the first of the major console makers: in December 1991 it launched the **Mega-CD** in Japan, an add-on that connected to the existing Mega Drive and turned it into a machine with a disc drive.

The unit reached the West in 1992 under the name **Sega CD** (in Europe the Mega-CD designation stuck) and immediately ran into its biggest problem — price. The add-on cost roughly as much as an entire console, and that was assuming you already had a Mega Drive at home. The result was a platform that won a handful of devoted fans, enormous publicity around a few controversial titles, and only a fraction of the sales Sega had hoped for. Even so, it remains one of the most fascinating pieces of hardware of its era.

The Mega-CD's legacy is genuinely split in two. On one side stand **Night Trap** and **Sewer Shark** — games assembled from live-action footage that became a symbol of technology becoming an end in itself. On the other stand **Sonic CD**, **Lunar: The Silver Star**, and Kojima's adventure **Snatcher** — titles that still rank among the best Sega released in its sixteen-bit era.

### Technology: graphics and sound

The Mega-CD isn't just a disc drive. The add-on brings its **own Motorola 68000 processor** clocked at roughly 12.5 MHz — faster than the one in the Mega Drive itself — and the two chips work in tandem. It also adds significantly more memory (several hundred kilobytes of program RAM plus a buffer for data from the disc) and, crucially, an **ASIC for scaling and rotation** — a hardware unit that can enlarge, shrink, and rotate graphics similarly to the famous Mode 7 on the rival SNES.

That chip is behind the platform's most striking effects: the rotating bonus stages in **Sonic CD**, the pseudo-3D flythroughs in **Silpheed**, or the moving backgrounds in action games. The color palette and resolution, however, remain dictated by the Mega Drive, so visually the Mega-CD is still a sixteen-bit console — just with more motion.

Sound is where the leap forward is greatest. Alongside the **Yamaha YM2612** FM chip came the **Ricoh RF5C164** PCM synthesizer with eight sample channels, and above all the ability to play regular **CD audio tracks**. Composers could for the first time work with real recordings, choirs, or live instruments, and the difference is audible on first listen — the Japanese and European soundtracks of Sonic CD rank among the cult recordings of the entire generation.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The hookup is typically Sega, meaning a bit convoluted. The Mega-CD connects to the console via an **expansion port** and edge connector, has its own power supply and its own audio cabling, which mixes with the Mega Drive's output. The controllers remain unchanged — the Mega-CD adds no ports of its own and is played with the same three-button and six-button gamepads.

The console keeps saved positions in built-in **battery-backed memory**, which could be expanded with a **Backup RAM Cart** slotted into the cartridge port. The same slot could also accept the **32X** add-on, creating the notorious "tower of power" — a trio of boxes with three power supplies that only a handful of games could actually take advantage of. When no game disc was inserted, the unit worked as an ordinary CD player with a graphical interface.

### Models and revisions

The original **Model 1** (1991) is a horizontal deck with a sliding disc tray, onto which the Mega Drive sits from above; it looks and was priced like an expensive hi-fi component. The revised **Model 2** (1993) switched to a cheaper top-loading disc mechanism and connects from the side next to the console, making the whole setup more compact and reliable. On older units, a dried-out belt in the tray mechanism and leaking capacitors are typical faults today.

Sega also released combined units. The **Sega CDX** (in Europe the **Multi-Mega**) packed both Mega Drive and Mega-CD into a case the size of a portable CD player and could also work as an ordinary discman. A collaboration with JVC produced the upscale **Wondermega** (sold in North America as the **X'Eye**) with better audio output, and Aiwa offered a micro system with a Mega-CD built directly into the tower.

### Clones and variants

Dedicated Mega-CD clones essentially never appeared — the mechanism with its BIOS was too complex and expensive to copy, so cheap knockoffs concentrated on the Mega Drive itself instead. There were, however, interesting licensed offshoots: the multimedia system **Pioneer LaserActive** could, after purchasing the **Mega LD** module, play Mega Drive and Mega-CD games as well as its own titles on LaserDiscs. It was one of the most expensive gaming devices of its time and is a collector's rarity today.

Competition in the disc space was ultimately fierce: NEC had its **PC Engine CD-ROM²**, Philips pushed the **CD-i**, and the mid-1990s brought the **3DO**, **Amiga CD32**, and eventually the Saturn and PlayStation, which closed the book on FMV games.

### Today's scene

Mega-CD emulation is well handled today — the **Genesis Plus GX** and **PicoDrive** cores run reliably even on weaker retro handhelds, while more powerful machines have access to more accurate emulators like **BlastEm** or **Ares**. Unlike the Mega Drive, there's one crucial difference: the platform **requires a BIOS file**, separately for the Japanese, American, and European versions. Without it the game won't launch, and this is the step where beginners most often get stuck.

In Batocera, RetroPie, and EmulationStation, the Mega-CD has its own folder (usually `segacd` or `megacd`), and discs are most commonly stored in the **CHD** format, which compresses both the disc image and audio tracks into a single file. With audio tracks, it's worth not skimping on quality.

A legal path to these games does exist, though it's narrow. **Sonic CD** was released in a modern version on today's platforms and also as part of the **Sonic Origins** collection, the **Lunar** series received an official remaster, and even **Night Trap** returned in an anniversary edition. A number of other titles — **Snatcher** chief among them — remain trapped on their original discs, whose prices on the collector's market have been steadily climbing.

sega-32x.history:
There are consoles that lost the battle for customers. And then there's the **SEGA 32X** — a device that lost the battle with its own company. In late 1994, Sega faced an uncomfortable realization: the 16-bit era was winding down, the competition was gearing up for 32 bits, and the **Saturn** wasn't yet ready for Western markets. The answer was supposed to be an add-on that would turn the existing **Mega Drive** into a cheap 32-bit console and bridge the gap until the real next generation arrived.

From the outside, it was a black "mushroom" mounted from above into the cartridge slot. Inside sat two **32-bit Hitachi SH-2 processors** — the same chip family that powered the Saturn itself. The idea sounded logical: a Mega Drive owner wouldn't have to throw away their old console, just buy a box to go with it and suddenly have textured polygons on screen. But the Saturn showed up barely a year after the 32X, and the whole plan fell apart. Customers didn't understand what they were supposed to buy, developers didn't know where to invest their time, and stores had three incompatible Segas sitting side by side on the shelf.

The 32X's lifespan can be measured in months rather than years. Its library stopped at roughly forty games, and Sega quietly wrote the add-on off to shift all its energy to the Saturn. Today the 32X is a textbook example of how bad strategy can fragment even a very strong brand.

### Technology: graphics and sound

The pair of **Hitachi SH-2** chips ran at somewhere in the higher tens of megahertz, and at launch that represented decent computing power — especially for the 3D math that the contemporary Mega Drive, with its **Motorola 68000**, could only handle with enormous compromises. Importantly, the 32X doesn't replace the original hardware but supplements it: the 68000 and the eight-bit **Zilog Z80** keep working, handling part of the logic and sound, while the SH-2 chips crunch the demanding stuff.
