The add-on brought its own **VDP** and, crucially, a **framebuffer**, which let it push far richer color onto the screen than the Mega Drive alone — instead of a few dozen colors at once, it was on the order of thousands. The final picture is built by compositing layers: whatever the 32X draws blends with the image from the Mega Drive. That's exactly where the typical look of games like **Virtua Racing Deluxe** or **Star Wars Arcade** comes from — rough but smoothly rotating polygon objects over a background that still looks "sixteen-bit."

Sound got a boost from a **PWM stereo channel**, so the 32X can play higher-quality samples and digitized speech than the **Yamaha YM2612** was capable of on its own. In practice, games usually mixed both.

### Connectivity and peripherals

Installation was a chapter of its own. The add-on slid into the cartridge slot, needed its **own power adapter**, plus a short **video link cable** running from the Mega Drive's output to the 32X. Some console revisions shipped with plastic spacers to make the assembly sit properly. The result was a knot of cables and two outlets occupied by a single gaming system.

The crowning glory was combining it with the **Mega-CD** (Sega CD). Anyone who owned both ended up stacking the infamous **tower of three devices**: the CD drive on the bottom, the console on top of it, the 32X on top of that, plus three separate power supplies. Games that used everything at once could be counted on one hand, and they were mostly titles built around full-motion video. As an image summing up Sega's mid-1990s, though, that tower is unbeatable.

Controllers stayed unchanged — the standard three-button and **six-button** Mega Drive gamepads worked without a second thought.

### Models and revisions

The 32X never got a major hardware revision — it simply wasn't on the market long enough. Across regions it launched under different names: **Super 32X** in Japan, **Genesis 32X** in North America, and **Mega Drive 32X** in Europe. After the failure, the price dropped steeply and the add-on lived out its days in clearance bins.

The most interesting model is the one that never shipped: the **Neptune**. Sega considered a single console that would integrate the Mega Drive and 32X in one housing, eliminating adapters, cables, and the tower altogether. The project died the moment it became clear that all attention had to go to the Saturn.

### Clones and variants

The 32X barely saw any clones at all — unlike the Mega Drive, which dozens of manufacturers still produce today, the add-on was too complex, too specific, and too unsuccessful for anyone to bother imitating it. In Brazil, where **Tectoy** holds the Sega license, it did reach the market, but even there it didn't cause the kind of wave that the Mega Drive itself still commands.

What can be considered variants are really software categories instead: regular 32X cartridges and a handful of **32X CD** titles that require the full setup with the Mega-CD. The second group is by far the hardest to find for collectors today.

### The scene today

The 32X library is small, but a few names still stick in memory. **Knuckles' Chaotix** is the only platformer from the Sonic family on this hardware, known for its unconventional mechanic of two characters joined by an elastic tether. **Virtua Racing Deluxe** ranked among the best home conversions of its time, **Star Wars Arcade** delivered space-fighter combat, and **Doom** showed that the add-on could handle the era's phenomenon too — albeit a trimmed-down version.

Emulation is the main way to try the 32X today. The best support comes from the **PicoDrive** core, which runs in **RetroArch** and on distributions like **Batocera** and handles the 32X even on modest retro handhelds; on PC, the classic **Kega Fusion** has also proven reliable. Watch out for a common mix-up: the popular **Genesis Plus GX** covers the Mega Drive, Master System, and Game Gear, but does not emulate the 32X itself — for this system you need to reach for PicoDrive.

Legal re-releases are scarce, since Sega practically never recycles this part of its catalog; exceptions like **Knuckles' Chaotix** in the **Sonic Gems Collection** just prove the rule. What's left is the collector's market, where prices for both the add-on and rarer cartridges have been climbing steadily. Surprisingly, a community scene is alive too — the best-known example is the fan project **Doom 32X Resurrection**, which squeezed considerably more out of the original conversion than was possible back in 1994. Three decades on, the 32X mainly works as a curiosity and a cautionary tale: a technically interesting piece of hardware that lacked just one thing to justify its existence — time.

sg-1000.history:
SEGA SG-1000 is a console few people know today, and yet without it there would be no Master System and no Mega Drive. It was **Sega's very first home console** — a company that until then had lived off arcade cabinets and building game cabinets for Japanese arcades. It launched in 1983, and fate handed it perhaps the most thankless start imaginable: it arrived on the market **on the very same day as the Nintendo Famicom**. Two consoles, one date, and utterly different continuations of the story.

In Japan, the SG-1000 didn't do badly at all. Interest in home gaming was surging at the time, Sega carried the reputation of an arcade brand, and it brought over titles people already knew from arcades onto the console. But the Famicom was technically further ahead, had stronger publisher support, and within a year or two the gap turned into a chasm. In the West, the SG-1000 was essentially never sold — it reached Europe and America only marginally, and in some countries not at all.

For today's retro gamer, it's a platform more for discovery than nostalgia. It offers a raw, early form of eight-bit gaming: short arcade pieces, harsh difficulty, and coarse-grained graphics without frills. And above all, it shows where Sega's whole eight-bit lineage grew from, one that a few years later culminated in the Master System.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At its core is the eight-bit **Zilog Z80** processor clocked at roughly 3.58 MHz — the same family known to owners of the ZX Spectrum, MSX, or Master System. Graphics are handled by the **Texas Instruments TMS9918** video chip (or its TMS9918A variant), a completely standard solution for its time. It manages a resolution of **256×192 pixels**, a palette of **16 colors**, and roughly three dozen sprites, though with a hard limit on the number of sprites per line — the source of the characteristic character flicker typical of this generation.

The choice of the TMS9918 is the key to understanding the whole platform. The same chip also powered **MSX** and **ColecoVision**, so games on these three systems looked very similar and porting between platforms was fairly easy. Quite a few titles therefore exist in nearly identical versions across several systems at once. Sound comes from the **SN76489** (PSG) with three tone channels and one noise channel — no synthesis, no samples, just typical eight-bit bleeps that nevertheless work surprisingly well in arcade conversions.

Memory was minimal, so games are inherently short and loop-based: one screen, one idea, rising difficulty.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The console connected to the TV the classic way, via an **RF modulator**; later versions and variants gained better outputs as well. It had a **Pause** button on the body, since the controller didn't yet handle pausing back then. The first model had the controller wired directly into the unit, which was a practical weakness — a damaged joystick meant a problem with the entire console.

More interesting is the accessory lineup that made the SG-1000 more than just a toy. There was a **keyboard**, which, once connected, turned the console into a simple home computer capable of running BASIC — Sega, after all, simultaneously offered a computer variant called the **SC-3000**, built on the same hardware. Also available were **Sega My Card** cartridges, a thin card-based medium cheaper than classic cartridges, which plugged into the console via an adapter called the Card Catcher. Sega later carried this dual media format over to the Master System as well.

### Models and revisions

The original **SG-1000** from 1983 was a boxy white-and-black unit with a hardwired joystick. It was followed by the **SG-1000 II** revision, which simplified and cleaned up the design and, crucially, introduced **detachable controllers** — a genuinely significant usability improvement in practice. Software-wise it stayed fully compatible, so both generations of players shared the same library.

The development line didn't stop there, though. The SG-1000 II was followed by the **Sega Mark III**, which significantly upgraded the hardware, and that in turn became the **Master System** for Western markets. That's exactly why the SG-1000 is, technically speaking, the direct ancestor of the Master System: it shares its processor, its philosophy, and part of its media ecosystem with it, just with a considerably weaker graphics chip.

### Clones and variants

A small but interesting family of related devices grew up around the SG-1000. The most important is the already-mentioned **SC-3000**, a fully-fledged home computer with a keyboard built on the same foundation — it sold even in countries where the console itself barely existed, and in some regions built up a decent user base. There were also licensed variants and devices from other manufacturers which, thanks to the shared TMS9918 chip, could run cartridges from multiple systems at once.

For a Czech gamer, this platform is a period curiosity: at a time when people here mainly played on the ZX Spectrum and its clone, the **Didaktik**, the SG-1000 practically never reached our households. It shows up here only in retrospect, through emulation and interest in Sega's history.

### The scene today

Today the SG-1000 is chiefly **historically interesting** — as the point where Sega entered the home console business. Its library consists of arcade conversions and simple action games, among which you'll find names like **Congo Bongo**, **Flicky**, **Zaxxon**, **Monaco GP**, or **Star Jacker**. The collection isn't large and varies quite a bit in quality, but that also makes it easy to get through the whole thing.

Emulation is completely trouble-free. The most widespread route is the **Genesis Plus GX** core, which handles the Master System, Game Gear, and the SG-1000 alongside the Mega Drive — so the entire Sega eight-bit lineage runs under one roof. In **RetroArch** and in ready-made distributions like **Batocera**, the platform has its own system folder and runs even on the cheapest Chinese handhelds, whose performance it doesn't stress at all. The legal route to the games runs through official compilations and re-releases into which Sega periodically folds part of its old catalog, or through original cartridges themselves — though collecting those isn't a cheap affair, precisely because of the limited distribution outside Japan.

Anyone who wants a picture of what the very beginnings of console Sega looked like has ideal material here: a few evenings, dozens of short games, and a pretty clear view of just how fast the eight-bit era moved forward.

virtual-boy.history:
The year 1995 was obsessed with virtual reality. The word "VR" was popping up in movies, in magazines and in press releases from manufacturers who promised that players would soon step directly inside a game. Nintendo sent **Virtual Boy** into that wave — a strange tabletop device on a tripod that you had to bury your face into like a binocular. Inside awaited a richly **red monochrome world** built from LEDs and oscillating mirrors. Nothing like it existed on the market, and as it turned out, there was a reason for that.

Behind the design stood **Gunpei Yokoi**, the engineer behind Game & Watch and the Game Boy, a man whose philosophy of "lateral thinking with withered technology" had worked flawlessly for a decade. This time, though, it failed him. Cheap red LEDs allowed for a sharp, high-contrast image at an affordable price, but the result was visually exhausting. The device couldn't be worn, couldn't be shared with a friend, and after half an hour of play many people got headaches. On top of that, Nintendo gave it only lukewarm marketing support — all its energy at the time was aimed at the upcoming Nintendo 64.

The result was an unambiguous flop. Fewer than a million units sold, the console never officially reached Europe at all, and Nintendo pulled it from the market roughly a year after launch. Yokoi left the company shortly afterward and tragically died in a traffic accident in 1997. Yet Virtual Boy hasn't disappeared from memory — quite the opposite. Today it's one of the most collectible pieces of gaming history, and several of its games rank among the best Nintendo published in the mid-1990s.

### Tech: graphics and sound

Inside Virtual Boy beats a surprisingly modern heart: a **32-bit RISC NEC V810 processor** clocked at around 20 MHz. On paper, that made it the most powerful Nintendo console of its time — more than the SNES, though less than the sixty-four then in the works.

The display side, however, was a whole different league of strangeness. No screen existed in the usual sense: each eye received a **single vertical row of red LEDs**, whose image was spread across a plane by a rapidly oscillating mirror. The resulting resolution was **384 × 224 dots per eye**, with a color depth of a mere **four shades of red**. Two independent "screens" with slightly different viewing angles created genuine **stereoscopic 3D** — and it worked remarkably convincingly. The depth in Red Alarm or in Galactic Pinball's pinball tables was something a flat television simply couldn't reproduce.

Sound was handled by the **VSU** chip with six channels — five wavetable channels plus one noise channel — with **stereo** output to the built-in headphone speakers. Sonically, Virtual Boy sounded cleaner and fuller than the Game Boy and often held its own against the SNES.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The Virtual Boy controller was prophetic for its time: **two D-pads** side by side, A and B buttons, two shoulder triggers, and a removable **battery module** for six AA batteries that could be swapped for a power adapter. The pair of D-pads allowed movement and aiming to be controlled separately — a principle that, a few years later in the form of two analog sticks, came to dominate action games.

The device also had a **link port** for connecting two units, but the corresponding cable never actually made it to retail, and no released game used it. Nintendo did include something else instead: the system had a built-in **automatic break reminder** hard-wired into it, which paused the game after a set time and prompted the player to rest. The box and manual both warned that the device wasn't suitable for children under seven.

### Models and revisions

Here the story is short. Virtual Boy saw only **a single hardware version** — between the Japanese and American releases, practically only the packaging and bundled game differed (in North America, **Mario's Tennis**). No slim model, no color variant, no successor. A European or Australian version never came out at all.

The library remained equally modest: **22 released games** in total, some of which appeared only in Japan. The undisputed highlight is **Virtual Boy Wario Land**, a full-fledged platformer that uses the 3D effect to shift between foreground and background and would easily hold its own on the SNES. Also aging gracefully are the robot duel game **Teleroboxer**, Atlus's dungeon crawler **Jack Bros.**, the arcade-style **Mario Clash**, and the fast-paced shooter **Red Alarm**. The rest of the catalog is, unfortunately, more a collection of experiments and quick cash-ins.

### Clones and variants

Virtual Boy clones practically don't exist — the device was too strange, too expensive and too unsuccessful for anyone to bother imitating it. Indirect successors, however, are plentiful: Sega never finished its Sega VR headset, Virtuality arcade systems rode the same wave in arcades, and the idea of glasses-free stereoscopic 3D returned to Nintendo only in 2011 with the **Nintendo 3DS**, this time with a considerably better result.

For Czech players, Virtual Boy is a strange chapter: it officially never reached here, so most people know it only from photos and videos. The units circulating here today arrived via import.

### Today's scene

Emulation is today the only realistic way to try out the Virtual Boy. The standard is the **Beetle VB** core (derived from Mednafen), available in both **RetroArch** and **Batocera**, and it runs fine even on a cheap retro handheld. The emulator offers several display modes: classic red-and-black 2D, side-by-side images for VR headsets, and above all an **anaglyph mode** — with ordinary red-blue paper glasses you can try the stereoscopic effect at home for pocket change. There's also a well-regarded emulator for the Nintendo 3DS, where the 3D effect can be reproduced without any glasses at all.

The community around the platform is alive too. **Homebrew** games and translations of Japanese titles are being made, flashcarts exist that let you run your own code on real hardware, and enthusiasts fix the typical defect of aging units — the detaching display ribbon cable that causes one eye's image to drop out. Nintendo itself eventually returned to Virtual Boy, making part of its catalog available to subscribers of its retro service on the Switch, including an add-on that reproduces the stereoscopic effect. The console once regarded as a symbol of failure has thus, three decades later, earned something like a rehabilitation.

ngpc.history:
The Neo Geo Pocket Color arrived in 1999 as SNK's last big attempt to reach players directly in their pocket. The company had legendary arcade cabinets and the home Neo Geo AES behind it, but it was a newcomer in handhelds — the previous monochrome **Neo Geo Pocket** from 1998 practically never made it beyond Japan. The color version was meant to be the real weapon: a faster 16-bit processor, a color display, and a library built on what SNK did best — fighting games.

The fight, however, was uneven from the start. On the other side stood Nintendo with the **Game Boy Color**, which had a huge installed base, Pokémon, and distribution in every supermarket; on the Japanese market the situation was further complicated by Bandai's **WonderSwan**. SNK entered with hardware that was in many respects better, but with marketing that barely reached players at all.

That's precisely why it's such a strange chapter today. Almost no one bought it back then, yet everyone who ever held one remembers it fondly — mainly because of the controls. The microswitch joystick with its distinctive click is still considered by many collectors to be **the best controller a handheld console ever received**. It wasn't a mushy rubber D-pad but a miniature arcade stick that rewarded every movement under your thumb with tangible feedback. In fighting games, that made an enormous difference.

### Tech: graphics and sound

Inside ticks a 16-bit **Toshiba TLCS-900/H** processor running at roughly **6 MHz**, supported by an auxiliary **Z80** that handles sound exclusively. On paper that's a significantly more capable setup than the 8-bit Game Boy Color — and it shows, both in the smoothness of the animations and in how many objects the console can keep on screen at once.

The display has a resolution of **160 × 152 dots** and draws from a palette of **4,096 colors**; around **146** are typically shown at once. The panel is reflective and unlit, so it needs good ambient light — by far the device's biggest weakness, and exactly the point where modders most often step in today. The upside of that same design, however, is **excellent battery life**: two AA batteries last for dozens of hours, considerably more than backlit color competitors of the era.

Sound comes from a chip in the **T6W28** family, related to proven PSG generators — three tone channels plus a noise channel, with stereo output to headphones. It has a characteristically sharp, purely chip-tune sound that suits the arcade nature of the library. The console also has a built-in **real-time clock** and calendar; on first power-up it asks the player for a name, date of birth, and favorite color.

### Connectivity and peripherals

Two units could be connected via a **link cable** for two-player battles — for fighting games and for SNK's card game SNK vs. Capcom: Card Fighters' Clash, this was the platform's main social feature. The most interesting peripheral, though, was the **Dreamcast link cable**. SNK and Sega grew close enough at the time that the handheld could communicate with the home Dreamcast and transfer data between select titles — the practical reach was small, but for its era it was a bold move.

Cartridges are small, region-free, and save progress directly to their own memory, so there's no issue with dying save batteries as with some period games elsewhere. The color console is also fully compatible with games made for the original monochrome Neo Geo Pocket.

### Models and revisions

Collectors distinguish two generations: the original **Neo Geo Pocket** (1998, monochrome, practically Japan-only) and the **Neo Geo Pocket Color** (1999). The color version was released in a single hardware form, but in a wide range of case colors — from silver and charcoal through various shades of blue to translucent "crystal" variants. In Japan several limited editions were added on top, which today rank among the most expensive pieces.

Production ended as early as **2001**. SNK ran into serious financial trouble, and distribution in Europe and the US had already been scaled back before that — which is why Western titles are also harder to find than Japanese ones.

### Clones and variants

Hardware clones practically don't exist; the platform was too niche for anyone to bother the way they did with famiclones or Game Boy knockoffs. The console officially never really reached Czechoslovakia/Czechia, and anyone who owned one back then got it through import — for most local players it's a console discovered only in retrospect, through emulation.

The more interesting "variant" today is the official re-release. Since 2020, SNK has been releasing individual titles as well as compiled collections — **Neo Geo Pocket Color Selection** — on Nintendo Switch and PC, so the classics can now be obtained completely legally and without hunting through swap meets.

### Today's scene

Emulation is very well handled. The standard is the **Beetle NeoPop** core in RetroArch, which handles the vast majority of the library without issues; on weaker devices, the more efficient **RACE** core is used instead. The `ngpc` system is included in **Batocera**, ArkOS, and other distributions for handheld emulation consoles — and that's exactly where it makes the most sense, since the format of its games is ideal for short play sessions.

From the library, the titles most recommended today are **SNK vs. Capcom: Match of the Millennium**, which many players consider the best fighting game ever released on a handheld console, along with **The King of Fighters R-2**, Samurai Shodown! 2, Gals' Fighters, and both Metal Slug entries. Outside of fighting games, **Sonic the Hedgehog Pocket Adventure** stands out — a surprisingly well-made version of the blue hedgehog by SNK, technically based on the Mega Drive Sonic. And then there's Card Fighters' Clash, a card-based RPG with a cult following that has lasted to this day.

It thus remains a textbook example of a console that lost the market but won its reputation. Anyone who picks it up today usually understands why within a minute. All it takes is a single click of the joystick.

wonderswan.history:
When Bandai launched its handheld console **WonderSwan** in Japan in 1999, this was no outsider's gamble. Behind the design stood **Gunpei Yokoi** — the engineer who created the Game & Watch, the cross-shaped D-pad, and the Game Boy itself for Nintendo. Yokoi had left Nintendo in the mid-1990s, founded his own studio **Koto Laboratory**, and teamed up with Bandai to build a machine meant to beat the Game Boy at its own game. He didn't live to see it finished: he died in a traffic accident in 1997, two years before the device launched. WonderSwan is thus his last piece of handheld hardware, and his fingerprints are visible in its design at first glance.

That philosophy can be summed up as "mature technology in a clever shell." The console doesn't chase spectacle — it chases endurance and low cost. It runs on a **single AA battery** and lasts dozens of hours on it — at a time when rival color handhelds chewed through two to six batteries in an afternoon, this was an argument that kept surfacing again and again in Japanese reviews. Its second peculiarity is the controls: WonderSwan has **two sets of buttons** and can be held horizontally like a normal game console or vertically like a book. The vertical mode was mainly used by puzzle games and text-heavy Japanese RPGs.

WonderSwan never officially reached the West. It remained a **Japan-only exclusive**, which paradoxically gave it the aura of a collector's rarity. In its home market, though, it managed to bite off a noticeable share of the Game Boy's market for a while, mostly thanks to its alliance with **Square**, which wasn't on good terms with Nintendo at the time and sent Bandai's console remakes of its classics. The end came with the arrival of the Game Boy Advance in 2001; Bandai wound down support over the following few years.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At the console's heart is a sixteen-bit **NEC V30 MZ** processor, a relative of the Intel 8086 family, clocked at around **3 MHz**. Compared to the eight-bit Sharp chip in the Game Boy, this was a more modern architecture with smoother scrolling and easier handling of larger amounts of data. The display has a resolution of **224 × 144 pixels** — noticeably wider than the Game Boy's — and in the original version shows **eight shades of gray** on a monochrome FSTN panel.

Color arrived only with the **WonderSwan Color** model, which works with a palette of **4096 colors** and can display several hundred on screen at once; it also got four times the working memory, so color games could be more elaborate. Sound is handled by **four channels** built on programmable wavetables, one of which can also handle noise and a simple voice sample. The built-in speaker is mono; stereo could be obtained through headphones, but only via a special adapter — the console has no standard headphone jack, probably the most frequently mentioned cost-cutting measure on the whole device.

### Connectivity and peripherals

Two WonderSwans could be linked with a **link cable** to play in tandem or exchange data. But Bandai also tried things ahead of their time: the **WonderWave** adapter added wireless infrared transfer, and **MobileWonderGate** connected it to a Japanese mobile phone, opening the door to the mobile data services of the era. A special chapter belongs to **WonderBorg**, a robotic beetle that the player programmed directly on the console and controlled via infrared commands.

But the most interesting accessory is **WonderWitch** — an official development kit that let anyone write their own games in C and load them onto a special cartridge. For a console from 1999, this was a remarkably open move, and Japan's amateur scene took to it eagerly.

### Models and revisions

The family has three members. The original **WonderSwan** (1999) is monochrome and the most power-efficient. **WonderSwan Color** (2000) added color and memory, grew slightly larger, and remained backward-compatible with older games. The last one, **SwanCrystal** (2002), is technically almost identical to the color model but swapped the display for a **TFT panel** with significantly better contrast and faster response time — the motion blur that plagued the color version disappears. For today's collector, SwanCrystal is clearly the most pleasant choice, though it tends to be pricier.

All models had colorful case variants and themed editions tied to licenses Bandai itself owned — Gundam and Digimon are right at home here.

### Clones and variants

WonderSwan practically never saw hardware clones; it was too regional and too short-lived for that. But the library itself is full of variations on familiar names: alongside **Final Fantasy**, **Final Fantasy II**, and **Final Fantasy IV** remakes from Square, there's a handheld **Makaimura** from the Ghosts'n Goblins series, **Rockman & Forte**, **Klonoa: Moonlight Museum**, **Guilty Gear Petit**, and the RPG **Riviera** from Sting. There's also the puzzle game **Gunpey**, named after Yokoi himself, and **Judgement Silversword** — a shooter that grew out of an amateur competition and became a cult classic.

The console never reached Czech lands during its active years at all. Anyone who owns one today either brought it back from Japan or ordered it through overseas auctions; a complete boxed unit is still fairly available, since Japanese players tend to preserve their hardware carefully.

### Today's scene

Emulating the WonderSwan today is trouble-free. The most widespread option is the **Beetle Cygne** core in RetroArch, which covers both the monochrome and color models and runs on practically anything — from PCs through Raspberry Pi to cheap Chinese handhelds. **Batocera** and other emulation distributions include WonderSwan by default and offer switching to vertical mode, which is essential for this platform: without rotating the screen, half the library is unplayable.

The main obstacle is language. Practically the entire library exists only in Japanese, so part of the community plays with **fan translations**, of which a decent number exist for the major RPGs and adventure games. Legal routes to the games are few but not zero — several of the best titles later got ports and remakes on other platforms, whether the Final Fantasy remakes on Game Boy Advance, Riviera on modern consoles, or Judgement Silversword released as part of collector's compilations by Qute. Anyone wanting the experience in its original form reaches for a SwanCrystal and a modern flash cartridge.

3do.history:
The **3DO Interactive Multiplayer** is a console that arrived too early and at too high a price. When **The 3DO Company**, led by **Trip Hawkins**, founder of Electronic Arts, launched it in the fall of 1993, it was the most powerful gaming machine an ordinary person could put under their TV. Except the word "ordinary" didn't quite fit: the launch price of **$699** was simply out of touch with reality at a time when the SNES and Mega Drive sold for a fraction of that. The console thus became famous more as an expensive technological marvel from advertisements than as a machine anyone actually had at home.

More interesting than the hardware, though, was the business model. 3DO wasn't a single company's console — the company itself made no boxes at all. Instead, it **licensed its design to electronics manufacturers**, exactly the way the VHS standard worked for video recorders. The console was thus built by **Panasonic**, **Sanyo**, and **GoldStar**, and in theory competition was supposed to drive prices down. In practice that didn't happen: manufacturers made no money on the hardware (3DO took a fee on every pressed disc, not on the consoles), and before prices could fall, **PlayStation** and **Sega Saturn** arrived on the market at half the price, and that was that.

Still, 3DO remains one of the most fascinating dead ends of the 1990s. It was the console where the very first **Need for Speed** came out, where **Road Rash** was born in a version with digitized rock music, and where the legendary **Star Control II** has its home.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At its base is a **32-bit ARM60 processor** clocked at 12.5 MHz, paired with **two graphics coprocessors** (so-called cel engines) and a math accelerator. This pair was what made the 3DO fast: it could churn out huge numbers of **smoothly scaled and rotated sprites** and warp them into arbitrary quadrilaterals. That's exactly where the typical 3D scenes of the era came from — textured surfaces built from stretched bitmaps, unthinkable on rival sixteen-bit consoles.

A **CD-ROM** drive (double-speed) was standard, along with 2 MB of working memory and separate video memory. The standard resolution was 320×240 pixels, but the machine also handled an interlaced higher-resolution mode for static screens and text. Sound was handled by its own **digital signal processor** with **16-bit stereo output** at CD quality, so games commonly used voiced dialogue and recorded music instead of chip synthesis.

The combination of a large disc and decent power had a dark side too: the library was flooded with **FMV**, games built on filmed video sequences. Interactive film was then hailed as the future of gaming, and 3DO became its flagship — with all the enthusiasm and the subsequent disillusionment that came with it.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The console has an unusual controller solution: instead of a row of ports, it has **a single connector, and controllers chain together**. A second gamepad plugs into the first, a third into the second, and so on up to eight players — hence the "Multiplayer" in the name. Each controller also carried its own **headphone jack with a volume wheel**, a very elegant idea for its time.

The rear **expansion port** mainly served the **MPEG decoder**, which once connected let the console play **Video CD** and offered much smoother video in games that supported it. Steering wheels, arcade sticks, and light guns were also made. Save games were handled by built-in battery-backed memory, so players couldn't avoid deleting old saves eventually. Video-wise, 3DO offers composite and S-Video, and European and Japanese units can also access RGB.

### Models and revisions

The best known is the **Panasonic FZ-1 REAL 3DO**, a hefty black box with a sliding disc tray that looked more like an expensive CD player than a toy. Its successor was the noticeably smaller, lighter, and cheaper **Panasonic FZ-10**, which replaced the tray with a flip-up lid — mechanically simpler, and therefore a more reliable choice for collectors today.

Alongside Panasonic, **GoldStar** (today's LG) built its own model, whose version was among the most affordable, and in Japan **Sanyo** sold its variant under the name **TRY**. All the machines are essentially identical inside, and games run on any of them without difference — that was the whole point of the standard. The planned successor platform **M2** never sold as a console at all: Matsushita bought the technology, and it ended up mainly in arcade machines.

### Clones and variants

3DO has no unofficial clones; the platform was too expensive and too short-lived for that. The most interesting variant is arguably the **3DO Blaster** from **Creative Labs** — a plug-in ISA card that turned a DOS PC into a full-fledged 3DO, complete with its own drive and output into a window in Windows. It was a curiosity for enthusiasts with very deep pockets.

In the former **Czechoslovakia**, the console was never officially sold at all, and given the prices of the time there was no demand for it either. Anyone who knew about it knew it from magazines and stunning screenshots that looked like they came from another planet. That's exactly why 3DO carries an aura here today of an exotic device that almost nobody ever saw in person.

### Today's scene

Emulation of the 3DO is in good shape today. The most common route is the **Opera** core (descended from the FreeDO and 4DO projects) in **RetroArch**, included in Batocera, RetroPie, and most portable Linux consoles. A key requirement is a **BIOS file** — without it nothing launches and the emulator just stays silent, usually the most common reason beginners think 3DO "doesn't work." The BIOS from the Panasonic FZ-10 or FZ-1 model is used most often.

Performance-wise, 3DO sits somewhere between PlayStation and more demanding systems: it stutters on weaker handhelds, but generally runs at full speed on H700-class chips and above. The legal route to the games runs through original discs, or through PC versions of some titles still sold today in digital stores. A lovely exception is **Star Control II**, whose 3DO-version source code its authors released, giving rise to the freely available project **The Ur-Quan Masters**. Anyone wanting a picture of what the gaming future looked like through the eyes of 1993 has everything they need at hand today.

cd-i.history:
**Philips CD-i** is the strangest device that ever found its way onto a list of game consoles. When Philips launched it in 1991, it didn't claim to be a console at all — it talked about a **home multimedia player**, a device meant to sit next to the TV and the VCR and offer the family encyclopedias, language courses, music, movies, and "a few games too." The abbreviation **Compact Disc Interactive** denoted an entire industry standard: its own disc format, its own operating system, and a fixed hardware specification that manufacturers had to follow so a disc would work anywhere.

That ambition was a decade ahead of its time — CD-i was meant to be what DVD and the smart TV later became, combined. But in 1991 that meant an expensive box that did everything by half. And above all: the device was controlled with a **remote control with a thumb joystick**, because Philips expected users to browse an encyclopedia, not dodge an enemy. Games took a hit from that they never recovered from.

CD-i did make history, though — just not the way anyone wished. It was on CD-i that **Link: The Faces of Evil**, **Zelda: The Wand of Gamelon**, and **Hotel Mario** were released — titles featuring Nintendo characters that emerged as a byproduct of failed negotiations over a **CD add-on for the SNES**. Nintendo licensed its characters to Philips as a consolation prize, Philips turned them into games with stiff animation and awkward voice acting, and two decades later the internet decided these discs would forever be the textbook example of how not to do it.

### Tech: graphics and sound

The heart of most players is the **Motorola 68070** processor — a variant of the 68000 chip with integrated controllers, clocked around 15 MHz. Graphics are handled by the **MCD 212** video chip series, which works with **two independent graphics planes** and can blend them with transparency: one carries a photographic background, the other sharp interface graphics.

Besides the usual palette modes (**CLUT**), the chip also supported **DYUV**, a compression format designed for photorealistic images. Thanks to it, static screens on CD-i looked better than the competition's — but the price was abysmal redraw speed. **CD-i had no hardware accelerator for sprites or scrolling**, so anything that moved had to be computed by the processor. That's the root of the notorious choppiness and "paper cutout" animation in many of its games.

Sound, on the other hand, was a strength. Alongside **16-bit stereo CD quality**, the standard offered several levels of **ADPCM** compression, which let hours of spoken word be crammed onto a disc and played back alongside data. Narrated commentary was standard on educational discs at a time when players on cartridge-based consoles could only dream of it.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The standard control device on the early models was an **infrared remote control** with a thumb joystick and two buttons. It was fine for browsing menus, but dreadful for playing — and because games had to be controllable with exactly this, many of them stick to a slow pace and screen-clicking. **Gamepads**, a **trackball**, a **mouse**, and even a **touchpad** were added later.

The most important accessory was the **Digital Video Cartridge**, a module with an **MPEG-1 decoder**. Only with it could a player handle **Video CD** and so-called Digital Video titles with full-screen video — and some games require it outright. Video-wise, the players offer composite and S-Video, with European units typically also including SCART.

### Models and revisions

The first generation is represented by the bulky desktop players of the **CD-i 910** series, indistinguishable from quality hi-fi components. Smaller and cheaper models followed in the **200** and **400** series, with the later 400 series explicitly targeting gamers and usually bundled with a gamepad. A special chapter belongs to the **professional models** for businesses, museums, and kiosks, with a more rugged chassis and expansion slots.

**Portable players** with their own LCD panel were also made. For collectors, one thing is essential: models differ in whether they have the **Digital Video Cartridge** fitted — and today the module is often pricier than the player itself.

### Clones and variants

Because CD-i was an openly licensed standard, no clones appeared, but rather **official variants from other brands**. In the USA it was sold under Philips's own house brand **Magnavox**, in Europe **Grundig** added its model, and Asian manufacturers took out licenses too, among them **GoldStar** (today's LG) and **Kyocera**. Internally these are essentially the same machines, and discs work between them without restriction — exactly what Philips was after.

In the former **Czechoslovakia**, CD-i sold only marginally, and given the prices of the time it was bought more by companies and schools than families. Anyone who remembers it usually knows it from demo kiosks in department stores.

### The scene today

CD-i emulation is among the **most demanding and least polished** in all of retro gaming. Furthest along are the specialized **CD-i Emulator** and the **same_cdi** driver based on MAME. Both require the **original system ROM of the specific player model**, without which nothing runs at all — and titles with digital video also run into problems emulating the MPEG module. Support exists in **Batocera**, but it's rather experimental and hits a performance ceiling on weaker handhelds.

The legal route to content is through original discs, which are plentiful in secondhand shops — educational titles were pressed in huge numbers and no one collected them. Only the Nintendo games that turned CD-i into an internet legend command collector prices. Anyone wanting to get to know the platform fairly, though, should also reach for something else: **Burn:Cycle** shows just how well Philips could do its own interactive movie, and hundreds of encyclopedic discs still remind us that this device never really wanted to be a console first.

vectrex.history:
There's only one home console you never had to plug into anything else. The **Vectrex** from **General Consumer Electronics** arrived on the market at the end of 1982 as a tall plastic cabinet with its own built-in screen, a built-in speaker, and a controller tucked into a recess at the front. You set it on a table, plugged it into an outlet, and played. No arguing with family over the TV, no fiddling with the antenna channel — exactly the kind of self-sufficiency that handheld consoles wouldn't offer again for another decade.

The reason for this unusual construction was technical. Vectrex didn't draw its picture from dots like every other console of its time, but **vectorially**: the beam inside the monochrome screen traveled directly along the shapes it was meant to draw, leaving behind sharp, bright white lines. It was exactly what people knew from arcades with machines like **Asteroids** or **Battlezone** — and something a regular television simply couldn't display. Color was solved in an admirably old-fashioned way: each game came with an **overlay** of transparent colored plastic that you fastened over the screen. Instantly space took on a blue tint, fuel gauges glowed red, and backgrounds gained artwork the hardware could never have managed on its own.

The timing, though, was brutal. Vectrex arrived literally on the doorstep of the **video game crash of 1983**, when the North American consumer electronics market collapsed under a wave of low-quality titles and price wars. Although the machine earned excellent reviews, GCE never recovered from the crash, and production ended after about a year and a half. What remained was a library of roughly **thirty official games** — and the most unusual console of the 1980s.

### Tech: graphics and sound

Inside runs an eight-bit **Motorola MC6809** processor, considerably more capable computationally than the 6502 in rival machines, backed by just a handful of kilobytes of RAM. The system software was stored in ROM right inside the console and gave programmers ready-made routines for drawing lines and working with text and music.

The display side is what really matters, though. In place of the usual graphics chip sits a **vector generator**: converters that turn numbers into voltages, and integrators driving the deflection coils. The game therefore fills no frame buffer at all — instead it feeds the hardware a list of line segments and brightness levels that have to be drawn before the image has time to fade. The more lines a scene contains, the dimmer and more flicker-prone the image gets, a permanent trade-off developers had to live with. The reward was perfectly smooth rotation and fluid scaling of objects that raster consoles of the era couldn't even fake.

Sound is handled by the **General Instrument AY-3-8912**, a three-channel sound chip with a noise generator — the same chip family later found in the ZX Spectrum 128 and Amstrad CPC home computers. Compared to the Atari 2600's two crude channels, this was an audible leap: Vectrex could handle simple melodies and spoken effects, and games used it inventively.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The controller is a fixed part of the experience: an **analog joystick** with a self-centering stick and four buttons in a row, housed behind a flip-down cover on the front of the cabinet. The console has two ports, so two people could play on the same screen. Analog control was a total rarity in homes in 1982, and it suited piloting or aiming games noticeably well.

GCE offered two peripherals for the Vectrex that are sought-after today. The **Light Pen** — a light pen used to draw directly on the screen — and above all the **3D Imager**, a goggle attachment with a spinning disc that alternately blocked each eye to create an impression of spatial depth while also letting colored segments of the disc show through. It was one of the very first attempts at a stereoscopic game in the living room; given the console's demise, only a handful of titles were released for the Imager, which today makes it one of the most expensive pieces of collectible retro gear.

### Models and revisions

The construction stayed essentially unchanged; mainly the badge on the front changed. The original machine carried the **GCE** logo; after the company was acquired it was sold as the **Milton Bradley Vectrex**, and it reached Europe in that form. In Japan, Bandai distributed it under the name **Kousokusen**.

The built-in game **Minestorm** — a variation on Asteroids stored right in the console's memory — launches whenever there's no cartridge inserted in the machine. Among the released titles, the most cited are the arcade conversion **Scramble**, the space duel **Star Castle**, and the maze game **Berzerk**; most of them came with their own overlay and cardboard frame.

### Clones and variants

The Vectrex has practically no classic unofficial clones — the vector screen was too expensive and specific for anyone to copy. There is, however, a lively ecosystem of modern accessories: **multicarts** with an entire game library in a single module, developer cartridges with flash memory, and add-ons that bring modern programming environments to the console. Collectors have **replica overlays** printed, since the originals fade and crack after four decades.

### The scene today

For its size, Vectrex has a remarkably tenacious **homebrew scene**. New games for it are still released today, often in physical form with cartridge, overlay, and manual — and sometimes they match the quality of period productions, because their authors now have modern tools and don't have to scrimp on every byte.

Anyone wanting just a taste of Vectrex can reach for the **Vecx** emulator. It's also available as a RetroArch core, so ready-made distributions like **Batocera** and ordinary gaming handhelds can run it too. A vector image never behaves quite the same on an LCD — it lacks that characteristic phosphor glow — but blur filters and a fading trail effect come close enough to make it work. The most legal route to games remains the titles homebrew authors release for free themselves, and modern re-releases of old games straight from the rights holders.

Vectrex never won any console war — it's remembered as a beautiful dead-end branch that brought the arcade's aesthetic home, screen included.

x68000.history:
When Sharp launched the X68000 in 1987, it wasn't a computer for everyone. It was expensive, sold only in Japan, and made clear at first glance that it belonged somewhere other than in front of the family television. The black case, made of two vertical towers joined by a shared base, earned the nickname **Manhattan shape** — it looked like a piece of the New York skyline placed on a desk. Inside ticked a **Motorola 68000** processor, surrounded by a chipset that held its own against the arcade cabinets of the day. That, in fact, was the whole point of the machine.

For players, the X68000 became a legend for one specific reason: arcade conversions on it looked and sounded almost exactly like the originals. While elsewhere an arcade hit turned into a pale imitation with half the colors and gutted music, on the X68000 the ports could stand comparison with the arcade board itself. **Capcom** brought over **Final Fight**, **Strider Hiryu**, and **Daimakaimura** (Ghouls 'n Ghosts); **Konami** bundled a port of **Gradius** with the very first model. For a Japanese fan, that meant one thing: an arcade at home in your own room.

The price matched the ambition. The X68000 was never a mass-market machine — it shared the Japanese market with the office-dominant **NEC PC-9801**, the cheaper **MSX2**, and, from 1989, the multimedia-focused **Fujitsu FM Towns**. It remained a computer for enthusiasts and people who wanted the best regardless of budget.

### Hardware: graphics and sound

The graphics side was extraordinary for 1987. The X68000 worked with a palette of **65,536 colors** and offered several independent graphics planes that could be layered, scrolled, and blended in color. On top of that it added **hardware sprites** and **hardware scrolling** — precisely the two things arcade action is built on. A programmer didn't have to invent tricks to get dozens of moving objects on screen: they had the same kind of tools available as in an arcade cabinet. Graphics modes reached resolutions around 512×512 pixels, and the machine paired with its own analog monitor capable of switching to frequencies close to arcade standards.

Sound was handled by the **Yamaha YM2151** (also known as **OPM**) — an eight-channel **FM synthesizer**, literally the same type of chip that rang out of arcade cabinets at the time. Alongside it ran a channel for playing back **ADPCM** samples, so music could have an FM backbone with drum or vocal samples taken from a real recording layered on top. The result is still recognizable at first listen today: X68000 soundtracks rank among the best of Japanese game music from the eighties and nineties, and many composers chose this machine specifically for that reason.

### Connectivity and peripherals

The equipment was generous by Japanese standards. The towers shipped from the factory with **two 5.25" floppy drives** stacked on top of each other, which saved endless disk-swapping during installation and play. The machine had ports for a mouse and a joystick, a serial and a parallel port, and was designed for expansion from the start — memory modules, **SCSI** controllers with hard drives, and later third-party accelerators and sound add-ons followed.

The operating system was **Human68k**, a Unix-flavored command line with its own filesystem, later running the graphical environment **SX-Window** on top. The combination of a capable 68000, decent memory, and a sensible operating system made the X68000 a popular development tool — in Japanese studios it was used to write code, draw graphics, and compose music for titles that then headed to completely different platforms.

### Models and revisions

The line grew gradually, mainly toward smaller cases and faster processors. After the original 1987 model came variants such as **ACE**, **EXPERT**, **PRO**, and **SUPER**, which added memory, room for a hard drive, or a different case shape. A turning point was the **X68000 XVI** with a **16 MHz** processor — double the original clock speed, and it showed immediately on more demanding games. A smaller variant called **Compact** also existed, abandoning the massive twin-tower design in favor of a compact box.

The final chapter was the **X68030** from 1993, with a **Motorola 68030** processor. It arrived, however, just as the Japanese market was starting to be taken over by PC-compatible machines running Windows, and the line said its goodbyes with it. Sharp ended development, and the X68000 remained what it had been all along — an expensive, admired exception.

### Clones and variants

Because of its own architecture and Japanese origin, the X68000 was never cloned the way PCs or the ZX Spectrum were. It was practically never sold outside Japan and reached other countries only as an import for collectors — for a long time it was known here more from magazine mentions than from firsthand experience.

More interesting than hardware clones, then, are the original games made for the X68000 and nowhere else. Konami released **Akumajō Dracula** (1993) here, its own version of Castlevania, which later got a remake on PlayStation. Studio Exact showed off **Geograph Seal**, one of the first fully 3D action games on a home computer. And because the community stayed active, later amateur gems appeared too — for instance the precise vertical shoot-'em-up **Chō Ren Sha 68K**.

### Today's scene

The X68000 is surprisingly easy to get into today. On PC, on handhelds, and in Batocera, the **PX68k** emulator runs (also available as a RetroArch core); on Windows, the most accurate options are **XM6** and its variant **XM6 TypeG**. The emulator needs system files from the original machine, typically an **IPL ROM** and the **CGROM** character set; Sharp allowed free distribution of the system software for non-commercial use in the past, so the situation around it is friendlier than for most machines of its era. Games are commonly distributed as floppy disk images, and it's worth expecting Japanese in the menus.

Anyone who wants an X68000 physically has two routes. Original machines are a **prized collector's item** — they were expensive to find even before, and today buyers also have to deal with dried-out capacitors and worn floppy drives. The other option is the modern miniature replica **X68000 Z** from Zuiki, which faithfully recreates the twin-tower shape at a smaller scale. Either way, the X68000 remains a symbol of an era when a home computer could take on an arcade cabinet — and win.

pc-98.history:
When **NEC** launched the **PC-9801** in October 1982, it didn't look like the start of a gaming legend. The beige office box with a sixteen-bit **Intel 8086** was aimed at Japanese companies, meant to handle spreadsheets and documents. But that's exactly where its greatest strength grew from: it handled Japanese properly. The **kanji** character set sat directly in ROM, and text was rendered in hardware, so Japanese on screen looked crisp at a time when other computers struggled with it.

During the eighties, the **PC-98** became a standard in Japan that the competition couldn't even dream of — it was in offices, in schools, and on desks at home. And wherever crowds of machines share the same architecture, games follow. Not action titles with dozens of sprites — the PC-98 wasn't built for that — but what Japanese players loved most: **adventure games**, **visual novels**, sprawling **strategy games**, and **RPGs**. The library grew into the thousands of titles, and most of it never left Japan.

The architecture, though, was paradoxical. Inside ticked an **x86** processor running **MS-DOS**, yet the PC-98 wasn't IBM PC compatible in the slightest — a different memory map, different I/O ports, different graphics. An American DOS program wouldn't run on it, and vice versa. It was its own world, bounded by both language and technology, and that's exactly why so many one-of-a-kind things were created on it.

### Hardware: graphics and sound

The graphical foundation was a **640×400 pixel** mode, which held throughout the entire era of the line. For its time, that was a fine resolution — and it was no accident, since legible kanji rendering needs a fine grid. Alongside the graphics plane ran an independent **text plane** with its own character generator, so games could draw an image and lay sharp Japanese text over it. The original models handled **8 colors**, later ones **16 colors from a palette of 4096**, and drawing was accelerated by the **GRCG** and later **EGC** chips; only the **PC-9821** line brought **256 colors**.

The platform had neither hardware sprites nor smooth scrolling, though, and that marked the whole game catalog. Action games exist here, you just notice the processor redrawing the screen. On the other hand, hand-drawn illustrations and character portraits, on which adventure games and visual novels are built, looked great.

Sound was a chapter of its own, since out of the box it offered only a **beeper**. Anyone who wanted music bought a sound card: the **PC-9801-26K** with a **Yamaha YM2203** (OPN) chip added **FM synthesis**, while the stronger **PC-9801-86** with a **YM2608** (OPNA) threw in more FM channels, rhythm samples, and **ADPCM**. Enthusiasts hooked up MIDI modules like the **Roland MT-32** or **SC-55** — so the same game could sound completely different depending on what the player had in their box.

### Connectivity and peripherals

Expansion relied on its own bus called **C-bus** — sound cards, **SCSI** controllers, network cards, and memory modules all went into it. The standard was **5.25" floppy drives**, later **3.5"** in newer models, and a hard drive went from luxury to a given.

Monitors deserve a separate mention. The PC-98 worked at its own frequency of around **24 kHz** and didn't get along with an ordinary PC monitor, which still complicates life for collectors today. System-wise it ran **MS-DOS** in NEC's Japanese version, later **Windows 3.1** and eventually **Windows 95** — and there lay the irony of the whole story: the more Windows could do, the less the kanji in ROM mattered.

### Models and revisions

The line branched out incredibly richly. A milestone was the **PC-9801VM** from the mid-eighties — so widespread that it became an unofficial baseline that game developers targeted for a long time afterward. Dozens of variants followed with **80286**, **80386**, and **80486** processors, labeled with codes like **VX**, **RA**, or **DA**, along with portable **98NOTE** units and oddities like the **PC-98DO**, which combined the PC-98 with the eight-bit **PC-8801**.

In 1992 came the **PC-9821** generation, with colors, CD-ROM, and multimedia ambitions. It was, however, the last big chapter. Meanwhile, standard PC-compatible machines stopped needing special hardware thanks to a software solution for Japanese, and with the arrival of **Windows 95**, the Japanese market flipped over to the global standard within a few years. NEC eventually started building PC-compatible computers itself, and PC-98 production ran out around the turn of the millennium.

### Clones and variants

The best-known chapter is **Epson**, which from the mid-eighties built legal PC-98-compatible computers in the **PC-286**, **PC-386**, and **PC-486** lines. NEC fought back both in court and technically — software sometimes checked whether it was running on a genuine machine, and programs appeared that got around that check.

Outside Japan, the PC-98 was practically never sold and reached European players only as a curiosity. Yet a great many things were made here that later made other platforms famous: **Nihon Falcom** delivered entries in **Ys**, **Sorcerian**, and **Brandish** here; **Koei** launched **Nobunaga's Ambition** and **Romance of the Three Kingdoms**; **Gainax** introduced **Princess Maker**. And above all — the first five games of the **Touhou Project** series came out on the PC-98 in the second half of the nineties, long before it became a worldwide phenomenon.

### Today's scene

Emulation is good today. The most widespread is **Neko Project II** and its newer variants for the PC-9821 line, also available as a **RetroArch** core, and therefore usable on handhelds and in **Batocera**; on Windows, **T98-Next** and **Anex86** hold their ground, and **DOSBox-X** can handle PC-98 mode too. The emulator needs system files from the original, mainly the **BIOS** and the **character ROM** with kanji, and games are distributed as floppy disk images in formats like **FDI**, **D88**, or **HDI**.

The biggest obstacle remains the language. The vast majority of the catalog exists only in Japanese, so a strong community of **fan translations** has formed around the platform, gradually making classic adventure games and visual novels available in English. A number of titles can legally be bought through the **Project EGG** service, which runs old games in emulation, and some series have gotten re-releases on Steam. The physical machine is a task for the patient: it has to be sourced in Japan, and buyers have to deal with dried-out capacitors, drives, and a non-standard monitor. For most people, then, the PC-98 is a platform you enter through an emulator — and the reward is a library you won't find anywhere else.
